name: Paddington Bear Experience
why:
This multi-room immersive Experience is London’s newest family attraction situated on London’s South Bank.

Step into Paddington’s world by helping him and the Brown family prepare for a VERY special occasion, The Marmalade Day Festival!
Board the train from Paddington Station to 32 Windsor Gardens and be transported to the Peruvian jungle, where you’ll meet beloved characters from the films, help them solve puzzles…
line: This multi-room immersive Experience is London’s newest family attraction situated on London’s South Bank.
address: Riverside Building, County Hall, Westminster Bridge Road, London, SE1 7PB

name: Crystal Maze Experience
why: The Crystal Maze LIVE Experience is over 60 minutes of frantic, frenetic, silly team fun that’s open to everybody aged 9 and over. Your goal is to get as much time in The Crystal Dome and score as many points as you can.
line: The Crystal Maze LIVE Experience is over 60 minutes of frantic, frenetic, silly team fun that’s open to everybody aged 9 and over.

name: Chimney Lift
why:
The chimney lift has been reimagined for its third birthday
Explore a recreation of architect Sir Giles Gilbert Scott’s office, power up sound and movement at an interactive wall illustrating the story of Battersea Power Station’s construction.
line: The chimney lift has been reimagined for its third birthday Explore a recreation of architect Sir Giles Gilbert Scott’s office, power up sound and movement at an interactive wall illustrating the story of Battersea Power Station’s construction.

name: Sea Life London Aquarium
why: London's big aquarium in County Hall, right by the London Eye: a gentoo penguin colony, the UK's largest jellyfish zone and its largest living coral reef, plus rock pools of creatures from British seas. A good rainy-day pick for families.
line: London's big aquarium in County Hall, right by the London Eye: a gentoo penguin colony, the UK's largest jellyfish zone and its largest living coral reef, plus rock pools of creatures from British seas.
address: County Hall Westminster Bridge Road London SE1 7PB

name: London Eye
why:
Marvel at iconic British landmarks like the Houses of Parliament, Big Ben and Buckingham Palace when visiting The London Eye.
Since its grand opening in 2000, the London Eye has been one of the city’s most popular attractions. It is the world’s largest cantilever observation wheel and is 135m tall.
line: Marvel at iconic British landmarks like the Houses of Parliament, Big Ben and Buckingham Palace when visiting The London Eye.

name: Tower Bridge Walkway
why: Walking across the Tower Bridge glass floor is a thrilling way to experience the landmark. Situated 42 metres (138 feet) above the River Thames, the transparent High-Level Walkway panels offer views of cars, pedestrians, and passing ships below. The floors span the East and West Walkways
line: Walking across the Tower Bridge glass floor is a thrilling way to experience the landmark.

name: Outernet London
why: Outernet London is an immersive arts and entertainment district located next to Tottenham Court Road station. About - Outernet London. It features Europe’s largest digital exhibition space, wrapping visitors in floor-to-ceiling, 360-degree Ultra HD LED screens.
line: Outernet London is an immersive arts and entertainment district located next to Tottenham Court Road station.

name: Mission: Breakout
why:
An escape room in London that goes beyond anything you ever thought possible

With its setting in the former South Kentish Town underground station, escape room games don’t get much more immersive than Mission: Breakout, escape room London.

You have 60 minutes to escape the room using your mind, good sense, and teamwork!
line: An escape room in London that goes beyond anything you ever thought possible  With its setting in the former South Kentish Town underground station, escape room games don’t get much more immersive than Mission: Breakout, escape room London.

name: Horizon 22
why: Horizon 22 is one of London’s newest and most impressive public viewing galleries. Located at the top of the 22 Bishopsgate skyscraper in the City of London, it offers spectacular panoramic views across the capital. Visitors can enjoy sights of famous landmarks such as The Shard, Tower Bridge, St Paul’s Cathedral, and the River Thames.
line: Horizon 22 is one of London’s newest and most impressive public viewing galleries.

name: Poolhouse
why: Pool, but not as you know it: games are projected onto the table and every shot is tracked, so even beginners can play. Good cocktails, good food, and a fun night out for groups.
line: Pool, but not as you know it: games are projected onto the table and every shot is tracked, so even beginners can play.

name: Electric Shuffle
why: Shuffleboard with a twist: the scoring's done for you while you play, drinks come to the table, and it gets lively after work. In the middle of King's Cross, a short walk from Coal Drops Yard.
line: Shuffleboard with a twist: the scoring's done for you while you play, drinks come to the table, and it gets lively after work.

name: Helix Tunnel Slide
why:
The world’s longest and tallest tunnel slide
Where art and adventure collide, Helix is the world’s longest and tallest tunnel slide spanning 178m in length, and located on the iconic ArcelorMittal Orbit sculpture.
line: The world’s longest and tallest tunnel slide Where art and adventure collide, Helix is the world’s longest and tallest tunnel slide spanning 178m in length, and located on the iconic ArcelorMittal Orbit sculpture.
address: Arcelor Mittal Orbit, Olympic Park Stratford

name: Policeman's Coat Hook
why:
On the right hand side of this building is a metal coat hook with the plaque "Metropolitan Police" above it.
Back in the 1930s, a policeman would stand in the six-way junction of St Martin's Lane and direct the traffic by hand.
The story goes that what is now 4 Great Newport Street was undergoing building works, and on the hoarding outside was a protruding nail.
line: On the right hand side of this building is a metal coat hook with the plaque "Metropolitan Police" above it.

name: Farting Lamp
why:
Lurking around the back of the world famous Savoy lies an ingenious – if not slightly nauseating – piece of Victorian engineering; London’s last remaining sewage lamp.

The Webb Patent Sewer Gas Lamp was invented in the late 19th century by the Birmingham inventor Joseph Webb.
line: Lurking around the back of the world famous Savoy lies an ingenious – if not slightly nauseating – piece of Victorian engineering; London’s last remaining sewage lamp.

name: Little Ben
why:
Everyone has heard of Big Ben but even lots of locals don’t know about Little Ben. 
Little Ben is a cast iron miniature clock tower, situated at the intersection of Vauxhall Bridge Road and Victoria Street, in the City of Westminster, close to the approach to Victoria station.
line: Everyone has heard of Big Ben but even lots of locals don’t know about Little Ben.
address: Vauxhall Bridge Road and Victoria Street Intersection

name: Nelson’s Fleet
why:
Whether myth or truth, stroll down the Mall from Admiralty Arch and look atop each of the lampposts and you will see a small ship on each one. 
Some say these represent the ships in Nelson’s Fleet which supported him at the Battle of Trafalgar.
line: Whether myth or truth, stroll down the Mall from Admiralty Arch and look atop each of the lampposts and you will see a small ship on each one.

name: Cockpit Steps
why:
Leading between Birdcage Walk and Old Queen Street is the small passageway of Cockpit Steps, named after its rather sinister connection to the age old pastime of cock fighting. The steps themselves are actually the last remaining parts of the old Royal Cockpit, a venue built in the 18th century for the upper classes to watch and wager on cock fights.

These steps are rumoured to be haunted by a headless lady!
line: Leading between Birdcage Walk and Old Queen Street is the small passageway of Cockpit Steps, named after its rather sinister connection to the age old pastime of cock fighting.
address: Birdcage Walk or Great Queen St

name: Brydges Place
why: Brydges Place is an alley between St Martin's Lane and Bedfordbury in the City of Westminster, Greater London, running alongside the Coliseum.
line: Brydges Place is an alley between St Martin's Lane and Bedfordbury in the City of Westminster, Greater London, running alongside the Coliseum.

name: Giro the Dog (London's only Nazi-era memorial)
why: Giro, a terrier owned by the German ambassador to the UK, Leopold von Hoesch, is buried at 9 Carlton House Terrace in London, with his 1934 grave often cited as the only Nazi-era memorial in the city. The dog was electrocuted after chewing a cable in the garden, and while his owner served the Nazi regime, he was considered an anti-Nazi.
line: Giro, a terrier owned by the German ambassador to the UK, Leopold von Hoesch, is buried at 9 Carlton House Terrace in London, with his 1934 grave often cited as the only Nazi-era memorial in the city.

name: Queenhithe Mosaic
why:
In a quiet spot along the North of the River Thames, you’ll find the Queenhithe Mosaic, an epic 30m artwork that charts the history of the City.
Welcome to Queenhithe, the site where Alfred the Great re-established the City in 886, after it had been abandoned by the Romans.
The artwork was commissioned by the City of London and 4C Hotel Group footed the bill.
line: In a quiet spot along the North of the River Thames, you’ll find the Queenhithe Mosaic, an epic 30m artwork that charts the history of the City.

name: Golden Boy of Pye Corner
why: The Golden Boy of Pye Corner is a small late-17th-century monument located on the corner of Giltspur Street and Cock Lane in Smithfield, central London.
line: The Golden Boy of Pye Corner is a small late-17th-century monument located on the corner of Giltspur Street and Cock Lane in Smithfield, central London.

name: Landseer Lions
why: Four huge bronze lions guard the foot of Nelson's Column. Sir Edwin Landseer was best known as a painter of animals and had never made a big sculpture before, so they took him years. They were unveiled in 1867, more than 20 years after the column went up. Look closely at the paws.
line: Four bronze lions at the foot of Nelson's Column. Look closely at the paws.
story: Landseer was sent a dead lion from London Zoo to model from, but it started to rot before he'd finished, and the paws went first. The story goes that he used his own cat for the paws instead, which is why they look more like a moggy's than a lion's. People also say the lions lie with their front legs stretched out like a dog, which a real lion doesn't do. And legend has it that if Big Ben ever strikes thirteen, they'll come to life.

name: Plaque Marking Centre of London
why: Where exactly is the centre of London? It's marked: a brass plaque in the pavement behind the statue of Charles I in Trafalgar Square, on the site of the original Charing Cross. Distances to London are still measured from here, and anyone working within six miles of it used to get London Weighting on their pay.
line: Where exactly is the centre of London?
address: King Charles I Island, Trafalgar Square

name: St Dunstan in the East Church Garden
why: St Dunstan in the East Church Garden is a truly unique space set within the ruins of a Wren church. This green oasis has benches and a fountain with greenery draping the historic walls.
line: St Dunstan in the East Church Garden is a truly unique space set within the ruins of a Wren church.

name: Watts Memorial to Heroic Self-Sacrifice
why: In September 1887, the Victorian artist George Frederic Watts wrote to The Times proposing a monument to honour everyday heroism as part of Queen Victoria’s golden jubilee.
line: In September 1887, the Victorian artist George Frederic Watts wrote to The Times proposing a monument to honour everyday heroism as part of Queen Victoria’s golden jubilee.
address: King Edward St Postman, London EC1A 7BT

name: Trinity Buoy Wharf
why:
Originally developed in the 19th century by Trinity House, Trinity Buoy Wharf served as a base for maintaining navigation buoys and testing lighthouse technology. Its lighthouse—associated with experiments by Michael Faraday—reflects its scientific and maritime heritage.

Today, the wharf is a vibrant creative hub in East London.
line: Originally developed in the 19th century by Trinity House, Trinity Buoy Wharf served as a base for maintaining navigation buoys and testing lighthouse technology.

name: The Astronomical Clock
why:
The Astronomical Clock is a fascinating modern installation that blends science, art, and timekeeping. Unlike historic medieval clocks, this piece is contemporary in design, featuring intricate mechanisms that display not only the time but also astronomical information such as planetary positions and lunar phases.

Created to celebrate humanity’s long-standing relationship with the cosmos, the clock serves both an…
line: The Astronomical Clock is a fascinating modern installation that blends science, art, and timekeeping.

name: Leake Street Arches
why: Linking South Bank and Waterloo, the epic 300-metre-long Leake Street tunnel that crosses beneath the tracks of Waterloo Station is the unofficial centre of south London graffiti culture.
line: Linking South Bank and Waterloo, the epic 300-metre-long Leake Street tunnel that crosses beneath the tracks of Waterloo Station is the unofficial centre of south London graffiti culture.

name: Stolperstein Golden Plaque
why:
The UK's first brass memorial plaque for a Holocaust victim was unveiled in the heart of London.
The Stolperstein stone was laid in Golden Square, Soho, where Ada von Dantzig worked. She was murdered, along with her family, at Auschwitz in 1943.
line: The UK's first brass memorial plaque for a Holocaust victim was unveiled in the heart of London.

name: Tiny Mouse Mansion
why:
The story behind this one relates to Hedonism Wines, the emporium established on Davies Street in 2012.

When they opened they took over no.s 3 and 7, the owner curious as to why there had never been a number 5 Davies Street.
They decided to create a mini number 5 in the form of a tiny mouse hole in the middle of the shop front which was in place until approx 2014.
But since the business has expanded the mouse hole…
line: The story behind this one relates to Hedonism Wines, the emporium established on Davies Street in 2012.

name: The Philpot Lane Mice
why:
Londons smallest statue!
If you look up at London’s 23 Philpot Lane, you will find a sculpture of two mice stirring – well, to be more exact, busily feasting on a block of cheese. This is the capital’s smallest public sculpture and was created as a memorial to two of the building’s construction workers who fell to their deaths during an altercation over who had eaten their cheese sandwiches.
line: If you look up at London’s 23 Philpot Lane, you will find a sculpture of two mice stirring – well, to be more exact, busily feasting on a block of cheese.

name: Baby Things, Mitten by Tracey Emin
why: Baby Things, Mitten is located outside the Foundling Museum - the UKs first children’s charity where mothers often left their children to be cared for as they could not. The Mitten recalls both the children (Foundlings) left behind, as well as the mothers brave enough to part with them. Many 18th-century mothers left a token with their child (a mitten) while keeping hold of its twin.
line: Baby Things, Mitten is located outside the Foundling Museum - the UKs first children’s charity where mothers often left their children to be cared for as they could not.
story: Easy to miss: it's tiny, and sits on the railings of the Foundling Museum. Pop inside to see the real tokens that inspired it.

name: Horselydown stairs
why: Horselydown Stairs in Southwark are a small but atmospheric gateway to the Thames, tucked just east of Tower Bridge beside Shad Thames. Once used by watermen, traders and brewery workers, the steps recall a time when the river was London’s highway and the Southwark waterfront bustled with boats, warehouses and industry.
line: Horselydown Stairs in Southwark are a small but atmospheric gateway to the Thames, tucked just east of Tower Bridge beside Shad Thames.

name: St Bride's Church crypt
why: The crypt of St Bride’s Church on Fleet Street offers a fascinating glimpse into London’s past. Beneath the famous church lies a collection of archaeological finds that reveal centuries of burial practices and daily life.
line: The crypt of St Bride’s Church on Fleet Street offers a fascinating glimpse into London’s past.

name: Thin House
why: The Thin House on Thurloe Square is one of London's most unusual buildings. Built in the nineteenth century, it appears impossibly narrow from certain angles, creating a striking visual illusion. The wedge-shaped structure resulted from railway construction that reduced the original plot, leaving only a slim frontage.
line: The Thin House on Thurloe Square is one of London's most unusual buildings.
address: 5 Thurloe Square, South Kensington, London SW7 2TA

name: Host Cafe
why: Host Café is a distinctive coffee shop inside St Mary Aldermary Church. Set beneath the church’s beautiful Gothic fan-vaulted ceiling, it offers a peaceful escape from the surrounding streets and offices. The café is an ethical, non-profit project run by the church, with a strong emphasis on hospitality and community.
line: Host Café is a distinctive coffee shop inside St Mary Aldermary Church.

name: Spy Lamp Post
why: The spy lamp post in Audley Square, London, has a fascinating connection to the Cold War. From the 1950s, Soviet KGB agents reportedly used the ordinary-looking lamp post as a secret “dead letter box.” Spies could place documents and messages behind a small door at the back of the post, allowing information to be exchanged without agents meeting face to face.
line: The spy lamp post in Audley Square, London, has a fascinating connection to the Cold War.

name: London's Roman Amphitheatre
why:
London's Roman Amphitheatre

Hidden beneath the historic Guildhall Yard in the City of London lies one of the capital’s most remarkable Roman remains: London’s Roman Amphitheatre.
line: London's Roman Amphitheatre  Hidden beneath the historic Guildhall Yard in the City of London lies one of the capital’s most remarkable Roman remains: London’s Roman Amphitheatre.

name: Maarten Baas’s Real Time clock
why:
Opposite Paddington Station, high above the entrance to 50 Eastbourne Terrace, is one of London’s most unusual public clocks. Real Time, created by Dutch artist and designer Maarten Baas, was installed in 2021 and combines art, film and traditional timekeeping.

Instead of ordinary mechanical hands, the clock shows a 12-hour filmed performance of a man appearing to stand inside the clock face.
line: Opposite Paddington Station, high above the entrance to 50 Eastbourne Terrace, is one of London’s most unusual public clocks.

name: Agatha Christie Memorial
why:
The memorial is located in the heart of London's theatre district. This was chosen to pay homage to Christie's contribution to theatre: her 1952 murder mystery play The Mousetrap is the world's longest-running show, and she was the first female playwright to have three plays performing simultaneously in the West End.

The memorial depicts a book with Christie at its centre.
line: The memorial is located in the heart of London's theatre district.
address: Great Newport St and Cranbourn St

name: Mercato Mayfair
why: Mercato Mayfair is set in the Grade I-listed St Mark’s Church, where stained glass and grand architecture create a striking welcome.
line: Mercato Mayfair is set in the Grade I-listed St Mark’s Church, where stained glass and grand architecture create a striking welcome.

name: Borough Market
why: Borough Market is generally considered worth visiting for food lovers, offering an incredible array of high-quality street food and fresh produce in a historic setting, though it gets extremely crowded, especially on weekends, making an early weekday visit or a mid-week trip ideal to avoid peak congestion. It's a must-visit for authentic London foodie experiences, but be prepared for crowds
line: Borough Market is generally considered worth visiting for food lovers, offering an incredible array of high-quality street food and fresh produce in a historic setting, though it gets extremely crowded, especially on weekends, making an early weekday visit or a mid-week trip ideal to avoid peak congestion.

name: Seven Dials Market
why: Seven Dials Market is widely considered worth visiting for its vibrant atmosphere, extensive variety of high-quality street food vendors (offering everything from burgers to bao), cocktails, and lively setting in the heart of Covent Garden. It's a great spot for a casual meal, pre-theatre dining, or a social outing, though it can get busy, making finding seats a potential challenge
line: Seven Dials Market is widely considered worth visiting for its vibrant atmosphere, extensive variety of high-quality street food vendors (offering everything from burgers to bao), cocktails, and lively setting in the heart of Covent Garden.

name: Market Place Food Hall Leicester Square
why: Now open in London’s West End, Market Place Food Hall Leicester Square is the largest food hall in Central London, located beneath Leicester Square Underground station. Home to 16 global street-food traders, two bars, and private hire spaces, it’s a vibrant, all-inclusive destination. Family- and dog-friendly, packed with flavour and energy.
line: Now open in London’s West End, Market Place Food Hall Leicester Square is the largest food hall in Central London, located beneath Leicester Square Underground station.

name: Market Halls Oxford Street
why: A hidden food hall upstairs just off Oxford Street, with a run of street-food kitchens, bars and a games hall under one roof. A good escape from the shopping crowds, and easy for a group that can't agree what to eat.
line: A hidden food hall upstairs just off Oxford Street, with a run of street-food kitchens, bars and a games hall under one roof.

name: Harrods Food Hall
why: The most famous food hall in the world: tiled Edwardian halls of seafood, exotic fruit, chocolates, and sourdough baked every day. Even if you buy nothing, it's worth walking through.
line: The most famous food hall in the world: tiled Edwardian halls of seafood, exotic fruit, chocolates, and sourdough baked every day.

name: Camden Market
why: Camden Market is one of London’s most vibrant and eclectic destinations, famous for its counter-culture roots, over 1,000 independent shops, and global street food stalls situated right along the Regent's Canal.
line: Camden Market is one of London’s most vibrant and eclectic destinations, famous for its counter-culture roots, over 1,000 independent shops, and global street food stalls situated right along the Regent's Canal.

name: Selfridges Food Hall and Restaurants
why: Obviously known for its shopping Selfridges also has a wealth of restaurants and places to eat plus an extensive food hall with food and sweets from all over the world.
line: Obviously known for its shopping Selfridges also has a wealth of restaurants and places to eat plus an extensive food hall with food and sweets from all over the world.

name: Tyburn Tree Stone
why: The Tyburn Tree stone is a small, circular commemorative plaque embedded in a traffic island at the junction of Edgware Road, Bayswater Road, and Oxford Street near Marble Arch in London. It marks the approximate site of the infamous "Tyburn Tree," a three-legged wooden gallows where over 50,000 people were executed between 1196 and 1783
line: The Tyburn Tree stone is a small, circular commemorative plaque embedded in a traffic island at the junction of Edgware Road, Bayswater Road, and Oxford Street near Marble Arch in London.
address: Traffic Island at junction between Bayswater Road, Edgeware Road and Marble Arch

name: St Helen's Bishopsgate
why: One of the city’s only medieval churches having survived the great fire on London in 1666. Founded in 1210 and apparently attended by William Shakespeare when he lived in the area.
line: One of the city’s only medieval churches having survived the great fire on London in 1666.

name: Kensington Gardens
why: Once the private gardens of Kensington Palace, laid out by Queen Caroline in the 1700s and now open to all. Grand tree-lined avenues, the Italian Gardens and the Peter Pan statue by the Long Water. A calmer, prettier neighbour to Hyde Park.
line: Once the private gardens of Kensington Palace, laid out by Queen Caroline in the 1700s and now open to all.

name: Parliament Square and its Statues
why:
Parliament Square is a green space which sits opposite the Houses of Parliament in London. It is known as a meeting place for protest and celebration. Parliament Square is also the home to a number of notable statues of political figures.

The statues of Parliament Square can often go unremarked. However they represent a microcosm of the history of Britain.
line: Parliament Square is a green space which sits opposite the Houses of Parliament in London.

name: Paradox Museum
why: A museum of mind-bending illusions on Brompton Road, built for photos. Rooms where you shrink, float or vanish. Fun for all ages and an easy stop on a Knightsbridge day.
line: A museum of mind-bending illusions on Brompton Road, built for photos.

name: Ibraaz
why:
A brave space for art, culture, and ideas from the global majority
A space for encounter and exchange. Ibraaz spans exhibitions, talks, screenings, and music, with residencies across its library, café, and bookshop.
line: A brave space for art, culture, and ideas from the global majority A space for encounter and exchange.

name: National Portrait Gallery
why: The Gallery is filled with the people, portraits and the life stories of a nation. Home to the most extensive collection of portraits in the world, visitors can explore over 220,000 works, from the 8th century to the present day.
line: The Gallery is filled with the people, portraits and the life stories of a nation.

name: Frameless Immersive Experience
why: The UK's largest permanent immersive art experience, near Marble Arch: 42 masterpieces by artists like Van Gogh and Monet projected across four galleries, so you walk right into the paintings. One ticket covers everything.
line: The UK's largest permanent immersive art experience, near Marble Arch: 42 masterpieces by artists like Van Gogh and Monet projected across four galleries, so you walk right into the paintings.

name: Moco London
why: A museum of modern and contemporary art near Marble Arch, the London sister of Amsterdam's Moco: Banksy, Warhol and big immersive digital rooms.
line: A museum of modern and contemporary art near Marble Arch, the London sister of Amsterdam's Moco: Banksy, Warhol and big immersive digital rooms.

name: Twist Museum
why: The main concept of Twist Museum London is exploring the fascinating relationship between the mind and reality through mind-bending illusions and large-scale interactive installations. As London’s Museum of Illusions, it is designed to challenge visitors’ perceptions and senses, making them question what is real.
line: The main concept of Twist Museum London is exploring the fascinating relationship between the mind and reality through mind-bending illusions and large-scale interactive installations.

name: Wallace Collection
why:
A national museum housing unsurpassed masterpieces of painting, sculpture, furniture, arms and armour, and porcelain.
Check website as exhibitions change.
line: A national museum housing unsurpassed masterpieces of painting, sculpture, furniture, arms and armour, and porcelain.

name: London Mithraeum Bloomberg Space
why: The ruins of a Roman temple to the god Mithras, put back where they were found, under Bloomberg's City offices. Free, with a sound-and-light show; book a slot.
line: The ruins of a Roman temple to the god Mithras, put back where they were found, under Bloomberg's City offices.

name: Design Museum
why:
Located in London, the world's leading museum devoted to contemporary design in every form. The Design Museum is a multifaceted museum, an ever-changing space for the public, industry and education to come together and explore new ideas.

Check before you go which designers are showing as this changes.
line: Located in London, the world's leading museum devoted to contemporary design in every form.

name: V&A East Storehouse
why: V&A East Storehouse is your access all areas experience of the V&A collection. Go behind the scenes and take your own path through the worlds of art, design, performance, fashion and more. Art Fund Museum of the Year 2026 Shortlisted.
line: V&A East Storehouse is your access all areas experience of the V&A collection.
address: Parkes Street, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, Hackney Wick, London, E20 3AX

name: Young V&A
why: The V&A's museum for children and families in Bethnal Green, rebuilt and named Art Fund Museum of the Year 2024. Kids can play, design and make things, and it's free.
line: The V&A's museum for children and families in Bethnal Green, rebuilt and named Art Fund Museum of the Year 2024.
address: Cambridge Heath Rd, Bethnal Green, London E2 9PA

name: V&A South Kensington
why: Welcome to V&A South Kensington, a world of creativity in the heart of London. From unmissable exhibitions to extraordinary collections, there is something for everyone at the global destination for art, design and performance.
line: From unmissable exhibitions to extraordinary collections, there is something for everyone at the global destination for art, design and performance.

name: Fashion & Textiles Museum
why: The UK's only museum devoted to contemporary fashion and textiles, founded by designer Zandra Rhodes on Bermondsey Street. There's no permanent display, just a changing run of exhibitions, so check what's on.
line: The UK's only museum devoted to contemporary fashion and textiles, founded by designer Zandra Rhodes on Bermondsey Street.

name: Leighton House
why: Created as his 'private palace of art', the former studio-home of leading Victorian artist, Fredric Leighton (1830-1896), showcases an exceptional collection of 19th c. art throughout its unique interiors, including the iconic Arab Hall, with a golden dome and a calming fountain.
line: Created as his 'private palace of art', the former studio-home of leading Victorian artist, Fredric Leighton (1830-1896), showcases an exceptional collection of 19th c.

name: Sambourne House
why:
Sambourne House is the family home of legendary Punch illustrator Linley Sambourne (1844 - 1910)

Sambourne House is definitely worth visiting for anyone interested in Victorian history, art, or architecture. It is an exceptionally well-preserved “time capsule” of upper-middle-class Victorian life (circa 1870–1900), featuring stunning William Morris wallpapers, intricate artwork, and original family
line: Sambourne House is the family home of legendary Punch illustrator Linley Sambourne (1844 - 1910)  Sambourne House is definitely worth visiting for anyone interested in Victorian history, art, or architecture.

name: Handel and Hendrix Museum
why:
Separated by a wall and 200 years. The homes of two musicians who chose London & changed music.
Handel Hendrix House is made up of two residences: Handel’s house at 25 Brook Street and Hendrix’s flat at the top floor of 23 Brook Street. The museum also offers exhibition spaces that further dive into the lives of the two musicians and their times in London.
line: Separated by a wall and 200 years.

name: Foundling Museum
why: The story of London's first children's charity, founded by Thomas Coram in 1739, with Hogarth and Handel among its backers. The tokens mothers left with their babies – a coin, a button, a scrap of ribbon – are the most moving thing you'll see in any London museum.
line: The story of London's first children's charity, founded by Thomas Coram in 1739, with Hogarth and Handel among its backers.
story: Look for Tracey Emin's little bronze mitten on the railings outside – a nod to those tokens. Mothers often left one of a pair and kept the other.

name: The London Model
why: The London Model at The London Centre is a giant 3D scale model that helps visitors understand the size, shape and future of the capital. Built at 1:2000 scale, it stretches 16.5 metres and covers more than 247 square kilometres of London, including 21 boroughs and 42 kilometres of the Thames. From above, people can spot familiar places, transport routes, parks, bridges, neighbourhoods and major development areas.
line: The London Model at The London Centre is a giant 3D scale model that helps visitors understand the size, shape and future of the capital.

name: Billingsgate Roman House & Baths
why: Billingsgate Roman House & Baths is one of the most important surviving Roman archaeological sites in London. Located beneath the streets of the City of London, the remains date from the second century AD, when London was known as Londinium.
line: Billingsgate Roman House & Baths is one of the most important surviving Roman archaeological sites in London.

name: Brunel Museum
why: The Museum is an educational charity and tells the story of one of the world’s great engineering dynasties. Brunel organised the world’s first underground concert party here in 1827, and the Museum celebrates and interprets music and theatre as well as engineering.
line: The Museum is an educational charity and tells the story of one of the world’s great engineering dynasties.
address: Brunel Museum, Railway Avenue Rotherhithe, London, SE16 4LF

name: Cinema Museum
why: A treasure trove of cinema history, run by enthusiasts in the old Lambeth Workhouse, where a young Charlie Chaplin was sent when his mother fell on hard times. Projectors, posters, usherette uniforms and old cinema fittings. Visits are by guided tour or event, so book ahead.
line: A treasure trove of cinema history, run by enthusiasts in the old Lambeth Workhouse, where a young Charlie Chaplin was sent when his mother fell on hard times.

name: Freud Museum
why: Sigmund Freud's last home, in Hampstead, kept as it was, with his famous couch in the study. A quiet, fascinating hour.
line: Sigmund Freud's last home, in Hampstead, kept as it was, with his famous couch in the study.

name: Dennis Severs House
why:
Dennis Severs came to Spitalfields in 1979 and bought a derelict house saved by the Spitalfields Trust. He reconfigured it to tell the story of an imaginary Huguenot family who had lived there since it was built in 1724.

Dennis moved into 18 Folgate Street with a candle, a chamber pot and a bedroll – and the house became his life’s work.

Born in southern California, he grew up loving historical dramas on…
line: Dennis Severs came to Spitalfields in 1979 and bought a derelict house saved by the Spitalfields Trust.

name: Old Operating Theatre Museum & Herb Garret
why: Europe's oldest surviving operating theatre, hidden in the roof of an old church by London Bridge, up a narrow spiral stair. Gruesome, fascinating, and great for older kids.
line: Europe's oldest surviving operating theatre, hidden in the roof of an old church by London Bridge, up a narrow spiral stair.

name: London Transport Museum
why: 200 years of London's buses, trams and Tube trains in the old Covent Garden flower market, with plenty to climb aboard. Ask about the Hidden London tours, which take you into disused Underground stations and wartime shelters.
line: 200 years of London's buses, trams and Tube trains in the old Covent Garden flower market, with plenty to climb aboard.
address: London Transport Museum 39 Wellington Street, London WC2E 7BB

name: Postal Museum
why: 500 years of the Royal Mail, and the chance to ride Mail Rail, the tiny underground railway that carried London's post for nearly 80 years. Great for kids, with its own play area, Sorted.
line: 500 years of the Royal Mail, and the chance to ride Mail Rail, the tiny underground railway that carried London's post for nearly 80 years.

name: V&A East Museum
why: The V&A's newest museum in the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park: five floors on how creativity and design change the world, made with young Londoners. The main Why We Make galleries are free.
line: The V&A's newest museum in the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park: five floors on how creativity and design change the world, made with young Londoners.
address: East Bank, 107 Carpenters Rd, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, Stratford, London E20 2AR

name: Museum of Illusions
why: A playful hour of optical illusions on Tottenham Court Road: tilted rooms, mirror tricks and photos that make no sense. Good fun with kids, or on a wet afternoon.
line: A playful hour of optical illusions on Tottenham Court Road: tilted rooms, mirror tricks and photos that make no sense.

name: Abbey Road Studios
why: The most famous recording studio in the world, where the Beatles recorded almost all their albums. The studio itself is private, but you can visit the shop and do the photo everyone comes for, on the zebra crossing outside. Watch out for the traffic: it's a real road.
line: The most famous recording studio in the world, where the Beatles recorded almost all their albums.

name: The Dublin Castle
why: Camden's most famous little music pub, with live bands most nights in the back room and DJs after the bands at weekends. It's a drinks-and-gigs pub rather than a food pub.
line: Camden's most famous little music pub, with live bands most nights in the back room.
story: Madness made their name here in the late 1970s, and it went on to launch bands through the Britpop years. Amy Winehouse was a regular.

name: The Beatles' Rooftop Concert (3 Savile Row)
why: On 30 January 1969, the Beatles performed a concert from the rooftop of their Apple Corps headquarters at 3 Savile Row, in central London's office and fashion district. Joined by guest keyboardist Billy Preston, the band played a 42-minute set before the Metropolitan Police arrived and ordered them to reduce the volume. It was the final public performance of their career.
line: On 30 January 1969, the Beatles performed a concert from the rooftop of their Apple Corps headquarters at 3 Savile Row, in central London's office and fashion district.

name: The Music Walk of Fame Camden
why: Camden’s Walk of Fame – London’s version of Hollywood’s – has the music record plaques dedicated to rock and roll greats embedded in the road along Camden High Street. With a phone app, you can find out about why each person appears and explore their connection to London’s music scene.
line: Camden’s Walk of Fame – London’s version of Hollywood’s – has the music record plaques dedicated to rock and roll greats embedded in the road along Camden High Street.

name: Jimi Hendrix Blue Plaque
why: The guitarist and songwriter Jimi Hendrix became an overnight sensation with the release of his band’s first single, ‘Hey Joe’, in 1966. His innovative fusion of blues and experimental rock – coupled with his extraordinary live performances – has continued to have a profound influence on popular music long after his death.
line: The guitarist and songwriter Jimi Hendrix became an overnight sensation with the release of his band’s first single, ‘Hey Joe’, in 1966.
story: Look up and you'll see two plaques side by side: Handel at No. 25, Hendrix at No. 23. Two musicians, 200 years apart, living next door to each other.

name: Ziggy Stardust Plaque
why: Rock and roll might be an auditory art form, but some images mean just as much to the history of the genre as any song. Such is the iconic image of David Bowie's Ziggy Stardust emerging into the night on the cover of his titular album. The moment is so iconic that there is even a plaque on the spot commemorating it.
line: Rock and roll might be an auditory art form, but some images mean just as much to the history of the genre as any song.

name: David Bowie Blue Plaque
why: Although there is no plaque on his birthplace, one was unveiled at 17 St Anne’s Court in Soho, the site of the Trident Recording Studio where Bowie made many of his early records. The plaque was unveiled by the singer Billy Bragg and Bowie’s friend the artist George Underwood. The Studio, closed in 1981, had been home to artists like Queen and Elton John and it was where the Beatles recorded Hey Jude.
line: Although there is no plaque on his birthplace, one was unveiled at 17 St Anne’s Court in Soho, the site of the Trident Recording Studio where Bowie made many of his early records.

name: Hope and Anchor
why: Everybody who was anybody passed through these doors in the 'Seventies and 'Eighties: The Clash, The Cure, The Jam, The Police, Dire Straits, The Specials, The Stranglers, The Damned, Dr Feelgood, X-Ray Specs, Eurythmics, Elvis Costello and Madness to name just a few!
line: Everybody who was anybody passed through these doors in the 'Seventies and 'Eighties: The Clash, The Cure, The Jam, The Police, Dire Straits, The Specials, The Stranglers, The Damned, Dr Feelgood, X-Ray Specs, Eurythmics, Elvis Costello and Madness to name just a few!

name: Kirsty MacColl's Bench
why: With the support and blessing of Kirsty MacColl’s family and management, a proposal was put to Westminster Council to place a Bench in Kirsty’s memory in Soho Square, central London. Soho Square is a garden in the middle of one of London’s busiest areas.
line: With the support and blessing of Kirsty MacColl’s family and management, a proposal was put to Westminster Council to place a Bench in Kirsty’s memory in Soho Square, central London.

name: Vortex Jazz Club
why: A volunteer-run jazz club in Dalston with almost 400 gigs a year, named by DownBeat magazine as one of the world's top jazz venues. Small, friendly and the real thing.
line: A volunteer-run jazz club in Dalston with almost 400 gigs a year, named by DownBeat magazine as one of the world's top jazz venues.

name: Little Italy
why: "It's a family story Little Italy with its combination of fine dining, an exceptional wine list, music and dancing has become one of the most popular and best known Italian restaurants in Soho. Opened in 1995, it traces its roots deep into the heart of the Italian community in London.
line: "It's a family story Little Italy with its combination of fine dining, an exceptional wine list, music and dancing has become one of the most popular and best known Italian restaurants in Soho.

name: Ronnie Scott's
why: London's most famous jazz club, in Soho since 1959. Miles Davis, Nina Simone, Ella Fitzgerald, Jimi Hendrix, Prince and Amy Winehouse have all played here, and it still has its old-school Soho charm. Book for the main show, or catch the late sets.
line: London's most famous jazz club, in Soho since 1959.

name: Zuma Bar
why:
The original Zuma is renowned as one of the best Japanese restaurants in the capital
embracing the rich culinary heritage of Japanese cuisine with contemporary dishes, inspired by the founder’s many years spent eating + drinking after work in traditional Tokyo izakayas, this is where the story began…
line: The original Zuma is renowned as one of the best Japanese restaurants in the capital embracing the rich culinary heritage of Japanese cuisine with contemporary dishes, inspired by the founder’s many years spent eating + drinking after work in traditional Tokyo izakayas, this is where the story began…

name: Zum Barbarossa
why: Zum Barbarossa will serve as an all-in-one cocktail bar and club. Guests can choose from a selection of uniquely crafted cocktails and enjoy live DJs
line: Zum Barbarossa will serve as an all-in-one cocktail bar and club.

name: Flute Rooftop Bar
why:
Soho's most loved rooftop bar

In the 19th century, Broadwick Street was home to a noted flute-maker who inspired the name of the rooftop dining and bar venue that crowns the hotel. Flute's landscaped wraparound outdoor terrace offers spectacular views over the Soho streets and London skyline.
line: Soho's most loved rooftop bar  In the 19th century, Broadwick Street was home to a noted flute-maker who inspired the name of the rooftop dining and bar venue that crowns the hotel.

name: Three Sheets Soho
why: The Soho branch of a much-loved cocktail bar, just off Greek Street: relaxed service, simple, perfectly made drinks, and British oysters with champagne or a cracking burger and chips.
line: The Soho branch of a much-loved cocktail bar, just off Greek Street: relaxed service, simple, perfectly made drinks, and British oysters with champagne or a cracking burger and chips.

name: Cahoots Underground
why: Cahoots Underground is a lively 1940s-inspired cocktail bar hidden beneath the streets of Soho, London. Set inside a recreated vintage Underground station, it captures the atmosphere of wartime Britain with tiled walls, old train seats, retro posters, and swing music. The venue is known for theatrical cocktails served in playful containers, from teacups to milk bottles, adding to its nostalgic charm.
line: Cahoots Underground is a lively 1940s-inspired cocktail bar hidden beneath the streets of Soho, London.

name: Wagtail
why: A rooftop restaurant and terrace bar on top of a grand art deco building in the City, with 360° views of Tower Bridge, St Paul's, the Shard and the Gherkin. Open late, with DJs some evenings.
line: A rooftop restaurant and terrace bar on top of a grand art deco building in the City, with 360° views of Tower Bridge, St Paul's, the Shard and the Gherkin.

name: The Nest
why: The rooftop bar of the Treehouse Hotel by Oxford Circus, with 360° views over the West End skyline. Open until 1am most nights.
line: The rooftop bar of the Treehouse Hotel by Oxford Circus, with 360° views over the West End skyline.

name: Joia Rooftop
why:
Located in the Artotel in Battersea Power Station. 
JOIA Rooftop is open every day. Escape above the city and enjoy sun-soaked afternoons, iconic skyline views and signature drinks that taste like summer.
line: Located in the Artotel in Battersea Power Station.

name: Savage Garden
why:
London's wildest rooftop bar

A study in experimentation and temptation, enter a decadent and twisted world, 12 storeys above, and far removed from the corporate streets of the city below. A bar where the atmosphere is unapologetically untamed, the cocktail serves theatrical and the food savagely good.

Take a walk on the wild side…
line: London's wildest rooftop bar  A study in experimentation and temptation, enter a decadent and twisted world, 12 storeys above, and far removed from the corporate streets of the city below.

name: Florattica Rooftop
why:
High above Aldgate on the 11th floor, Florattica is a rooftop spot with some of the best views in London. From St Paul’s to Canary Wharf, the city skyline is always part of the experience, whether you’re here for after-work drinks, a weekend catch-up, or a special night out.

Rooted in East London’s heritgae
Florattica’s design takes inspiration from the silk weavers of Spitalfields, whose creativity once shaped…
line: High above Aldgate on the 11th floor, Florattica is a rooftop spot with some of the best views in London.
address: 11-15 Minories St, London EC3N 1AX, United Kingdom

name: Los Mochis City
why: Explore the diverse settings of Los Mochis London City, featuring a vibrant main dining room, scenic rooftop terrace, captivating sushi bar, and a luxurious agaveria & lounge.
line: Explore the diverse settings of Los Mochis London City, featuring a vibrant main dining room, scenic rooftop terrace, captivating sushi bar, and a luxurious agaveria & lounge.

name: Cé La Vi
why: West London's highest rooftop, on the 17th and 18th floors of Paddington Square: modern Asian food, a sky bar and a terrace with views from Hyde Park to the London Eye and the Shard.
line: West London's highest rooftop, on the 17th and 18th floors of Paddington Square: modern Asian food, a sky bar and a terrace with views from Hyde Park to the London Eye and the Shard.
address: 1 PADDINGTON SQUARE 17th & 18th Floor, London England, W2 1DL

name: One Hundred Shoreditch Kaso Rooftop Bar
why:
flavours of the east med with views of the east end

Kaso blends the relaxed rhythm of the Mediterranean and Aegean regions with the energy of East London - channelling year-round sun-soaked vibes alongside killer cocktails and an eclectic, club classics playlist with DJs spinning every Friday and Saturday night. Check the menus and artist line-ups below.
line: flavours of the east med with views of the east end  Kaso blends the relaxed rhythm of the Mediterranean and Aegean regions with the energy of East London - channelling year-round sun-soaked vibes alongside killer cocktails and an eclectic, club classics playlist with DJs spinning every Friday and Saturday night.

name: Yasmin
why: A Middle Eastern rooftop restaurant and bar high above Soho: sharing plates, good cocktails and a sunny terrace in summer. Works for a date, a celebration or drinks with friends.
line: A Middle Eastern rooftop restaurant and bar high above Soho: sharing plates, good cocktails and a sunny terrace in summer.

name: Sachi
why: A glass-walled rooftop restaurant and bar on Motcomb Street, Belgravia, serving Japanese favourites with a Pan-Asian twist. Bright for lunch, relaxed for after-work drinks.
line: A glass-walled rooftop restaurant and bar on Motcomb Street, Belgravia, serving Japanese favourites with a Pan-Asian twist.

name: Jurema
why:
Nestled in the heart of Fitzrovia, the Jurema terrace is a cosy alfresco escape from the city’s hustle and bustle. The space features a striking glass structure that offers warmth and comfort alongside uninterrupted views of Jurema’s iconic hanging garden.

Guests are invited to enjoy plates from the Eastern Mediterranean, made to share, paired with expertly crafted cocktails, creating a vibrant dining experience…
line: Nestled in the heart of Fitzrovia, the Jurema terrace is a cosy alfresco escape from the city’s hustle and bustle.

name: Forza Wine
why: A natural wine and cocktail bar at the National Theatre with views over the Thames, with Italian-ish sharing plates. Perfect before or after a show on the South Bank.
line: A natural wine and cocktail bar at the National Theatre with views over the Thames, with Italian-ish sharing plates.

name: 1864 Rooftop Bar
why: A rooftop bar and kitchen on the 6th floor of John Lewis on Oxford Street: city views, cocktails and a seasonal menu. A handy reward after a day's shopping.
line: A rooftop bar and kitchen on the 6th floor of John Lewis on Oxford Street: city views, cocktails and a seasonal menu.

name: Jazz Cafe
why: One of the world's iconic live music venues. Daily shows, a mezzanine restaurant and club nights every weekend.
line: One of the world's iconic live music venues.

name: Apollo's Muse
why: A hidden cocktail lounge inside Bacchanalia in Mayfair, surrounded by ancient antiquities. Named one of the top 10 bars in Europe by Tales of the Cocktail. Walk-ins welcome.
line: A hidden cocktail lounge inside Bacchanalia in Mayfair, surrounded by ancient antiquities.

name: SAMBAROOM at SUSHISAMBA
why: A cocktail bar and lounge on the 39th floor of Heron Tower in the City, reached through a gilded entrance and a mirrored walkway. DJs, bar bites and huge views over east London.
line: A cocktail bar and lounge on the 39th floor of Heron Tower in the City, reached through a gilded entrance and a mirrored walkway.

name: Red Room at The Connaught
why: A secret wine bar inside The Connaught, reached through a velvet curtain from the Champagne Room. A small, intimate room hung with red artworks by four women artists, and a superb wine list.
line: A secret wine bar inside The Connaught, reached through a velvet curtain from the Champagne Room.

name: Eve Bar
why:
Dimly lit lounge preparing imaginative cocktails in a hip, stylishly decorated hideaway

Cocktail, Champagne and caviar bar, in the heart of London’s Theatreland
line: Dimly lit lounge preparing imaginative cocktails in a hip, stylishly decorated hideaway  Cocktail, Champagne and caviar bar, in the heart of London’s Theatreland

name: Archive and Myth
why: A hidden cocktail bar under the Hippodrome Casino, from the team behind Magic Mike Live. Moody, theatrical and full of curiosities. Use the Magic Mike Live entrance on Cranbourn Street, and book ahead.
line: A hidden cocktail bar under the Hippodrome Casino, from the team behind Magic Mike Live.

name: Punch Room at The London Edition
why: From its humble beginnings on 17th century trade ships and in raucous dockside taverns to gracious presence at balls and garden parties of the aristocracy, Punch has always made the most of its surroundings.
line: From its humble beginnings on 17th century trade ships and in raucous dockside taverns to gracious presence at balls and garden parties of the aristocracy, Punch has always made the most of its surroundings.

name: Mr Fogg's Society of Exploration
why: A cocktail bar in Mayfair dressed as the Victorian home of an explorer inspired by Around the World in 80 Days. Fun, theatrical and good for a group.
line: A cocktail bar in Mayfair dressed as the Victorian home of an explorer inspired by Around the World in 80 Days.

name: The Mulwray
why: A wine bar hidden above The Blue Posts on the edge of Soho, specialising in fine and natural wines from lesser-known growers. The list changes weekly, so there's always something new to try by the glass.
line: A wine bar hidden above The Blue Posts on the edge of Soho, specialising in fine and natural wines from lesser-known growers.

name: Phoenix Arts Club
why:
A Home for Theatre, Cabaret and Late-Night Soho

Founded in 1988 and hidden beneath the Phoenix Theatre in the heart of Soho, The Phoenix Arts Club is one of London’s last truly independent performance venues — a place where theatre spills off the West End stage and into the night.

For nearly four decades, the Club has been a meeting place, rehearsal room, performance space and creative refuge for artists working…
line: A Home for Theatre, Cabaret and Late-Night Soho  Founded in 1988 and hidden beneath the Phoenix Theatre in the heart of Soho, The Phoenix Arts Club is one of London’s last truly independent performance venues — a place where theatre spills off the West End stage and into the night.

name: Weezie's
why: Weezie’s is an all-day pizza restaurant in Eccleston Yards, Belgravia, London, from amie founders Abbie Roden and Will Sandbach. Located next door to amie wine studio, Weezie’s will serve thin-crust pizzas made fresh daily, alongside small plates, pints, cocktails and exceptional wine.
line: Weezie’s is an all-day pizza restaurant in Eccleston Yards, Belgravia, London, from amie founders Abbie Roden and Will Sandbach.

name: Village Underground
why: A converted Victorian warehouse in Shoreditch, famous for the old Tube carriages on its roof. One of east London's best independent venues for gigs and club nights, from new acts to big names.
line: A converted Victorian warehouse in Shoreditch, famous for the old Tube carriages on its roof.

name: The Orange
why: A grand four-storey pub on Pimlico Road, built as a brewery in the 1800s and said to be named after William of Orange. Hidden in the basement is the Blood Orange Bar, a cocktail bar for later on.
line: A grand four-storey pub on Pimlico Road, built as a brewery in the 1800s and said to be named after William of Orange.

name: Selene
why: A glamorous Greek-mythology-themed late-night venue in Fitzrovia, open Friday to Sunday only. Dress up, and book ahead.
line: A glamorous Greek-mythology-themed late-night venue in Fitzrovia, open Friday to Sunday only.

name: 42 Mayfair
why: The cocktail bar upstairs at Gymkhana in Mayfair, inspired by the captain's quarters of India's old Gymkhana clubs: cocktails with Indian flavours, rare whiskies and Gymkhana bar snacks. DJs on Friday and Saturday nights until 2am.
line: The cocktail bar upstairs at Gymkhana in Mayfair, inspired by the captain's quarters of India's old Gymkhana clubs: cocktails with Indian flavours, rare whiskies and Gymkhana bar snacks.

name: St James's Park
why: London's oldest Royal Park, with the best view in town: stand on the Blue Bridge and you've got Buckingham Palace one way and the turrets of Whitehall the other. Come at 2.30pm to see the pelicans fed. They've lived here since a Russian ambassador gave the first ones to Charles II in 1664.
line: London's oldest Royal Park, with the best view in town: stand on the Blue Bridge and you've got Buckingham Palace one way and the turrets of Whitehall the other.

name: Hyde Park
why:
This is where suffragettes gave fiery speeches, where the Rolling Stones rocked out by the lake, where the UK’s first Pride march began and where Nelson Mandela took the stage. No wonder it’s nicknamed ‘The People’s Park’. 

This vast open space in the heart of the city is packed with things to discover.
line: This is where suffragettes gave fiery speeches, where the Rolling Stones rocked out by the lake, where the UK’s first Pride march began and where Nelson Mandela took the stage.

name: Regent's Park and Primrose Hill
why:
If you’re after horticultural excellence, head for Queen Mary’s Gardens. In the summer, when the heady scent of 8,000 jewel-like roses fills the air, you’ll understand why poet Sylvia Plath described it as a ‘wonderland’. Next, visit Avenue Gardens for vibrant floral displays that wrap around historic fountains and ornate planters.

Did you know that the park boasts London’s largest outdoor sports area?
line: If you’re after horticultural excellence, head for Queen Mary’s Gardens.

name: The Green Park
why: The quiet one between Hyde Park and St James's Park: shady avenues, open grass and deckchairs in summer. Charles II created it in 1660 so he could walk between the two parks without leaving royal land. His daily 'constitutional' here is said to have given nearby Constitution Hill its name.
line: The quiet one between Hyde Park and St James's Park: shady avenues, open grass and deckchairs in summer.

name: Victoria Tower Gardens
why:
Nestled between the sweeping River Thames and the spectacular Houses of Parliament, this park is a little pocket of peace at the heart of political power.

The theme of freedom is woven through this tranquil green space in the form of memorials commemorating some of the most important political movements in British History. This is why some have called this space ‘The Garden of Conscience’.
line: Nestled between the sweeping River Thames and the spectacular Houses of Parliament, this park is a little pocket of peace at the heart of political power.

name: Holland Park
why:
Holland Park is spread across 54 acres of what used to be the grounds of Cope Castle, a large Jacobean mansion hidden in the woods. Sir Walter Cope built it in the early 17th century. He became Chancellor of the Exchequer under King James I.

It was renamed Holland House after the Earl of Holland’s wife Lady Rich inherited the property.

Holland House was badly damaged during World War 2.
line: Holland Park is spread across 54 acres of what used to be the grounds of Cope Castle, a large Jacobean mansion hidden in the woods.

name: Battersea Park and Zoo
why: Battersea Park is a large (200 acre) Victorian park, built between 1854 and 1870. It has a riverside promenade, a large lake, many notable trees and ecological areas, children's play areas, a children's zoo, the Pump House gallery, ceremony venue and sports facilities.
line: Battersea Park is a large (200 acre) Victorian park, built between 1854 and 1870.

name: The Old Bank of England
why:
The Old Bank is one of the most stunning pub interiors in the City of London.

The pub resides in the old Law Court’s branch of the previous Bank of England which operated from 1888 to 1975. The location is also famously directly between Sweeney Todd’s barber shop and Mrs Lovett’s pie shop!
line: The Old Bank is one of the most stunning pub interiors in the City of London.

name: Trafalgar Tavern
why: The Trafalgar was built on the site of the long-established Old George Tavern, whose landlord Charles Hart continued at the helm of the Trafalgar until his death in 1863.
line: The Trafalgar was built on the site of the long-established Old George Tavern, whose landlord Charles Hart continued at the helm of the Trafalgar until his death in 1863.

name: The Churchill Arms
why: Dripping in flowers and crammed with memorabilia, The Churchill Arms is one of London’s most recognisable and famous watering holes. Built in 1750, the pub was frequented by Churchill’s grandparents and is known for serving real ales and authentic Thai cuisine.
line: Dripping in flowers and crammed with memorabilia, The Churchill Arms is one of London’s most recognisable and famous watering holes.

name: Cutty Sark Pub
why: Nestled on the banks of the River Thames at Ballast Quay, The Cutty Sark has been a beloved institution for over 200 years, offering top-notch seasonal dishes made from premium British ingredients, complemented by exquisite wines from around the world and real ales Popular for its Sunday roast.
line: Nestled on the banks of the River Thames at Ballast Quay, The Cutty Sark has been a beloved institution for over 200 years, offering top-notch seasonal dishes made from premium British ingredients, complemented by exquisite wines from around the world and real ales

name: Newman Arms
why: A Fitzrovia institution since 1730, the Newman Arms is a pub built on proper pints, legendary pies, and a touch of indulgence. From a perfectly pulled pint to a glass of Pol Roger Champagne — or even a classic Black Velvet — you’ll find something to suit every mood.
line: A Fitzrovia institution since 1730, the Newman Arms is a pub built on proper pints, legendary pies, and a touch of indulgence.

name: Ship Tavern
why: A classic ale house tucked down a little alley by Lincoln's Inn Fields, serving pints since 1549. Run by the same family for over 20 years: wood panelling, open fires and a proper dining room upstairs.
line: A classic ale house tucked down a little alley by Lincoln's Inn Fields, serving pints since 1549.

name: Mayfair Bar
why: Welcome to The May Fair Bar, a dining and drinking experience set by the iconic Berkeley Square in Mayfair. Recently transformed with a new look and spirit, The May Fair Bar welcomes you for breakfast, lunch, night bites and all-day cocktails, accompanied by the occasional live music performance befitting the elegant location
line: Recently transformed with a new look and spirit, The May Fair Bar welcomes you for breakfast, lunch, night bites and all-day cocktails, accompanied by the occasional live music performance befitting the elegant location

name: The Pig's Ear
why: Tucked long Old Church Street, this place is an absolute local favourite for a reason. Think farm to fork seasonal menus, fresh oysters, wines from their own Sussex vineyard and the kind of warm, welcoming atmosphere that makes you want to come back
line: Tucked long Old Church Street, this place is an absolute local favourite for a reason.

name: Grenadier
why: One of the cutest and oldest pubs in London. The Grenadier is a tiny hidden gem on a mews street in Belgraviabut a world away from the nearby flashy department stores. There’s a few tables outside in summer.
line: One of the cutest and oldest pubs in London.

name: Compton Arms
why: A tiny 200-year-old Islington pub on a quiet back lane, famous for its cheeseburger. The kitchen is run by a guest restaurant (currently Rake, Wednesday to Sunday), and it has one of London's best little beer gardens.
line: A tiny 200-year-old Islington pub on a quiet back lane, famous for its cheeseburger.

name: Drapers Arms
why: A neighbourhood gastropub with a classic British menu with a French twist. More of a food destination than a casual drinking spot though the courtyard is a great place to sit and enjoy a drink. Popular for its Sunday roast.
line: A neighbourhood gastropub with a classic British menu with a French twist.

name: Elephant and Castle
why: A small, quiet pub on one of Kensington's prettiest streets, covered in flowers in summer and best enjoyed at a table outside. Good pints and proper pies.
line: A small, quiet pub on one of Kensington's prettiest streets, covered in flowers in summer and best enjoyed at a table outside.

name: Spurstowe Arms
why: A buzzy Hackney local known for its Sunday roast and its pizzas, with a lovely terrace for spritzes in summer. It fills up fast, so get there early.
line: A buzzy Hackney local known for its Sunday roast and its pizzas, with a lovely terrace for spritzes in summer.

name: De Beauvoir Arms
why: A Victorian corner pub in De Beauvoir with food at its heart: Mediterranean-inspired chalkboard menus, good wine and big shared wooden tables. Walk-in only, so come a bit early.
line: A Victorian corner pub in De Beauvoir with food at its heart: Mediterranean-inspired chalkboard menus, good wine and big shared wooden tables.

name: Pelican
why: A Notting Hill neighbourhood pub on All Saints Road, serious about its food: seasonal cooking with meat and produce from named British farms. Relaxed downstairs, with a dining room upstairs.
line: A Notting Hill neighbourhood pub on All Saints Road, serious about its food: seasonal cooking with meat and produce from named British farms.

name: The Hart
why:
Located on the corner of Chiltern Street and Blandford Street, The Hart is a neighbourhood pub and dining room celebrating British farmers with real focus on bringing back the weekday pub lunch.

The Hart takes its name from the Hart family, who ran a pub on this very site in the 1840s.
line: Located on the corner of Chiltern Street and Blandford Street, The Hart is a neighbourhood pub and dining room celebrating British farmers with real focus on bringing back the weekday pub lunch.

name: The Marlborough
why: A proper Mayfair pub on North Audley Street, and the home of Crisp Pizza, one of London's most talked-about pizzas. Sister pub to The Devonshire in Soho.
line: A proper Mayfair pub on North Audley Street, and the home of Crisp Pizza, one of London's most talked-about pizzas.

name: The Blue Stoops
why: The Blue Stoops is a pub in Kensington masterminded by Jamie Allsopp, who revived his family’s heritage brewing brand in 2021 and has been going from strength to strength ever since. This venture is the latest part of the brand’s almost 300-year history which includes the invention of the IPA by Jamie’s family seven generations ago.
line: The Blue Stoops is a pub in Kensington masterminded by Jamie Allsopp, who revived his family’s heritage brewing brand in 2021 and has been going from strength to strength ever since.

name: Blue Boar Pub and Restaurant
why: A relaxed modern pub in the heart of Westminster, a few minutes from Parliament and St James's Park. Proper British pub food, good beers and cocktails. A handy stop between the sights.
line: A relaxed modern pub in the heart of Westminster, a few minutes from Parliament and St James's Park.

name: Seven Stars
why: Twinkling is what stars are intended to do, of course. And its devoted attendees certainly think "brilliant" is a justifiable word to describe The Seven Stars: a perfect, ancient London boozer. Roxy Beaujolais, its legendary publican-- the Alewife For the Ages, as a pub critic has called her-- might personally be thought of as a substantial sparkler rather than a coy twinkler.
line: Twinkling is what stars are intended to do, of course.

name: Hoop and Grapes
why: One of the City's oldest pubs, built in 1593 and one of the very few timber buildings to survive the Great Fire of 1666, which stopped just 50 yards away. Step inside the tall, narrow building and you're stepping back 400 years.
line: One of the City's oldest pubs, built in 1593 and one of the very few timber buildings to survive the Great Fire of 1666, which stopped just 50 yards away.

name: Spaniards Inn
why: A 1585 coaching inn on the edge of Hampstead Heath where Dickens and Keats drank, and where highwayman Dick Turpin is said to haunt the corridors. Lovely big garden, and a perfect stop after a walk on the Heath.
line: A 1585 coaching inn on the edge of Hampstead Heath where Dickens and Keats drank, and where highwayman Dick Turpin is said to haunt the corridors.

name: The Grapes
why: One of London's oldest pubs, on the river at Limehouse. Dickens drank here and wrote it into *Our Mutual Friend*, and it's in the Good Pub Guide every year. Small, peaceful, and it feels a world away from Canary Wharf down the road.
line: One of London's oldest pubs, on the river at Limehouse.
story: Famous landlords: Sir Ian McKellen is one of the owners, and the staff he carried as Gandalf stands behind the bar. Go down to the little riverside terrace at the back.

name: The Mayflower
why:
The Mayflower pub is a hidden gem in the heart of Rotherhithe, London.

A traditional English pub surrounded by cobbled streets, the outside decked jetty and cosy candlelit restaurant have stunning river views. At low tide you can spot the original 1620 mooring point of the Pilgrim Father’s Mayflower ship.
line: The Mayflower pub is a hidden gem in the heart of Rotherhithe, London.

name: Ye Olde Mitre
why: Built in 1546 for the servants of the Bishops of Ely, The Ye Olde Mitre is famous for having a cherry tree, (now supporting the front) that Queen Elizabeth once danced around with Sir Christopher Hatton. The pub was actually a part of Cambridge (Ely being in Cambridge) and the licencees used to have to go there for their licence.
line: Built in 1546 for the servants of the Bishops of Ely, The Ye Olde Mitre is famous for having a cherry tree, (now supporting the front) that Queen Elizabeth once danced around with Sir Christopher Hatton.

name: The George Inn
why: London's last galleried coaching inn, rebuilt after the Southwark fire of 1676 and now looked after by the National Trust. Dickens knew it well. Sit in the cobbled yard and picture the stagecoaches pulling in.
line: London's last galleried coaching inn, rebuilt after the Southwark fire of 1676 and now looked after by the National Trust.
address: George Yard 75-77 Borough High Street Southwark Greater London England SE1 1NH

name: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese
why: Probably the most famous pub in the world, Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese is one of London’s few remaining 17th Century chophouses. The sawdust on the floor is changed twice daily, It is a pub and eating house offering unpretentious fare in wooden bays provided by high-backed church pews and served by waiters. The site formed part of the 13th century Carmelite monastery and since 1538 a pub has stood here.
line: Probably the most famous pub in the world, Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese is one of London’s few remaining 17th Century chophouses.

name: The Prospect of Whitby
why: Said to be the oldest riverside pub in the country, built around 1520 on the Thames at Wapping. Sailors, smugglers and film stars have all walked its 400-year-old stone floor. Sit out on the river terrace and look for the noose hanging over the water, a reminder of nearby Execution Dock.
line: Said to be the oldest riverside pub in the country, built around 1520 on the Thames at Wapping.

name: Cittie of Yorke
why: A pub has stood on this site since 1430. The first pub was approximately a quarter of the size of today’s ground floor bar and stood between the back door of the main hall and the stove. The pub that stood here in 1666, survived the Great Fire of London, due to the fire stopping by Holborn Circus.
line: A pub has stood on this site since 1430.

name: The Eagle Farringdon
why:
The Eagle Farringdon. It’s what a pub should be. Good food and drink with great people behind the bar. 
The Food 

It’s always been about getting the sort of skills and ingredients from the best restaurants in town to a truly egalitarian, good value pub.
line: It’s what a pub should be.

name: Lore of the Land
why: Owned by film producer Guy Ritchie and used in the film The Gentleman. Seasonal sharing plates, pints and premium spirits in a classic setting housing a pub since 1829.
line: Owned by film producer Guy Ritchie and used in the film The Gentleman.

name: The Audley
why: Traditional neighbourhood pub open 7 days a week & set in a restored Victorian building.
line: Traditional neighbourhood pub open 7 days a week & set in a restored Victorian building.

name: The Devonshire
why: A Soho pub that's become famous in no time for its Guinness – it sells more than almost anywhere in Britain. Downstairs is a proper pub with food from its own butcher and bakery; upstairs, a wood-fired grill with Scottish beef, Oban langoustines and Devon scallops.
line: A Soho pub that's become famous in no time for its Guinness – it sells more than almost anywhere in Britain.
story: Famous landlords: it's run by Oisín Rogers, probably London's best-known publican. If you see a crowd on the pavement off Piccadilly Circus, you've found it.

name: The Fat Badger
why: A pub and dining room above a café on Portobello Road, with hearty British cooking. A good stop after the market.
line: A pub and dining room above a café on Portobello Road, with hearty British cooking.

name: Thomas Cubitt
why: A smart Belgravia pub named after Thomas Cubitt, the builder who created much of Belgravia, with a dining room upstairs and a good Sunday roast.
line: A smart Belgravia pub named after Thomas Cubitt, the builder who created much of Belgravia, with a dining room upstairs and a good Sunday roast.

name: The George
why: An 18th-century Grade II listed pub on Great Portland Street, once a meeting place for radicals and later for writers and poets. Two floors, good food and a proper Fitzrovia local feel.
line: An 18th-century Grade II listed pub on Great Portland Street, once a meeting place for radicals and later for writers and poets.

name: The Cow Irish Pub
why: A Notting Hill favourite for Guinness and oysters: an Irish-style pub with a famous seafood platter, a hearty fish stew and proper bangers and mash. Lively and friendly, especially at weekends.
line: A Notting Hill favourite for Guinness and oysters: an Irish-style pub with a famous seafood platter, a hearty fish stew and proper bangers and mash.

name: The Lamb
why: A beautiful Victorian pub on Lamb's Conduit Street, with its original snob screens still over the bar. Charles Dickens visited, and Sylvia Plath and Ted Hughes were regulars. One of Bloomsbury's best.
line: A beautiful Victorian pub on Lamb's Conduit Street, with its original snob screens still over the bar.
address: 94 Lamb’s Conduit Street, Bloomsbury, London, WC1N 3LZ

name: The Toucan Irish Pub
why: A tiny Irish pub in Soho, famous for one of the best pints of Guinness in London. In the 60s the basement was a music club. Small, packed and a lot of fun.
line: A tiny Irish pub in Soho, famous for one of the best pints of Guinness in London.

name: Waxy O’Connors Irish Pub
why:
Receive a warm Irish welcome at the award-winning Waxy O’Connor’s, London’s biggest and best Irish bar.

Located on Rupert Street at the edge of Soho, it’s a labyrinth of four unique bars over six levels, each with its own atmosphere and personality, as well as the famous Waxy’s tree found at the heart of the pub. There’s something for everyone at Waxy’s!
line: Receive a warm Irish welcome at the award-winning Waxy O’Connor’s, London’s biggest and best Irish bar.

name: The Blue Posts
why: An original Georgian pub from 1739, hidden on a corner between Soho and Chinatown. People have been drinking here for nearly 300 years. Look out for The Mulwray wine bar upstairs.
line: An original Georgian pub from 1739, hidden on a corner between Soho and Chinatown.

name: The Wigmore
why: The pub next door to The Langham hotel, with food overseen by Michel Roux Jr. Famous for its cheese toastie, and good for a Sunday roast near Oxford Circus.
line: The pub next door to The Langham hotel, with food overseen by Michel Roux Jr.
address: 15 Langham Place, Regent Street, London, W1B 3DE

name: The Lamb and Flag
why:
Great London pubs don't get much more historic than this. The very first mention of a pub on this site is in 1772, when it was known as The Coopers Arms (the name changed to The Lamb & Flag in 1833).

The building's brickwork is circa 1958 and conceals what may be an early 18th century frame of a house, replacing the original one built in 1638.

The pub acquired a reputation in the early nineteenth century for…
line: Great London pubs don't get much more historic than this.
address: The Lamb & Flag, 33 Rose Street, Covent Garden, London, WC2E 9EB

name: Bat and Ball
why: A games pub in Covent Garden: ping pong, darts, shuffleboard, pool and karaoke rooms, plus live sport on big screens and DJs later on. Great for groups.
line: A games pub in Covent Garden: ping pong, darts, shuffleboard, pool and karaoke rooms, plus live sport on big screens and DJs later on.

name: Bloodsports by MeatLiquor
why:
Welcome to bloodsports by meatliquor
Live sport. Cult horror. 30+ screens. BLOODsports is your late-night hangout where match-day madness meets horror and the drinks never stop flowing.

Spitting distance from Seven Dials and Covent Garden Piazza, BLOODsports is your after-dark playground. With 30+ screens, arcade games and heavy pours, this is where the night *actually* starts.
line: BLOODsports is your late-night hangout where match-day madness meets horror and the drinks never stop flowing.

name: The Kings Sports Bar
why:
Screens in every direction, an unbeatable matchday atmosphere, budweiser on tap and game-day food brought straight to your table - all without missing a second of the action.

Looking for a sports bar in London or somewhere to watch live sport?
line: Screens in every direction, an unbeatable matchday atmosphere, budweiser on tap and game-day food brought straight to your table - all without missing a second of the action.
address: Empire Casino 5-6 Leicester Square London WC2H 7NA

name: Pig and Butcher
why: A handsome 1850s Islington pub from when the fields around here were used to rest cattle on their way to Smithfield market. Fittingly, it's known for its meat, with a daily-changing seasonal menu from top British farms. The Sunday roast is a favourite.
line: A handsome 1850s Islington pub from when the fields around here were used to rest cattle on their way to Smithfield market.

name: The Trafalgar Chelsea
why: A grand Edwardian pub on the King's Road from 1909, designed by the architect of Chequers. Now beautifully restored, with craft beers, cocktails, live music and sport.
line: A grand Edwardian pub on the King's Road from 1909, designed by the architect of Chequers.

name: The Boundary
why: A lively neighbourhood bar on the Fulham end of the King's Road, with live music, big-screen sport, cocktails and fresh pizza. A good spot to watch the match.
line: A lively neighbourhood bar on the Fulham end of the King's Road, with live music, big-screen sport, cocktails and fresh pizza.

name: Crisp W1 in The Marlborough
why: Crisp Pizza's Mayfair kitchen inside The Marlborough pub: thin, crispy-edged pizzas that queue-for-them fans rate among London's best. Eat in the pub with a pint.
line: Crisp Pizza's Mayfair kitchen inside The Marlborough pub: thin, crispy-edged pizzas that queue-for-them fans rate among London's best.

name: Gymkhana
why:
Gymkhana is inspired by the elite clubs of India where members of high society socialise, eat, drink, celebrate and play sport.
The London restaurant has two Michelin stars
