line: Gymkhana is inspired by the elite clubs of India where members of high society socialise, eat, drink, celebrate and play sport.

name: Cicchetti
why: Italian family owned, Cicchetti Piccadilly has been named as one of the most authentic Italian restaurants in London.
line: Italian family owned, Cicchetti Piccadilly has been named as one of the most authentic Italian restaurants in London.

name: Sale e Pepe
why: For 50 years, Sale e Pepe of Knightsbridge has been, and continues to be, one of London's most iconic and celebrated restaurants serving classic Italian cuisine with authentic Italian hospitality.
line: For 50 years, Sale e Pepe of Knightsbridge has been, and continues to be, one of London's most iconic and celebrated restaurants serving classic Italian cuisine with authentic Italian hospitality.

name: Gunpowder
why: A modern take on traditional Indian cuisine, offering an experience that is distinctively different from the typical Indian fare found across the UK. Inspired by the rich and varied flavours of India.
line: A modern take on traditional Indian cuisine, offering an experience that is distinctively different from the typical Indian fare found across the UK.

name: Pizza Pilgrims
why: In 2012, founders Thom & James decided to quit their jobs and fly to the toe-end of Italy, and drive the 4,500km back to London, learning all they could about the true art of pizza making.
line: In 2012, founders Thom & James decided to quit their jobs and fly to the toe-end of Italy, and drive the 4,500km back to London, learning all they could about the true art of pizza making.

name: China Tang
why: China Tang at The Dorchester, is widely heralded as home to some of the finest authentic Cantonese food outside China.
line: China Tang at The Dorchester, is widely heralded as home to some of the finest authentic Cantonese food outside China.

name: Frog by Adam Handling
why: It’s a place to really immerse yourself in a theatrical show. You’re facing the kitchen, the chefs come to your table in this Michelin-starred restaurant.
line: It’s a place to really immerse yourself in a theatrical show.

name: NAC North Audley Cantine
why: NAC (North Audley Cantine) is a relaxed and stylish new bistro and cocktail bar offering French sharing plates and exquisite desserts.
line: NAC (North Audley Cantine) is a relaxed and stylish new bistro and cocktail bar offering French sharing plates and exquisite desserts.

name: Zuma
why: The original Zuma is renowned as one of the best Japanese restaurants in the capital embracing the rich culinary heritage of Japanese cuisine with contemporary dishes, inspired by the founder’s many years spent eating + drinking after work in traditional Tokyo izakayas, this is where the story began…
line: The original Zuma is renowned as one of the best Japanese restaurants in the capital embracing the rich culinary heritage of Japanese cuisine with contemporary dishes, inspired by the founder’s many years spent eating + drinking after work in traditional Tokyo izakayas, this is where the story began…

name: Straker’s
why: The chef who built a huge following with his lockdown cooking videos on TikTok, then opened this small Notting Hill restaurant so fans could taste the real thing. Book ahead – it's small and it's popular.
line: The chef who built a huge following with his lockdown cooking videos on TikTok, then opened this small Notting Hill restaurant so fans could taste the real thing.

name: Holy Carrot
why: Plant-based cooking that even meat-eaters rave about. The kitchen cooks over fire and uses fermentation to get serious flavour out of vegetables. A good stop on a Portobello Market day.
line: Plant-based cooking that even meat-eaters rave about.

name: Acre
why:
Acre is restaurant and delicatessen from famed influencer chef Thomas Straker, joining Straker’s as the chef’s second site in Notting Hill. 
Acre is more relaxed than Straker’s although it operates as a casual restaurant, it also has a delicatessen where you can buy produce.
line: Acre is restaurant and delicatessen from famed influencer chef Thomas Straker, joining Straker’s as the chef’s second site in Notting Hill.

name: Briciole
why: An Italian trattoria, café bar and deli under one roof in a quiet corner of Marylebone. Italian staff who know their wines, dishes from all over Italy, and a few tables outside in summer.
line: An Italian trattoria, café bar and deli under one roof in a quiet corner of Marylebone.

name: HG Soho
why:
One of Europes most popular plant based restaurants opened in Soho London. Bringing you Real Food, because a healthy lifestyle is a basic human right. No processing, no preservatives, nothing unnecessary, just Real Food done right.

The restaurant first opened in Barcelona in 2017 and has spread to more European cities since then.
line: One of Europes most popular plant based restaurants opened in Soho London.

name: Chutney Mary
why:
Chutney Mary – a London restaurant institution of over three decades

At the forefront of fine dining Indian restaurants since its opening it has earned innumerable accolades, including twice winning the award of Best Indian Restaurant in UK, and gained a reputation as one of the finest restaurants of its style in the Britain.
line: Chutney Mary – a London restaurant institution of over three decades  At the forefront of fine dining Indian restaurants since its opening it has earned innumerable accolades, including twice winning the award of Best Indian Restaurant in UK, and gained a reputation as one of the finest restaurants of its style in the Britain.

name: Yaatra
why:
From the Sanskrit word yaatra meaning “journey”, comes a dining experience that transcends the ordinary. 

Here, the rich culinary traditions of Northern India are reimagined with elegance and artistry by award-winning Michelin chef Krishnapal Negi, whose creations honour the past while embracing the present.
line: From the Sanskrit word yaatra meaning “journey”, comes a dining experience that transcends the ordinary.
address: Old Westminster Fire Station 4 Greycoat Place London, SW1P 1SB

name: Nobu
why: Europes original Nobu restaurant is located on Old Park Lane. London also is home to Nobu Portman Square located in Nobu Hotel.
line: Europes original Nobu restaurant is located on Old Park Lane.

name: Roka
why: With an exclusive London address, ROKA Mayfair on North Audley Street is fashioned to be a relaxed, yet elegant dining destination located in this sophisticated neighbourhood. Minutes away from the shopping hub of Oxford Street, ROKA brings its unique style of contemporary Japanese robatayaki cuisine and urban flair to Mayfair.
line: With an exclusive London address, ROKA Mayfair on North Audley Street is fashioned to be a relaxed, yet elegant dining destination located in this sophisticated neighbourhood.

name: Roka
why: In 2004 the first ROKA opened its doors on Charlotte Street, London with a flaming robata grill at its heart, and a striking yet informal interior that reflects the strength and energy of fire. Welcome to ROKA's distinctive, sensory environment designed to wrap each diner in a comfortable cocoon of warmth, welcome and hospitality.
line: In 2004 the first ROKA opened its doors on Charlotte Street, London with a flaming robata grill at its heart, and a striking yet informal interior that reflects the strength and energy of fire.

name: Scott's
why:
Serving exceptional British seafood since 1851. Perfectly situated on Mayfair’s Mount Street, Scott’s menu reflects its glittering heritage, serving the finest traditional British fish and shellfish dishes alongside a variety of seasonal favourites.
As of May 2025, children under six are only permitted at lunch time on Saturday and Sunday, bank holidays and school breaks.
line: Serving exceptional British seafood since 1851.

name: Noodle Inn
why: Hand-pulled biang biang noodles from north-west China, made in an open kitchen you can watch from the queue. No bookings and there will be a queue, but it moves and it's worth it.
line: Hand-pulled biang biang noodles from north-west China, made in an open kitchen you can watch from the queue.

name: Kung Fu Burger
why:
No seating or reservations
 A Viral sensation — Inspired by the street food phenomenon across the ESEA region, Chinese burger concept Kung Fu Burger’s menu is centred around a sourdough Chinese-style bun and a variety of fillings, from shredded pork belly – the most popular version – to chicken, or vegetables.

name: Din Tai Fung
why:
Mr Bing-Yi Yang, the founder of Din Tai Fung, was born in 1927 in China’s Shanxi Province. He moved to Taiwan at a young age in search of better prospects.
Unlike traditional restaurants, Din Tai Fung’s approach is that of an artist.

From food preparation to service, all aspects are held to strict standards, in order to redefine Chinese cuisine, allowing customers not simply a taste of fine dining, but a taste of…
line: Mr Bing-Yi Yang, the founder of Din Tai Fung, was born in 1927 in China’s Shanxi Province.

name: Sael
why: Jason Atherton's tribute to British food in St James's – proper British cooking from a Michelin-starred chef, and a strong choice for Sunday roast in the West End.
line: Jason Atherton's tribute to British food in St James's – proper British cooking from a Michelin-starred chef, and a strong choice for Sunday roast in the West End.

name: Napoli on the Road NOTR
why:
Napoli on the Road has gained international acclaim. The pizzeria was named Europe’s No.1 Pizzeria 2024 and 2025 (making it the top in the UK) and World’s 5th Best Pizzeria 2025 by the prestigious 50 Top Pizza Awards, the leading global guide for pizzerias.

Michele was named Best Pizza Maker in the World in 2023, and his signature pizza ‘Ricordi d’Infanzia’ won Best Pizza in the World in 2025.

name: Ambassadors Clubhouse
why: The UK's first Punjabi restaurant to win a Michelin star, inspired by the party mansions of Dalhousie. Big flavours, generous plates and a lively crowd, just off Regent Street.
line: The UK's first Punjabi restaurant to win a Michelin star, inspired by the party mansions of Dalhousie.

name: Crust Brothers
why: Started as a street-food van after a road trip round Italy, now serving Neapolitan pizza in Covent Garden. Light, blistered crusts and a relaxed spot before or after the theatre.
line: Started as a street-food van after a road trip round Italy, now serving Neapolitan pizza in Covent Garden.

name: Cinquecento Chelsea
why: Two friends from Naples, an old family dough recipe and Italian D.O.P. ingredients. One of Chelsea's best neighbourhood pizzerias, tucked away off the King's Road.
line: Two friends from Naples, an old family dough recipe and Italian D.O.P.

name: Sarastro
why: Named after a character in Mozart's Magic Flute and open since 1996, it's a theatrical, over-the-top dining room in theatreland, with Mediterranean food with a Turkish twist and live music nights. Known as "the show after the show."
line: Named after a character in Mozart's Magic Flute and open since 1996, it's a theatrical, over-the-top dining room in theatreland, with Mediterranean food with a Turkish twist and live music nights.

name: Le Cafe
why:
Where french tradition meets bold creativity
Each creation blends emotion, precision, and artistry, from the signature brioche, a reimagined childhood classic, to drinks crafted like desserts, turning every sip into an experience.

Nicolas Rouzaud is a celebrated pâtissier originally from France, known for his exquisite fruit-driven creations and his signature patisserie at The Connaught in London’s Mayfair.
line: Where french tradition meets bold creativity Each creation blends emotion, precision, and artistry, from the signature brioche, a reimagined childhood classic, to drinks crafted like desserts, turning every sip into an experience.

name: Legado
why:
A contemporary Spanish restaurant by Chef Nieves Barragán Mohacho.

Moving beyond the familiar, Legado celebrates the diverse regional food cultures of Spain and its islands, allowing the lesser-known to take centre stage.
People suggest to try the suckling pig and skate wing tortilla.

line: The menu pays homage to beloved British dishes and home to arguably the most expensive fish and chips in London.

name: Helene Darroze at The Connaught
why: Three Michelin stars inside The Connaught hotel. Your menu is built around the ingredients you choose, and the produce comes from farmers and growers Hélène Darroze picks herself. One for a very special occasion.
line: Three Michelin stars inside The Connaught hotel.
address: The Connaught Hotel Carlos Place, Mayfair

name: Restaurant Gordon Ramsay
why: Gordon Ramsay's first restaurant, opened in 1998 and holding three Michelin stars since 2001. Modern French cooking and faultless service in a small, quiet Chelsea dining room.
line: Gordon Ramsay's first restaurant, opened in 1998 and holding three Michelin stars since 2001.

name: Sketch - Lecture Room and Library
why: The website link below contains details from the Michelin Guide and press reports.
line: The website link below contains details from the Michelin Guide and press reports.

name: The Ledbury
why:
The Ledbury is located the heart of Notting Hill.

Since opening in 2005, it has become one of London's more established restaurants, gaining 3 Michelin stars in 2024.

The restaurant prides itself on showcasing seasonal ingredients along with their own Deer, Jersey Cows and Iberian Pigs which are reared by Chef/Owner Brett Graham.
line: The Ledbury is located the heart of Notting Hill.

name: Mayfair Chippy
why: Fish and chips done properly, in a smart take on a classic chippy – chequered floor, booths and all. Since 2015 it's been a favourite with locals and visitors who want the British classic without leaving Mayfair.
line: Fish and chips done properly, in a smart take on a classic chippy – chequered floor, booths and all.

name: Mayfair Chippy Knightsbridge
why: The Mayfair Chippy's Knightsbridge branch: fish and chips and other British classics all day, plus a gin bar and tables outside.
line: The Mayfair Chippy's Knightsbridge branch: fish and chips and other British classics all day, plus a gin bar and tables outside.

name: The Golden Hind Fish and Chips
why: A Marylebone chippy that has been frying for 100 years. Proper, no-fuss fish and chips in a warm, old-fashioned room.
line: A Marylebone chippy that has been frying for 100 years.

name: Rock and Sole Plaice Fish and Chips
why: London's oldest fish and chip shop, frying since 1871 in the middle of Covent Garden. Sustainable British fish, two cosy floors, and tables outside on summer evenings.
line: London's oldest fish and chip shop, frying since 1871 in the middle of Covent Garden.

name: Poppies Fish and Chips Soho
why: Proper fish and chips in the heart of Soho, in a fun retro setting with a 1950s feel. A perfect after-theatre stop.
line: Proper fish and chips in the heart of Soho, in a fun retro setting with a 1950s feel.

name: Poppies Fish and Chips Notting Hill
why: Fish and chips on Portobello Road in a fun retro dining room. Open seven days a week from lunch until late, and an ideal pit stop on a market day.
line: Fish and chips on Portobello Road in a fun retro dining room.

name: Seashell of Lisson Grove
why: One of London's best-loved chippies, near Marylebone station. Fish delivered fresh every morning and never frozen, hand-prepared fillets, generous portions and chips made from British potatoes.
line: One of London's best-loved chippies, near Marylebone station.

name: Golden Union Fish and Chips
why: A friendly Soho chippy serving real British comfort food since 2008. Fish cooked to order, responsibly sourced, and good value for the West End.
line: A friendly Soho chippy serving real British comfort food since 2008.

name: Claridge's
why:
The story of Afternoon Tea at Claridge’s begins more than 120 years ago. A tradition rewritten, today each element has its own tale to tell, from the beautifully designed jade teacups to the Foyer & Reading Room that sets the scene.

For a contemporary twist, opt for Thibault Hauchard at The Painter's Room - where cocktails and painterly courses combine amidst Annie Morris artworks and plush pink marble decor.
line: The story of Afternoon Tea at Claridge’s begins more than 120 years ago.

name: The Ritz
why: The most famous afternoon tea in London, in the gilded Palm Court of The Ritz. Finger sandwiches, warm scones with Cornish clotted cream, beautiful pastries, 20 loose-leaf teas and champagne if you like. Dress smartly and book well ahead.
line: The most famous afternoon tea in London, in the gilded Palm Court of The Ritz.

name: Fortnum & Mason
why: Afternoon tea in the Diamond Jubilee Tea Salon on Fortnum's fourth floor, reopened by Queen Elizabeth II in 2012. Teas have been served here for around 100 years. Coronation chicken sandwiches, scones and Fortnum's own teas. Classic and very British.
line: Afternoon tea in the Diamond Jubilee Tea Salon on Fortnum's fourth floor, reopened by Queen Elizabeth II in 2012.

name: The Lanesborough
why: An elegant afternoon tea in the grand Regency dining room of The Lanesborough at Hyde Park Corner, with beautiful cakes from the hotel's pastry team. One for a real treat.
line: An elegant afternoon tea in the grand Regency dining room of The Lanesborough at Hyde Park Corner, with beautiful cakes from the hotel's pastry team.
address: The Lanesborough Hyde Park Corner, London, SW1X 7TA, United Kingdom

name: The Savoy
why: When one thinks of afternoon tea in London, the first place that springs to mind is, of course, The Savoy. Opened in 1889 by Richard D’Oyly Carte, it was Britain’s first purpose-built luxury hotel and has a timeless appeal that has endured for generations. As you enter the Gallery, the hotel’s newer dining destination, you’re welcomed into a vast, peach-hued space that instantly transports you to another era.
line: When one thinks of afternoon tea in London, the first place that springs to mind is, of course, The Savoy.

name: Ham Yard Hotel
why: Stepping into Ham Yard is always a cloud-lifting experience. The playfully designed hotel and its orangery – all glass ceiling and huge windows – is a light-drenched oasis in the middle of Soho and an excellent spot for one of the more creative afternoon teas in town. Ham Yard’s trademark quirkiness carries through in its patisserie options.
line: Stepping into Ham Yard is always a cloud-lifting experience.

name: Dalloway Terrace
why: Afternoon tea in a pretty, plant-filled garden terrace at the Bloomsbury Hotel, inspired by Virginia Woolf's Mrs Dalloway. Covered and heated, so it works all year. A short walk from the British Museum.
line: Afternoon tea in a pretty, plant-filled garden terrace at the Bloomsbury Hotel, inspired by Virginia Woolf's Mrs Dalloway.

name: The Dorchester
why: Afternoon tea at The Dorchester's Promenade on Park Lane: silk drapes, velvet sofas and marble columns, with a crowd of celebrities and visitors from all over the world. Old-school luxury at its best.
line: Afternoon tea at The Dorchester's Promenade on Park Lane: silk drapes, velvet sofas and marble columns, with a crowd of celebrities and visitors from all over the world.

name: The Langham
why: Afternoon tea at The Langham, the hotel that claims to have started the tradition in the 1860s. A Victorian-inspired menu with a modern twist, served with champagne in the Palm Court.
line: Afternoon tea at The Langham, the hotel that claims to have started the tradition in the 1860s.

name: Raffles at the OWO
why: This unique afternoon tea pays homage to the secret history and the characters associated with the former Old War Office – today known as The OWO and home to Raffles London. The building played its part in the evolution of the Military Intelligence Service into its modern form of MI5 and MI6. 20th century spies were briefed here.
line: This unique afternoon tea pays homage to the secret history and the characters associated with the former Old War Office – today known as The OWO and home to Raffles London.

name: The Connaught
why: A playful, modern afternoon tea from Jean-Georges at The Connaught in Mayfair, with a few surprises along the way. A lighter, more contemporary take on the classic.
line: A playful, modern afternoon tea from Jean-Georges at The Connaught in Mayfair, with a few surprises along the way.

name: The Goring
why: The Goring’s Veranda certainly stakes a claim as London’s most elegant setting for afternoon tea. In the hotel and through the glitzy lounge, where plush banquettes and armchairs await for post-indulgence cocktails if you wish, lies one of two sprawling dining spaces – the other being the Dining Room, where afternoon tea can be taken on Saturdays.
line: The Goring’s Veranda certainly stakes a claim as London’s most elegant setting for afternoon tea.

name: The Stafford
why: Afternoon tea at The Stafford, a hidden-away hotel in St James's, from Michelin-starred chef Michael Caines. Classic and beautifully made, in a quiet, refined lounge.
line: Afternoon tea at The Stafford, a hidden-away hotel in St James's, from Michelin-starred chef Michael Caines.

name: Scalini
why:
Established in 1988, welcome to Scalini, the beloved Italian neighbourhood restaurant in the heart of Chelsea, London, known for its tradition, quality and warm hospitality for over
thirty-five years.
With an extensive seasonal menu packed with regional favourites and Scalini classics, experience memorable, authentic Italian dining
Tuesday to Sunday.

Now with locations in Dubai, Doha, Cannes, Istanbul, Bahrain and…
line: Established in 1988, welcome to Scalini, the beloved Italian neighbourhood restaurant in the heart of Chelsea, London, known for its tradition, quality and warm hospitality for over thirty-five years.

name: Amaya
why:
Amaya - Finest Indian Restaurant - Knightsbridge, London

Amaya, opened where fashionable Knightsbridge meets elegant Belgravia, in 2004 to wide acclaim.
line: Amaya - Finest Indian Restaurant - Knightsbridge, London  Amaya, opened where fashionable Knightsbridge meets elegant Belgravia, in 2004 to wide acclaim.

name: Joia
why:
Located in the Artotel in Battersea Power Station. 

JOIA showcases Henrique Sá Pessoa’s culinary heritage and is influenced by the robust flavours and cooking techniques of Catalonia and Portugal, using the best of British and Iberian produce offering guests a taste of the Mediterranean in the heart of Battersea, London.
line: Located in the Artotel in Battersea Power Station.

name: Hutong at the Shard
why:
Hutong's cuisine takes its inspiration from the dishes served in the imperial palaces of what was then Peking. Based on the “Lu school” cuisine of Shandong Province, the menu artfully captures the subtlety and surprises of Northern Chinese cooking.

A cocktail selection inspired by ingredients used in traditional Chinese medicine, and a stunning traditional Chinese interior with red lanterns and beautiful…
line: Hutong's cuisine takes its inspiration from the dishes served in the imperial palaces of what was then Peking.

name: Ting at the Shard
why: A restaurant and lounge on the 35th floor of The Shard, in the Shangri-La hotel, with Asian-inspired dishes and huge views. Good for afternoon tea too.
line: A restaurant and lounge on the 35th floor of The Shard, in the Shangri-La hotel, with Asian-inspired dishes and huge views.

name: Bleeker Burger
why: Started by a New York corporate lawyer who quit to make the burger he'd fallen for in the East Village. Simple, juicy, properly made burgers that regularly top London's best-burger lists. Several branches around town.
line: Started by a New York corporate lawyer who quit to make the burger he'd fallen for in the East Village.

name: Meatstop
why: Burgers done properly in Shoreditch, inside The Commercial Tavern: dry-aged Essex beef ground fresh, custom brioche buns and a short, tight menu. Simple food, big flavour.
line: Burgers done properly in Shoreditch, inside The Commercial Tavern: dry-aged Essex beef ground fresh, custom brioche buns and a short, tight menu.
address: The Commercial Tavern 142 Commercial St, London E1 6NU

name: Burger and Beyond Soho
why: One of London's top burger spots, on Old Compton Street in Soho: classic burgers taken seriously, with fine-dining care over every detail. Great sides too.
line: One of London's top burger spots, on Old Compton Street in Soho: classic burgers taken seriously, with fine-dining care over every detail.

name: Burger and Beyond Shoreditch
why: The Shoreditch branch of one of London's top burger spots: classic burgers taken seriously, with fine-dining care over every detail. Great sides and a lively East London crowd.
line: The Shoreditch branch of one of London's top burger spots: classic burgers taken seriously, with fine-dining care over every detail.

name: Supernova Burger Soho
why:
Why the Supernova London burger is so good

Both burgers arrive wrapped and satisfyingly heavy. Each one is built around two smashed patties made from a blend of dry-aged British beef. The patties are smashed aggressively enough that the edges become thin and lacy, almost crisp, while the centre stays juicy and rich.

This is where the Supernova burger in London really shines.
line: Why the Supernova London burger is so good  Both burgers arrive wrapped and satisfyingly heavy.

name: Dishoom Carnaby
why:
what a terrific trip! In the ‘60s, young Indians started hankering after Western styles. ‘Beat’ bands in Bombay belted out versions of the latest rock’n’roll hits. A whirlwind of excitement shook both London and Bombay.
Dishoom Carnaby – and its accompanying vinyl ‘Slip Disc’ – shares this little-known intersection of time, place and culture. There is a separate gluten-free menu.
line: In the ‘60s, young Indians started hankering after Western styles.

name: Dishoom Kensington
why: Art deco extravagance and quick tempo’d Jazz roared through the city in 1940s Bombay. Swarms of high society were pulled in by sell-out bands, “hot” new music spilled out onto the street. Inside Dishoom Kensington, the golden age of Bombay Jazz is both remembered and reimagined. In the voluptuous curves and chandeliers. In the glitz, glimmer and shine. All are welcome. There is a separate gluten-free menu.
line: Art deco extravagance and quick tempo’d Jazz roared through the city in 1940s Bombay.

name: Dishoom Covent Garden
why:
Early silver screen talkies brought an intoxicating world of adventure and liberty to Bombay. Thrilling “all talking, singing, dancing” Indian-made dramas cast a glamorous spell over picture houses, and over the city.
The thrill and amazement of the Talkies era is captured within ‘New’ Dishoom Covent Garden. Open all day, every day, serving Bombay comfort food for breakfast, lunch, dinner and evening tipples. There is a separate gluten-free menu.
line: Early silver screen talkies brought an intoxicating world of adventure and liberty to Bombay.

name: Ave Mario
why: Big Mamma's wildest London trattoria, in Covent Garden: six-metre ceilings, a bar lined with 3,500 bottles and a retro 80s room downstairs. Homemade Italian food, and plenty of theatre.
line: Big Mamma's wildest London trattoria, in Covent Garden: six-metre ceilings, a bar lined with 3,500 bottles and a retro 80s room downstairs.

name: The Barbery Covent Garden
why:
Located in the iconic Neal’s Yard in Covent Garden, the restaurant takes inspiration from the Barbary Coast, identified by 16th century Europeans as the area settled by the Berbers in the Atlas Mountains, with dishes served across lunch and dinner at the counter.

The Barbary tells a story of trade, travel and culture – people voyaging along the coast, collecting and sharing ingredients and recipes, gathering…
line: Located in the iconic Neal’s Yard in Covent Garden, the restaurant takes inspiration from the Barbary Coast, identified by 16th century Europeans as the area settled by the Berbers in the Atlas Mountains, with dishes served across lunch and dinner at the counter.

name: Slayer NY Pizzeria
why: Proper crunchy New York-style pizza in Notting Hill, made with Italian flour, meats and cheeses. Grab a slice from the shop, or sit down in the restaurant.
line: Proper crunchy New York-style pizza in Notting Hill, made with Italian flour, meats and cheeses.
address: 226 Westbourne Grove Notting Hill London W11 2RH

name: Fonda
why:
Contemporary Mexican inspired by the traditional fonda – a family-owned eatery – along with the vibrant cooking and colours of Mexican markets and homes.
Fonda serves regional Mexican classics through Chef Patron Santiago Lastra’s lens, focussing on British ingredients, creative preparation, and modern techniques.

Fonda is the second restaurant from Chef Santiago Lastra following the critically acclaimed KOL.
Born…
line: Contemporary Mexican inspired by the traditional fonda – a family-owned eatery – along with the vibrant cooking and colours of Mexican markets and homes.
address: 12 Heddon Street, London, United Kingdom W1B 4BZ

name: Kutir
why: An elegant Chelsea townhouse restaurant from chef Rohit Ghai. Refined Indian cooking inspired by India's heritage and wildlife: special-occasion food in a calm, intimate setting.
line: An elegant Chelsea townhouse restaurant from chef Rohit Ghai.

name: Blacklock City
why: A modern chophouse in the City: chops and steaks cooked over charcoal, great value, and one of the best Sunday roasts in London. Book ahead for Sundays.
line: A modern chophouse in the City: chops and steaks cooked over charcoal, great value, and one of the best Sunday roasts in London.

name: Blacklock Covent Garden
why: A modern chophouse in Covent Garden: chops and steaks cooked over charcoal, great value, and one of the best Sunday roasts in London. Book ahead for Sundays.
line: A modern chophouse in Covent Garden: chops and steaks cooked over charcoal, great value, and one of the best Sunday roasts in London.

name: Blacklock Soho
why: The original Blacklock, in a basement in Soho: chops and steaks cooked over charcoal, great value, and one of the best Sunday roasts in London. Book ahead for Sundays.
line: The original Blacklock, in a basement in Soho: chops and steaks cooked over charcoal, great value, and one of the best Sunday roasts in London.

name: Smith & Wollensky
why: The New York steakhouse's first restaurant outside the US, in the grand art deco Adelphi Building off the Strand. Classic American steaks and a big, buzzy dining room. The name was picked at random from a phone book!
line: The New York steakhouse's first restaurant outside the US, in the grand art deco Adelphi Building off the Strand.
address: The Adelphi Building John Adam Street

name: Schnitzel Heaven
why: Crispy hand-breaded schnitzels (chicken, veal or veggie), fried golden and served with fresh lemon. A simple idea, done really well, in Hoxton.
line: Crispy hand-breaded schnitzels (chicken, veal or veggie), fried golden and served with fresh lemon.

name: Chelsea Grill
why: A neighbourhood grill on the King's Road, built around fire and smoke: meat, fish and seafood butchered, aged and grilled in-house, made for sharing, with a good wine list.
line: A neighbourhood grill on the King's Road, built around fire and smoke: meat, fish and seafood butchered, aged and grilled in-house, made for sharing, with a good wine list.

name: Shoryu Ramen Soho
why: Rich, creamy Hakata tonkotsu ramen with thin, straight noodles, the Fukuoka style, created by a chef born and raised there. Just off Piccadilly Circus, and good for a quick, warming bowl.
line: Rich, creamy Hakata tonkotsu ramen with thin, straight noodles, the Fukuoka style, created by a chef born and raised there.

name: Shoryu Ramen Covent Garden
why: Rich, creamy Hakata tonkotsu ramen with thin, straight noodles, the Fukuoka style, created by a chef born and raised there. By Covent Garden and handy before or after a show. A quick, warming bowl.
line: Rich, creamy Hakata tonkotsu ramen with thin, straight noodles, the Fukuoka style, created by a chef born and raised there.

name: Ramo Ramen
why: Japanese ramen meets Filipino flavours in Soho: inventive bowls you won't find anywhere else, with no frills. Just good noodles.
line: Japanese ramen meets Filipino flavours in Soho: inventive bowls you won't find anywhere else, with no frills.

name: Kinoya, Harrods Food Hall
why: A ramen counter inside Harrods Food Hall: a bowl of noodles at the bar when you need a break from shopping in Knightsbridge.
line: A ramen counter inside Harrods Food Hall: a bowl of noodles at the bar when you need a break from shopping in Knightsbridge.

name: Tenmaru
why: A popular Japanese spot near Oxford Circus, known for authentic and creative cooking. The original is in Finsbury Park. Walk-ins only, so expect a short wait at busy times.
line: A popular Japanese spot near Oxford Circus, known for authentic and creative cooking.

name: Lucky Cat Mayfair
why: Gordon Ramsay's Asian restaurant and bar on Grosvenor Square, styled on the drinking dens of 1930s Tokyo. Dark, buzzy and good for a late dinner with cocktails.
line: Gordon Ramsay's Asian restaurant and bar on Grosvenor Square, styled on the drinking dens of 1930s Tokyo.

name: Lucky Cat Bishopsgate
why: Gordon Ramsay's Lucky Cat near the top of 22 Bishopsgate, the City's tallest tower, billed as London's highest restaurant. Asian small plates and cocktails with the whole of London laid out below you. Book a window table.
line: Gordon Ramsay's Lucky Cat near the top of 22 Bishopsgate, the City's tallest tower, billed as London's highest restaurant.

name: Spring Street Pizza
why: New York-style 18-inch pizzas under a railway arch in Southwark, led by Michelin-starred chef Tom Kemble. House-made dough, great toppings and a fun, lively room.
line: New York-style 18-inch pizzas under a railway arch in Southwark, led by Michelin-starred chef Tom Kemble.
address: Arch 32 The Lowline, Southwark, London, SE11 TE

name: Trishna
why: Located in the heart of London’s Marylebone Village, Trishna delivers a contemporary taste of Indian coastal cuisine, and an extensive wine list that focuses on emerging regions and fine wines from niche producers and boutique wineries from all over the world.
line: Located in the heart of London’s Marylebone Village, Trishna delivers a contemporary taste of Indian coastal cuisine, and an extensive wine list that focuses on emerging regions and fine wines from niche producers and boutique wineries from all over the world.
address: 15-17 Blandford Street Marylebone Village London W1U 3DG

name: The Ninth
why: A Michelin-starred neighbourhood restaurant on Charlotte Street, holding its star for ten years running. Mediterranean-inspired seasonal cooking, and the set lunch is one of the best-value Michelin meals in town.
line: A Michelin-starred neighbourhood restaurant on Charlotte Street, holding its star for ten years running.

name: Dim Sum Library
why: Hong Kong-style dim sum in Covent Garden, made in front of you at the open counter: wagyu beef puffs, black truffle har gau and xiaolongbao, plus clever tea-based cocktails.
line: Hong Kong-style dim sum in Covent Garden, made in front of you at the open counter: wagyu beef puffs, black truffle har gau and xiaolongbao, plus clever tea-based cocktails.

name: Anglo Thai
why: A Michelin-starred restaurant from husband and wife John and Desiree Chantarasak, cooking Thai recipes with the best seasonal British produce. Bold, balanced and unlike any other Thai restaurant in London.
line: A Michelin-starred restaurant from husband and wife John and Desiree Chantarasak, cooking Thai recipes with the best seasonal British produce.

name: Swiss Butter
why: A friendly neighbourhood steakhouse on Southampton Row, near Russell Square: good steaks without the West End fuss or prices.
line: A friendly neighbourhood steakhouse on Southampton Row, near Russell Square: good steaks without the West End fuss or prices.

name: Hakkasan
why: The Mayfair branch of the famous modern Cantonese restaurant: dramatic, dark interiors, excellent dim sum and cocktails. Popular for its weekend brunch.
line: The Mayfair branch of the famous modern Cantonese restaurant: dramatic, dark interiors, excellent dim sum and cocktails.

name: Fallow
why: A busy, sustainability-minded British restaurant on St James's Market, near Piccadilly Circus, using whole animals and seasonal produce. Its corn ribs and mushroom parfait have a cult following.
line: A busy, sustainability-minded British restaurant on St James's Market, near Piccadilly Circus.

name: Bolo by Gennaro
why:
Some people may recognise Gennaro from Jamie Oliver books and programmes or various TV cooking shows. 

Named after the Bolognese that made him famous, BOLO brings Gennaro Contaldo’s larger-than-life spirit to an intimate 32-seat trattoria in Piccadilly. 

The menu speaks for itself. It’s built around Bolognese, including Gennaro’s famous original as well as some very, very delicious twists. Oh my my!
line: Some people may recognise Gennaro from Jamie Oliver books and programmes or various TV cooking shows.

name: Darjeeling Express
why: Asma Khan's restaurant, made famous by Netflix's *Chef's Table*, with an all-women kitchen cooking home-style Indian food inspired by family matriarchs. Full of heart, and full of flavour.
line: Asma Khan's restaurant, made famous by Netflix's *Chef's Table*, with an all-women kitchen cooking home-style Indian food inspired by family matriarchs.

name: Heard Burger Soho
why:
Heard. was born out of Jordan Bailey ’s desire turn an everyday comfort food into something exceptional.

Jordan uses his expertise and relationships with top suppliers to make burgers that are deceptively simple yet made with the same care and precision as a Michelin-starred dish.

Heard. isn’t just a burger, 
it’s a new standard.
line: was born out of Jordan Bailey ’s desire turn an everyday comfort food into something exceptional.

name: KOL
why: Santiago Lastra's Michelin-starred Mexican restaurant in Marylebone, cooking Mexican flavours with British ingredients. A tasting menu like nothing else in London, and a brilliant mezcal bar downstairs.
line: Santiago Lastra's Michelin-starred Mexican restaurant in Marylebone, cooking Mexican flavours with British ingredients.

name: 26 Grains
why: An ongoing story  of community, food,  & connection. A place where quality  ingredients & genuine  experiences meet.
line: An ongoing story  of community, food,  & connection.

name: Willett’s
why: A smart, relaxed bistro in the Cadogan hotel on Sloane Street, where Belgravia, Knightsbridge and Chelsea meet. Seasonal British produce and daily specials, cooked in the spirit of a classic bistro.
line: A smart, relaxed bistro in the Cadogan hotel on Sloane Street, where Belgravia, Knightsbridge and Chelsea meet.

name: Bar Finch
why: New in 2026 from film producer Charles Finch, the man behind Chuc's: a Roman-style all-day bar and restaurant on Mayfair's art gallery street. Pasta-led Mediterranean cooking, forgotten-classic cocktails, and a regular crowd of actors and artists. Phones are discouraged, which is half the charm.
line: New in 2026 from film producer Charles Finch, the man behind Chuc's: a Roman-style all-day bar and restaurant on Mayfair's art gallery street.

name: Westfield Shopping Centre White City
why: A Westfield shopping is more than a mall - it's a dynamic entertainment destination where you can eat, shop and play in some of the most iconic cities
line: A Westfield shopping is more than a mall - it's a dynamic entertainment destination where you can eat, shop and play in some of the most iconic cities

name: Westfield Shopping Centre Stratford
why: One of Europe's biggest shopping centres, next to the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park at Stratford, with hundreds of shops, restaurants and a cinema.
line: One of Europe's biggest shopping centres, next to the Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park at Stratford, with hundreds of shops, restaurants and a cinema.

name: Harrods
why: Harrods is a luxury department store on Brompton Road in Knightsbridge, London, England. The building was designed by C. W. Stephens for Charles Digby Harrod, and opened in 1905; it replaced the first store on the grounds founded by his father Charles Henry Harrod in 1849, which burned down in 1881.
line: Harrods is a luxury department store on Brompton Road in Knightsbridge, London, England.

name: Hamleys Toy Shop
why: Head to Hamleys, London, for seven floors of toys, games, crafts and fun. It's London's oldest and largest toy shop, having been founded in 1760.
line: Head to Hamleys, London, for seven floors of toys, games, crafts and fun.

name: Selfridges
why: Voted the best department store in the world, Selfridges has all the latest designer collections, must-have toys & gifts for all the family.
line: Voted the best department store in the world, Selfridges has all the latest designer collections, must-have toys & gifts for all the family.

name: Spitalfields Market
why: East London's best-known market, under a Victorian roof by Liverpool Street: independent fashion, art, vintage, records and a big run of street-food stalls. Best from Thursday to Sunday.
line: East London's best-known market, under a Victorian roof by Liverpool Street: independent fashion, art, vintage, records and a big run of street-food stalls.

name: Raffles Spa Whitehall
why: A four-floor Guerlain spa inside Raffles London at The OWO, the restored Old War Office on Whitehall. Treatments, fitness and nutrition all in one, in a building once used by Churchill.
line: A four-floor Guerlain spa inside Raffles London at The OWO, the restored Old War Office on Whitehall.

name: Agua - Sea Containers Hotel
why: A calm, design-led spa in the Sea Containers hotel on the South Bank, offering personalised treatments and a new wellness studio. A good reset after a day of sightseeing.
line: A calm, design-led spa in the Sea Containers hotel on the South Bank, offering personalised treatments and a new wellness studio.

name: Biome by Corinthia London
why: Corinthia London's spa and wellbeing space just off Whitehall, offering tailored treatments for body and mind in a calm, natural setting. One of London's most luxurious spas.
line: Corinthia London's spa and wellbeing space just off Whitehall, offering tailored treatments for body and mind in a calm, natural setting.

name: Aire Ancient Baths
why:
In the modern, eclectic, and forever emblematic city of London, minutes away from Covent Garden, you will find an oasis, seamlessly intertwined with its enticing energy, comprising a touristic and local public.

An environment constructed right in Westminster, a worldwide recognised area, especially known for its cultural patrimony and its architectural milestones, landmarks, and overall history.
line: In the modern, eclectic, and forever emblematic city of London, minutes away from Covent Garden, you will find an oasis, seamlessly intertwined with its enticing energy, comprising a touristic and local public.

name: Hawksmoor Seven Dials
why: One of London's most famous Sunday roasts: dry-aged rump of beef with all the trimmings, or a big sharing cut from the blackboard. A proper steakhouse with an old-warehouse feel, tucked behind Covent Garden.
line: One of London's most famous Sunday roasts: dry-aged rump of beef with all the trimmings, or a big sharing cut from the blackboard.

name: Roast
why: A restaurant built around the roast, in the glass Floral Hall above Borough Market. Pork belly is the house favourite, with views over the market stalls below. A good way to finish a morning at the market.
line: A restaurant built around the roast, in the glass Floral Hall above Borough Market.
address: The Floral Hall, Stoney Street, London SE1 1TL

name: Temper Soho
why: A fire-cooking restaurant whose Sunday 'Three Beast Feast' brings beef, pork and smoked lamb shoulder to share. Big flavours, and a lively basement room in the middle of Soho.
line: A fire-cooking restaurant whose Sunday 'Three Beast Feast' brings beef, pork and smoked lamb shoulder to share.

name: Cora Pearl
why: A small, elegant Covent Garden dining room named after a famous Victorian courtesan. Roast sirloin of Highland beef with horseradish cream on Sundays, and a lovely spot before a matinee.
line: A small, elegant Covent Garden dining room named after a famous Victorian courtesan.

name: The Libertine
why: Sunday roast in a former bank vault beneath the Royal Exchange: dry-aged sirloin under vaulted brick ceilings. The City is quiet on a Sunday, which makes it all the more of a find.
line: Sunday roast in a former bank vault beneath the Royal Exchange: dry-aged sirloin under vaulted brick ceilings.
address: The Royal Exchange, Cornhill, London EC3V 3LR

name: The Jugged Hare
why: A handsome game-focused pub by the Barbican, known for its meat. On Sundays choose beef, pork belly, lamb or rotisserie chicken with all the trimmings.
line: A handsome game-focused pub by the Barbican, known for its meat.

name: The Harwood Arms
why: The Michelin-starred pub in Fulham, famous for its game and its venison Scotch egg. Sunday lunch is a set three-course menu and a real treat. Book well ahead.
line: The Michelin-starred pub in Fulham, famous for its game and its venison Scotch egg.

name: The Cleveland Arms
why: A friendly neighbourhood pub a few minutes from Paddington station, known for its trio-of-meats roast and giant Yorkshire puddings. Handy if you're arriving by train from the west.
line: A friendly neighbourhood pub a few minutes from Paddington station, known for its trio-of-meats roast and giant Yorkshire puddings.

name: Holly Bush
why: A tiny 18th-century pub hidden up a lane in Hampstead village, all low ceilings and open fires. Slow-braised lamb shoulder on Sundays, and perfect after a walk on the Heath.
line: A tiny 18th-century pub hidden up a lane in Hampstead village, all low ceilings and open fires.

name: The Good Oak
why: A relaxed Notting Hill pub with one of London's best vegetarian roasts (a celeriac 'steak'), alongside the classic meat roasts. A good pick when your group doesn't all eat meat.
line: A relaxed Notting Hill pub with one of London's best vegetarian roasts (a celeriac 'steak'), alongside the classic meat roasts.

name: Marksman
why: A Victorian East End pub turned award-winning dining room. Sundays are a three-course seasonal menu, and it's one of the most talked-about roasts in London.
line: A Victorian East End pub turned award-winning dining room.

name: Padella
why: The original home of London's favourite fresh pasta, by Borough Market: pici cacio e pepe and pappardelle with beef shin ragu, made by hand every day. Great value. Expect a queue, but it moves.
line: The original home of London's favourite fresh pasta, by Borough Market: pici cacio e pepe and pappardelle with beef shin ragu, made by hand every day.

name: OMA
why: Michelin-starred Greek sharing plates, including clay-pot stews, in the heart of Borough Market. Downstairs, its sister AGORA is a more casual souvlaki bar.
line: Michelin-starred Greek sharing plates, including clay-pot stews, in the heart of Borough Market.

name: Kolae
why: Zingy Thai sharing plates cooked over charcoal, a few steps from Borough Market. Lots for vegetarians, and the set menu is good value.
line: Zingy Thai sharing plates cooked over charcoal, a few steps from Borough Market.

name: Rambutan
why: Sri Lankan cooking with a focus on the north of the island: curries and cashew-chilli chicken wings, in a small, busy room on Stoney Street. Book ahead.
line: Sri Lankan cooking with a focus on the north of the island: curries and cashew-chilli chicken wings, in a small, busy room on Stoney Street.

name: The Anchor & Hope
why: The pub that helped start London's gastropub boom: a changing menu of hearty European cooking on The Cut, near the Old Vic and Young Vic theatres. A favourite with locals and theatre-goers. Sunday lunch is big sharing dishes – a suckling pig leg or slow-cooked lamb – in one sitting; book well ahead.
line: The pub that helped start London's gastropub boom: a changing menu of hearty European cooking on The Cut, near the Old Vic and Young Vic theatres.

name: Lasdun
why: A restaurant inside the National Theatre from the Marksman team, with modern British cooking in a classic 1970s setting. Ideal before a show, and save room for the brown butter and honey custard tart.
line: A restaurant inside the National Theatre from the Marksman team, with modern British cooking in a classic 1970s setting.
address: National Theatre, Upper Ground, London SE1 9PX

name: Dishoom King's Cross
why: Dishoom in a huge old railway goods warehouse off Granary Square. Bombay café classics, the famous black dal and the bacon naan roll at breakfast. Handy before a train from King's Cross. There is a separate gluten-free menu.
line: Dishoom in a huge old railway goods warehouse off Granary Square.
address: 5 Stable Street, Granary Square, London N1C 4AB

name: Barrafina King's Cross
why: Spanish tapas cooked in front of you at a marble counter, upstairs in Coal Drops Yard. Sit at the bar and watch the chefs at work.
line: Spanish tapas cooked in front of you at a marble counter, upstairs in Coal Drops Yard.

name: Caravan King's Cross
why: All-day dining and one of London's best brunches, in a converted Victorian grain store on Granary Square. Roasts its own coffee too.
line: All-day dining and one of London's best brunches, in a converted Victorian grain store on Granary Square.
address: The Granary Building, 1 Granary Square, London N1C 4AA

name: Hoppers King's Cross
why: Sri Lankan street food (hoppers, dosas and fiery curries) at the biggest branch of this much-loved London favourite, a short walk from the station.
line: Sri Lankan street food (hoppers, dosas and fiery curries) at the biggest branch of this much-loved London favourite, a short walk from the station.

name: Booking Office 1869
why: All-day dining in the old Victorian ticket office of St Pancras station, now part of the hotel, with soaring ceilings and live jazz. Perfect for breakfast before the Eurostar. On Sundays: dry-aged sirloin or chicken with all the trimmings.
line: All-day dining in the old Victorian ticket office of St Pancras station, now part of the hotel, with soaring ceilings and live jazz.
address: St Pancras Renaissance Hotel, Euston Road, London NW1 2AR

name: St. John
why: The restaurant that made 'nose-to-tail' eating famous, in an old smokehouse by Smithfield meat market. Michelin-starred but plain and unfussy, and the warm madeleines are legendary.
line: The restaurant that made 'nose-to-tail' eating famous, in an old smokehouse by Smithfield meat market.

name: Cloth Cornhill
why: Simpson's Tavern, one of the City's oldest chophouses (from the 18th century), revived: chops and steaks served in wood-panelled booths down a tiny alley off Cornhill.
line: Simpson's Tavern, one of the City's oldest chophouses (from the 18th century), revived: chops and steaks served in wood-panelled booths down a tiny alley off Cornhill.

name: Bob Bob Ricard City
why: Glamorous, high up in the Leadenhall Building, with a famous 'Press for Champagne' button at every table. A Franco-Russian menu and a real sense of occasion.
line: Glamorous, high up in the Leadenhall Building, with a famous 'Press for Champagne' button at every table.
address: The Leadenhall Building, 122 Leadenhall Street, London EC3V 4AB

name: Hawksmoor Guildhall
why: A wood-panelled City steakhouse, famous for its beef, a few minutes from St Paul's and the Guildhall. Also open for a hearty breakfast on weekdays.
line: A wood-panelled City steakhouse, famous for its beef, a few minutes from St Paul's and the Guildhall.

name: Lutyens Grill
why: A grand steakhouse inside The Ned, in the old Midland Bank building designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens. Old-school City glamour.
line: A grand steakhouse inside The Ned, in the old Midland Bank building designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens.

name: The Golden Chippy
why: A much-loved fish and chip shop near Greenwich station, with light, crisp batter and grilled fish if you prefer. Perfect after a day at the Cutty Sark and the Observatory.
line: A much-loved fish and chip shop near Greenwich station, with light, crisp batter and grilled fish if you prefer.

name: The Guildford Arms
why: A Greenwich gastropub with a big garden, known for its Sunday roasts and their side dishes. A short walk from the Cutty Sark.
line: A Greenwich gastropub with a big garden, known for its Sunday roasts and their side dishes.

name: Hullabaloo
why: Vegetarian Indian street food and thalis, right by the Cutty Sark. Quick, cheap and full of flavour.
line: Vegetarian Indian street food and thalis, right by the Cutty Sark.

name: Matiz On The Hill
why: A neighbourhood spot on pretty Royal Hill, mixing Mediterranean cooking with South American dishes like ceviche and tamales.
line: A neighbourhood spot on pretty Royal Hill, mixing Mediterranean cooking with South American dishes like ceviche and tamales.

name: Tower of London
why: Nearly 1,000 years of history in one place: the Crown Jewels, the White Tower, the ravens and the Beefeaters' famous tours. Allow at least half a day, and go first thing to beat the queue for the Jewels.
line: Nearly 1,000 years of history in one place: the Crown Jewels, the White Tower, the ravens and the Beefeaters' famous tours.
story: Every night at 9.53pm the Tower is locked in the Ceremony of the Keys, as it has been for around 700 years. Tickets are free but get snapped up months ahead.

name: Westminster Abbey
why: Where England's kings and queens have been crowned since 1066, and where many are buried. Poets' Corner, the Coronation Chair and the tomb of Elizabeth I are all inside.
line: Where England's kings and queens have been crowned since 1066, and where many are buried.
story: Look for the grave of the Unknown Warrior just inside the west door. It's the only tomb in the Abbey that nobody walks on.

name: Houses of Parliament and Big Ben
why: The Palace of Westminster and its famous clock tower, the most recognisable view in London. Guided tours run on many Saturdays and during recesses, and anyone can watch a debate from the public galleries.
line: The Palace of Westminster and its famous clock tower, the most recognisable view in London.
story: Big Ben is the bell, not the tower. The tower was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012. When the light above the clock is on, Parliament is sitting.

name: Buckingham Palace
why: The Royal Household's headquarters and the setting for state occasions and balcony appearances. Watch the Changing of the Guard outside for free (check the days before you go), and in summer you can tour the State Rooms. A big refurbishment is due to finish around March 2027, after which more of the palace is set to open to visitors.
line: The Royal Household's headquarters and the setting for state occasions and balcony appearances.
story: The King doesn't actually live here. He and Queen Camilla chose to stay at Clarence House, a few minutes up The Mall, and keep the palace as the royal headquarters.

name: Clarence House
why: The King and Queen's London home, on The Mall next to St James's Palace. Built by John Nash in the 1820s and home to the Queen Mother for nearly 50 years. Charles has lived here since 2003 and stayed on after becoming King. It's not normally open inside, but you can see it from The Mall.
line: The King and Queen's London home, on The Mall next to St James's Palace.
story: Princess Anne was born here in 1950, when the young Princess Elizabeth and Prince Philip lived here before she became Queen.

name: St James's Palace
why: Henry VIII's Tudor palace on Pall Mall, with its red-brick gatehouse and clock. Still the most senior royal palace: new monarchs are proclaimed from the balcony over Friary Court, as King Charles was in 2022. Not open inside, but the outside and the guards are worth a look.
line: Henry VIII's Tudor palace on Pall Mall, with its red-brick gatehouse and clock.
story: No monarch has lived here since Queen Victoria moved to Buckingham Palace in 1837, yet foreign ambassadors are still sent to 'the Court of St James's'. On Changing the Guard days, watch the Old Guard form up in Friary Court: it's much less crowded than the palace railings.

name: St Paul's Cathedral
why: Sir Christopher Wren's masterpiece, rebuilt after the Great Fire. Climb up to the Whispering Gallery inside the dome, then right to the top for one of the best views in the City.
line: Sir Christopher Wren's masterpiece, rebuilt after the Great Fire.
story: Wren is buried in the crypt under a simple stone. The Latin says: if you seek his monument, look around you.

name: Trafalgar Square
why: London's main square, with Nelson's Column, the Landseer lions and the National Gallery along one side. Free, central and always lively.
line: London's main square, with Nelson's Column, the Landseer lions and the National Gallery along one side.
story: In the south-east corner, one of the stone lamp posts was hollowed out as a tiny police lookout post, often called Britain's smallest police station.

name: Churchill War Rooms
why: The secret bunker under Whitehall where Churchill and his cabinet ran the Second World War, left almost exactly as it was in 1945. A brilliant pick for a wet day.
line: The secret bunker under Whitehall where Churchill and his cabinet ran the Second World War, left almost exactly as it was in 1945.
story: Churchill's hotline to the American President was hidden in a cupboard disguised as his private toilet.

name: Kensington Palace
why: A royal home since the 1600s, in the middle of Kensington Gardens. See the King's and Queen's State Apartments and the exhibitions, then walk the gardens outside.
line: A royal home since the 1600s, in the middle of Kensington Gardens.
story: Queen Victoria was born here in 1819 and grew up in the palace.

name: Horse Guards Parade
why: Mounted troopers of the King's Life Guard stand sentry on Whitehall all day, and the Household Cavalry Museum shows the horses in their stables. Trooping the Colour takes place here every June.
line: Mounted troopers of the King's Life Guard stand sentry on Whitehall all day, and the Household Cavalry Museum shows the horses in their stables.
story: The daily 4pm inspection is said to go back to Queen Victoria finding the guards drunk on duty.

name: Banqueting House
why: The only surviving part of the old Whitehall Palace, with a magnificent ceiling painted by Rubens. A quick, quiet visit right on Whitehall.
line: The only surviving part of the old Whitehall Palace, with a magnificent ceiling painted by Rubens.
story: Charles I commissioned the Rubens ceiling, then walked beneath it in 1649 to his execution on a scaffold outside.

name: The Royal Mews
why: The working royal stables behind Buckingham Palace, home to the Gold State Coach and the horses and carriages used on state occasions. Opening is seasonal, so check before you go.
line: The working royal stables behind Buckingham Palace, home to the Gold State Coach and the horses and carriages used on state occasions.
story: The Gold State Coach weighs around four tonnes and needs eight horses to pull it.

name: Hampton Court Palace
why: Henry VIII's palace by the Thames, with Tudor kitchens, the Great Hall and the famous maze. A full day out, about an hour from central London.
line: Henry VIII's palace by the Thames, with Tudor kitchens, the Great Hall and the famous maze.
story: The maze was planted around 1700 and is the oldest surviving hedge maze in Britain.
address: Hampton Court Way, East Molesey KT8 9AU

name: 10 Downing Street
why: The Prime Minister's front door. You can't go up the street, but you can look through the gates from Whitehall, a short walk from Parliament.
line: The Prime Minister's front door.
story: Until the gates went up in 1989, anyone could walk up to the door and take a photo.

name: The Monument
why: The column built to remember the Great Fire of 1666. Climb its 311 steps for a view over the City, and you get a certificate at the bottom to prove it.
line: The column built to remember the Great Fire of 1666.
story: It's 202 feet tall, exactly the distance from where the fire started in a baker's shop on Pudding Lane.

name: Piccadilly Circus
why: The famous lights and the statue everyone calls Eros, at the heart of the West End. Best after dark.
line: The famous lights and the statue everyone calls Eros, at the heart of the West End.
story: The statue isn't really Eros. It's his brother Anteros, put up in memory of the Victorian reformer Lord Shaftesbury.

name: The View from The Shard
why: The highest viewing platform in the UK, on floors 69 and 72 of the UK's tallest building. On a clear day you can see for miles.
line: The highest viewing platform in the UK, on floors 69 and 72 of the UK's tallest building.
story: The top floor is partly open to the air, so you can feel the wind at the top of London.

name: Sky Garden
why: A free indoor garden at the top of the 'Walkie Talkie' building, with terraces looking over the Thames and Tower Bridge. Book a free slot online ahead.
line: A free indoor garden at the top of the 'Walkie Talkie' building, with terraces looking over the Thames and Tower Bridge.
story: When it was being built in 2013, its curved glass focused the sun so strongly it melted parts of a car parked below.

name: Garden at 120
why: A free rooftop garden on the 15th floor of 120 Fenchurch Street, with close-up views of the City's towers. Quieter than Sky Garden. Check opening times before you go.
line: A free rooftop garden on the 15th floor of 120 Fenchurch Street, with close-up views of the City's towers.
tags: Public garden; free, check opening times

name: Shakespeare's Globe
why: A reconstruction of Shakespeare's open-air theatre on the South Bank. Take the tour, or stand in the yard for a play in summer, just as audiences did 400 years ago.
line: A reconstruction of Shakespeare's open-air theatre on the South Bank.
story: It has the only thatched roof allowed in London since the Great Fire of 1666.

name: HMS Belfast
why: A Second World War cruiser moored by Tower Bridge. Climb through nine decks, from the bridge down to the engine rooms. Great for families.
line: A Second World War cruiser moored by Tower Bridge.
story: Her front guns are said to be aimed at London Gateway services on the M1, about 12 miles away.

name: Cutty Sark
why: The world's last surviving tea clipper, raised up in a glass dock in Greenwich so you can walk underneath her hull.
line: The world's last surviving tea clipper, raised up in a glass dock in Greenwich so you can walk underneath her hull.
story: In her day she was one of the fastest ships in the world, racing tea home from China.

name: Royal Observatory and the Prime Meridian
why: Stand with one foot in each hemisphere on the Prime Meridian line, then enjoy the view from the top of Greenwich Park over Canary Wharf and the City.
line: Stand with one foot in each hemisphere on the Prime Meridian line, then enjoy the view from the top of Greenwich Park over Canary Wharf and the City.
story: The red Time Ball on the roof drops at exactly 1pm every day, so ships on the Thames could set their clocks.

name: ZSL London Zoo
why: The world's oldest scientific zoo, on the edge of Regent's Park. Penguins, gorillas, lions and the walk-through monkey and butterfly areas.
line: The world's oldest scientific zoo, on the edge of Regent's Park.
story: It opened in 1828, and Winnie the bear lived here. She inspired A.A. Milne's Winnie-the-Pooh.
address: Outer Circle, Regent's Park, London NW1 4RY

name: Madame Tussauds
why: The famous waxworks on Marylebone Road: royals, film stars and sporting heroes to pose with. Book online, as it's cheaper and quicker.
line: The famous waxworks on Marylebone Road: royals, film stars and sporting heroes to pose with.
story: Madame Tussaud made death masks during the French Revolution before bringing her waxworks to Britain.

name: The London Dungeon
why: A scary, funny walk through London's grisliest history, with actors, rides and Jack the Ripper. Best for older children and adults.
line: A scary, funny walk through London's grisliest history, with actors, rides and Jack the Ripper.
address: County Hall, Westminster Bridge Road, London SE1 7PB

name: Warner Bros. Studio Tour – The Making of Harry Potter
why: The real sets, costumes and props from the Harry Potter films, including the Great Hall and Diagon Alley. Just outside London at Leavesden, so book well ahead and allow time to get there.
line: The real sets, costumes and props from the Harry Potter films, including the Great Hall and Diagon Alley.

name: IFS Cloud Cable Car
why: A cable car ride high across the Thames between Greenwich Peninsula and the Royal Docks, with views of the O2, Canary Wharf and the river.
line: A cable car ride high across the Thames between Greenwich Peninsula and the Royal Docks, with views of the O2, Canary Wharf and the river.
story: Opened for the 2012 Olympics. A cheap way to see Canary Wharf and the river from above.

name: Up at The O2
why: Climb over the top of the O2 arena on a walkway across the roof, in a harness with a guide, with views down the river from the summit.
line: Climb over the top of the O2 arena on a walkway across the roof, in a harness with a guide, with views down the river from the summit.
story: Built as the Millennium Dome for the year 2000. Its twelve yellow masts are said to stand for the months of the year.

name: British Museum
why: Two million years of human history under one roof: the Rosetta Stone, the Egyptian mummies, the Parthenon sculptures and the Sutton Hoo helmet. Free, and far too big for one visit, so pick a few galleries.
line: Two million years of human history under one roof: the Rosetta Stone, the Egyptian mummies, the Parthenon sculptures and the Sutton Hoo helmet.
story: The Rosetta Stone is said to be the most visited object in the whole museum. Go first thing, or late on a Friday, to get close to it.

name: National Gallery
why: One of the world's great collections of paintings, from the 1200s to the 1900s: Van Gogh's Sunflowers, Turner, Constable, Leonardo and Rembrandt. Free, right on Trafalgar Square.
line: One of the world's great collections of paintings, from the 1200s to the 1900s: Van Gogh's Sunflowers, Turner, Constable, Leonardo and Rembrandt.
story: On the terrace wall outside are the official Imperial measures, brass markers showing exactly how long a foot, a yard and a chain should be.

name: Natural History Museum
why: Hope the blue whale skeleton, the dinosaurs and the earthquake room, in a building that looks like a cathedral. Free and brilliant for families.
line: Hope the blue whale skeleton, the dinosaurs and the earthquake room, in a building that looks like a cathedral.
story: Look closely at the outside: the building is covered in terracotta animals, with living species on the west side and extinct ones on the east.

name: Science Museum
why: Rockets, steam engines and the story of medicine, flight and computers. Free, with the hands-on Wonderlab gallery as a paid extra.
line: Rockets, steam engines and the story of medicine, flight and computers.
story: It looks after the Apollo 10 command module and Puffing Billy, the oldest surviving steam locomotive in the world.

name: Tate Modern
why: Modern and contemporary art in the old Bankside Power Station, with Picasso, Warhol and Rothko in the free collection. Go up to the viewing level for the view across to St Paul's.
line: Modern and contemporary art in the old Bankside Power Station, with Picasso, Warhol and Rothko in the free collection.
story: The power station's chimney is said to have been kept lower than the dome of St Paul's, out of respect for Wren's cathedral across the river.

name: Tate Britain
why: British art from 1500 to today on Millbank, with the best collection of Turner anywhere. Usually much quieter than Tate Modern.
line: British art from 1500 to today on Millbank, with the best collection of Turner anywhere.
story: It stands on the site of the old Millbank Penitentiary, where convicts were held before being shipped to Australia.

name: Imperial War Museum London
why: The story of war from 1914 to today: a Spitfire hanging in the atrium, tanks, the Holocaust Galleries and moving personal stories. Free.
line: The story of war from 1914 to today: a Spitfire hanging in the atrium, tanks, the Holocaust Galleries and moving personal stories.
story: The building was once Bethlem Royal Hospital, the original 'Bedlam'.

name: National Maritime Museum
why: Ships, explorers and sea battles in Greenwich, a few minutes from the Cutty Sark. Free, with lots for children.
line: Ships, explorers and sea battles in Greenwich, a few minutes from the Cutty Sark.
story: It has the coat Nelson was wearing at Trafalgar, with the bullet hole that killed him.

name: Sir John Soane's Museum
why: The house of the architect of the Bank of England, left exactly as he arranged it in the 1830s: every wall crammed with paintings, statues and curiosities, and an Egyptian sarcophagus in the basement. Free.
line: The house of the architect of the Bank of England, left exactly as he arranged it in the 1830s: every wall crammed with paintings, statues and curiosities, and an Egyptian sarcophagus in the basement.
story: Hogarth's Rake's Progress hangs on hinged panels that swing open to reveal more pictures behind. Ask the staff to show you.

name: Wellcome Collection
why: A free museum about health and the human body, opposite Euston station, with a great bookshop and café. Thought-provoking and often surprising.
line: A free museum about health and the human body, opposite Euston station, with a great bookshop and café.

name: Hunterian Museum
why: The surgeon John Hunter's 18th-century collection of anatomy specimens, at the Royal College of Surgeons. Free, but not for the squeamish, and best for ages 10 and up.
line: The surgeon John Hunter's 18th-century collection of anatomy specimens, at the Royal College of Surgeons.

name: Royal Academy of Arts
why: Big art exhibitions in Burlington House on Piccadilly, and the famous Summer Exhibition every year. A short walk from Fortnum & Mason.
line: Big art exhibitions in Burlington House on Piccadilly, and the famous Summer Exhibition every year.
story: The Summer Exhibition has run every year since 1769, and anyone can send in a work to be considered.

name: The Courtauld Gallery
why: A small gallery full of masterpieces at Somerset House: Impressionists and Post-Impressionists including Manet, Van Gogh and Cézanne. You can see it all in a couple of hours.
line: A small gallery full of masterpieces at Somerset House: Impressionists and Post-Impressionists including Manet, Van Gogh and Cézanne.
story: Look for Van Gogh's Self-Portrait with Bandaged Ear and Manet's A Bar at the Folies-Bergère.

name: Saatchi Gallery
why: Contemporary art in the old Duke of York's barracks just off the King's Road. Many shows are free, so check what's on.
line: Contemporary art in the old Duke of York's barracks just off the King's Road.
address: Duke of York's HQ, King's Road, London SW3 4RY

name: Serpentine Galleries
why: Two free contemporary galleries in Kensington Gardens, on either side of the Serpentine lake. Pair it with a walk in the park.
line: Two free contemporary galleries in Kensington Gardens, on either side of the Serpentine lake.
story: Every summer a different famous architect designs a temporary pavilion on the lawn.

name: Hayward Gallery
why: Big contemporary art shows in the concrete Southbank Centre, by Waterloo Bridge.
line: Big contemporary art shows in the concrete Southbank Centre, by Waterloo Bridge.
address: Southbank Centre, Belvedere Road, London SE1 8XX

name: Barbican
why: Art and design exhibitions inside the Barbican, the famous concrete estate in the City. Don't miss the Conservatory, a tropical garden hidden in the concrete (open on selected days).
line: Art and design exhibitions inside the Barbican, the famous concrete estate in the City.

name: Whitechapel Gallery
why: A free gallery in the East End that has shown new art since 1901.
line: A free gallery in the East End that has shown new art since 1901.
story: Picasso's Guernica was shown here in 1939, to raise money for the Spanish Civil War.

name: Lightroom
why: A huge immersive gallery at King's Cross, where art and music fill four walls and the floor. Shows change every few months.
line: A huge immersive gallery at King's Cross, where art and music fill four walls and the floor.
story: Now showing: David Bowie: You're Not Alone (to 10 Jan 2027). Next: Matisse: Joy (27 Jan to 8 May 2027).

name: London Museum (Smithfield)
why: The new home of the London Museum, opening on 28 November 2026 in the restored Victorian market buildings at Smithfield. The whole story of London, from prehistory to today. Check opening times and tickets before you go.
line: The new home of the London Museum, opening on 28 November 2026 in the restored Victorian market buildings at Smithfield.
story: Meat has been traded at Smithfield for over 800 years, and the museum shares the site with the market's history.

name: London Museum Docklands
why: The story of the river, the docks and the people who worked them, in a Georgian sugar warehouse at West India Quay. Free, with a play area for under-8s.
line: The story of the river, the docks and the people who worked them, in a Georgian sugar warehouse at West India Quay.
story: The warehouse it's in was built in 1802, when this was the busiest port in the world.

name: Charles Dickens Museum
why: Dickens's only surviving London home, where he wrote Oliver Twist. His study, desk and family rooms, set out as they were.
line: Dickens's only surviving London home, where he wrote Oliver Twist.

name: Sherlock Holmes Museum
why: The famous address, 221b Baker Street, set out as Holmes and Watson's Victorian lodgings. Fun for fans of all ages. Expect a queue.
line: The famous address, 221b Baker Street, set out as Holmes and Watson's Victorian lodgings.
story: 221B didn't actually exist when Conan Doyle wrote the stories. Baker Street wasn't numbered that high.

name: Florence Nightingale Museum
why: The story of the founder of modern nursing, at St Thomas' Hospital opposite Parliament.
line: The story of the founder of modern nursing, at St Thomas' Hospital opposite Parliament.
story: Look out for Athena, her pet owl, who she rescued in Athens and carried around in her pocket.
address: St Thomas' Hospital, 2 Lambeth Palace Road, London SE1 7EW

name: Garden Museum
why: The history of British gardens in an old church next to Lambeth Palace, with a lovely café and garden.
line: The history of British gardens in an old church next to Lambeth Palace, with a lovely café and garden.
story: Captain Bligh, of the Mutiny on the Bounty, is buried in the churchyard.

name: Horniman Museum
why: A much-loved family museum in Forest Hill: natural history, musical instruments, an aquarium and big gardens with a view over London. The main museum is free.
line: A much-loved family museum in Forest Hill: natural history, musical instruments, an aquarium and big gardens with a view over London.
story: Its famous walrus was stuffed so full by Victorians who'd never seen one that it has no wrinkles at all.
address: 100 London Road, Forest Hill, London SE23 3PQ

name: Museum of the Home
why: 400 years of living rooms, from the 1600s to today, in old almshouses in Hoxton. Free.
line: 400 years of living rooms, from the 1600s to today, in old almshouses in Hoxton.

name: National Army Museum
why: The story of the British Army, next to the Royal Hospital Chelsea, home of the Chelsea Pensioners. Free.
line: The story of the British Army, next to the Royal Hospital Chelsea, home of the Chelsea Pensioners.
story: It has the skeleton of Marengo, the horse Napoleon rode at Waterloo.

name: RAF Museum London
why: Over 100 aircraft, from First World War biplanes to the Spitfire and the Vulcan, at the old Hendon aerodrome. Free, and a big hit with kids.
line: Over 100 aircraft, from First World War biplanes to the Spitfire and the Vulcan, at the old Hendon aerodrome.

name: Kenwood House
why: A grand house on the edge of Hampstead Heath with a free collection of old masters, including a Rembrandt self-portrait and a Vermeer. Perfect after a walk on the Heath.
line: A grand house on the edge of Hampstead Heath with a free collection of old masters, including a Rembrandt self-portrait and a Vermeer.

name: Dulwich Picture Gallery
why: England's first purpose-built public art gallery, designed by Sir John Soane and opened in 1817, in leafy Dulwich Village.
line: England's first purpose-built public art gallery, designed by Sir John Soane and opened in 1817, in leafy Dulwich Village.

name: The King's Gallery
why: Exhibitions from the Royal Collection in a gallery attached to Buckingham Palace, open all year.
line: Exhibitions from the Royal Collection in a gallery attached to Buckingham Palace, open all year.

name: Grant Museum of Zoology
why: A small, packed Victorian-style room of skeletons and specimens in jars, run by UCL. Free and wonderfully odd.
line: A small, packed Victorian-style room of skeletons and specimens in jars, run by UCL.
story: Look for the jar packed with 18 moles.

name: London Wall at Tower Hill
why: The tallest surviving stretch of the wall that ringed London for 1,500 years: Roman stone at the bottom, medieval on top. Right next to Tower Hill station.
line: The tallest surviving stretch of the wall that ringed London for 1,500 years: Roman stone at the bottom, medieval on top.
story: The statue in front is of a Roman emperor, often said to be Trajan.
address: Wakefield Gardens, Tower Hill, London EC3N

name: London Wall, Noble Street
why: A long run of the old City wall, including the corner of a Roman fort, sunk below the modern street near the Barbican.
line: A long run of the old City wall, including the corner of a Roman fort, sunk below the modern street near the Barbican.
story: It lay hidden behind buildings for centuries until the Blitz flattened them and uncovered it.

name: All Hallows by the Tower
why: The oldest church in the City, founded in 675, with a Roman floor and Saxon arch in the crypt. A short walk from the Tower.
line: The oldest church in the City, founded in 675, with a Roman floor and Saxon arch in the crypt.
story: Samuel Pepys climbed its tower to watch the Great Fire. William Penn was baptised here, and US President John Quincy Adams was married here.

name: London Stone
why: A battered lump of limestone behind a grille on Cannon Street, part of London's story for at least 900 years. Nobody knows exactly what it was for.
line: A battered lump of limestone behind a grille on Cannon Street, part of London's story for at least 900 years.
story: Legend says that as long as the stone is safe, London will flourish. The rebel Jack Cade struck it with his sword in 1450, claiming to be lord of the city.

name: Pudding Lane
why: The little street near the Monument where the Great Fire of London began, in the early hours of 2 September 1666. A plaque marks the spot.
line: The little street near the Monument where the Great Fire of London began, in the early hours of 2 September 1666.
story: It started in Thomas Farriner's bakery. He swore he'd put his oven out before going to bed.

name: Temple Church
why: The round church of the Knights Templar, consecrated in 1185, hidden among the lawyers' courtyards off Fleet Street. Stone knights lie on the floor.
