line: The round church of the Knights Templar, consecrated in 1185, hidden among the lawyers' courtyards off Fleet Street.
story: It's where Robert Langdon goes looking for a knight's tomb in The Da Vinci Code.

name: St Bartholomew-the-Great
why: London's oldest surviving parish church, founded in 1123, through a Tudor gatehouse off Smithfield. Dark, ancient and beautiful.
line: London's oldest surviving parish church, founded in 1123, through a Tudor gatehouse off Smithfield.
story: The fourth wedding in Four Weddings and a Funeral was filmed here, and so were scenes from Shakespeare in Love.

name: William Wallace memorial
why: A plaque on the wall of St Bartholomew's Hospital marks where the Scottish hero William Wallace was executed in 1305.
line: A plaque on the wall of St Bartholomew's Hospital marks where the Scottish hero William Wallace was executed in 1305.
story: Scots still leave flowers and flags here.

name: Cleopatra's Needle
why: A 3,500-year-old Egyptian obelisk on the Victoria Embankment, guarded by two bronze sphinxes. Older than London itself.
line: A 3,500-year-old Egyptian obelisk on the Victoria Embankment, guarded by two bronze sphinxes.
story: Look at the base and the right-hand sphinx: the holes are shrapnel damage from a German air raid in 1917. A Victorian time capsule is buried underneath.

name: Execution Dock
why: Where pirates were hanged at the low-tide mark in Wapping, their bodies left for three tides to wash over them. The exact spot is disputed, but the riverside here is the place.
line: Where pirates were hanged at the low-tide mark in Wapping, their bodies left for three tides to wash over them.
story: Captain Kidd was hanged here in 1701. The rope broke the first time.

name: Bunhill Fields
why: A peaceful old burial ground off City Road, the resting place of William Blake, Daniel Defoe and John Bunyan.
line: A peaceful old burial ground off City Road, the resting place of William Blake, Daniel Defoe and John Bunyan.

name: The Clink Prison Museum
why: On the site of one of England's oldest prisons, on Clink Street in Southwark. Grim, hands-on and good for older kids.
line: On the site of one of England's oldest prisons, on Clink Street in Southwark.
story: It's where the phrase 'in the clink' comes from.

name: Golden Hinde
why: A full-size reconstruction of Sir Francis Drake's ship, squeezed into a little dock by Southwark Cathedral. Climb aboard.
line: A full-size reconstruction of Sir Francis Drake's ship, squeezed into a little dock by Southwark Cathedral.
story: This copy has sailed around the world itself, just like the original.
address: St Mary Overie Dock, Cathedral Street, London SE1 9DE

name: Winchester Palace
why: The ruined wall and rose window of the medieval palace of the Bishops of Winchester, on Clink Street.
line: The ruined wall and rose window of the medieval palace of the Bishops of Winchester, on Clink Street.
story: The bishops also licensed the local brothels. The women were nicknamed 'Winchester Geese'.

name: Cross Bones Graveyard
why: A small memorial garden on Redcross Way, the old unconsecrated burial ground for the poor of Southwark. The gates are covered in ribbons and messages.
line: A small memorial garden on Redcross Way, the old unconsecrated burial ground for the poor of Southwark.
story: Many of the 'Winchester Geese' were buried here, outside the churchyard.

name: Whitechapel and the Ripper streets
why: The streets of Whitechapel and Spitalfields where five women were murdered in 1888. Best seen on a guided walk that tells the women's own stories.
line: The streets of Whitechapel and Spitalfields where five women were murdered in 1888.

name: Dr Johnson's House
why: The house in a hidden square off Fleet Street where Samuel Johnson wrote his famous Dictionary of the English Language.
line: The house in a hidden square off Fleet Street where Samuel Johnson wrote his famous Dictionary of the English Language.
story: Outside is a statue of his cat Hodge, with empty oyster shells. Johnson used to go out and buy oysters for him.

name: Twinings, 216 Strand
why: A narrow tea shop that has been on the same spot on the Strand since 1706. Stop in for a tasting.
line: A narrow tea shop that has been on the same spot on the Strand since 1706.
story: The gold lion over the door has been there since 1787.

name: The Old Curiosity Shop
why: A crooked little 16th-century building near Lincoln's Inn Fields, one of the oldest shopfronts in London.
line: A crooked little 16th-century building near Lincoln's Inn Fields, one of the oldest shopfronts in London.
story: It took its name from Dickens's novel, though it probably wasn't the shop he had in mind.

name: Seven Noses of Soho
why: Small plaster noses stuck to buildings around Soho and Covent Garden. A fun hunt to do with kids.
line: Small plaster noses stuck to buildings around Soho and Covent Garden.
story: An artist stuck them up in 1997 as a protest against CCTV. There's a story that tapping the nose on Admiralty Arch brings luck.
address: Admiralty Arch, The Mall, London SW1A 2WH

name: Platform 9¾, King's Cross
why: The luggage trolley disappearing into the wall at King's Cross station, and the Harry Potter shop beside it. Expect a queue for the photo.
line: The luggage trolley disappearing into the wall at King's Cross station, and the Harry Potter shop beside it.
story: The Hogwarts Express scenes were actually filmed at platforms 4 and 5. There's no wall between 9 and 10 at all.

name: Leadenhall Market
why: A Victorian covered market of painted ironwork and cobbles in the City, with pubs and shops. Used as Diagon Alley in Harry Potter.
line: A Victorian covered market of painted ironwork and cobbles in the City, with pubs and shops.
story: The blue door in Bull's Head Passage was the entrance to the Leaky Cauldron in the first film. The shops close at weekends.

name: Cabmen's shelters
why: The little green huts dotted around London are cabmen's shelters, built from 1875 so cab drivers could get a hot meal without leaving their cabs. Only 13 are left. Cabbies eat inside, but anyone can buy a tea or a sandwich from the hatch. This one is in Russell Square.
line: The little green huts dotted around London are cabmen's shelters, built from 1875 so cab drivers could get a hot meal without leaving their cabs.
story: They're no bigger than a horse and cart, because that was the most a hut on a public road was allowed to take up. Ask any cabbie which one does the best bacon roll.

name: Highgate Cemetery
why: A Victorian cemetery of overgrown tombs and catacombs on the hill at Highgate. Karl Marx is buried in the East Cemetery; the West Cemetery is seen on guided tours.
line: A Victorian cemetery of overgrown tombs and catacombs on the hill at Highgate.

name: Brompton Cemetery
why: A grand, peaceful Victorian cemetery between Earl's Court and Fulham, now a haven for wildlife.
line: A grand, peaceful Victorian cemetery between Earl's Court and Fulham, now a haven for wildlife.
story: Beatrix Potter lived nearby, and some of the names on the gravestones, like Nutkins and Peter Rabbett, are said to have inspired her characters.

name: The Charterhouse
why: A hidden Tudor mansion and almshouse on Charterhouse Square, still home to a community of elderly 'Brothers'. The small museum is free.
line: A hidden Tudor mansion and almshouse on Charterhouse Square, still home to a community of elderly 'Brothers'.
story: Elizabeth I stayed here before her coronation.

name: Ely Place
why: A private gated road off Holborn Circus, with its own beadle who locks the gates at night. Home to St Etheldreda's church and Ye Olde Mitre pub.
line: A private gated road off Holborn Circus, with its own beadle who locks the gates at night.
story: It once belonged to the Bishops of Ely, and for centuries it was counted as part of Cambridgeshire, not London.

name: Wellington Arch
why: The triumphal arch at Hyde Park Corner, topped by a huge bronze of a chariot and horses. You can go inside and out onto the balconies.
line: The triumphal arch at Hyde Park Corner, topped by a huge bronze of a chariot and horses.
story: For years the arch had a tiny police station inside it.

name: Southwark Cathedral
why: London's oldest Gothic church, right by Borough Market and London Bridge. A calm escape from the crowds.
line: London's oldest Gothic church, right by Borough Market and London Bridge.
story: There's a memorial to Shakespeare inside, and his brother Edmund is buried here.

name: Denmark Street (Tin Pan Alley)
why: London's 'Tin Pan Alley', a short street of guitar shops off Charing Cross Road that was the heart of the British music business in the 1950s and 60s. Still full of instrument shops today.
line: London's 'Tin Pan Alley', a short street of guitar shops off Charing Cross Road that was the heart of the British music business in the 1950s and 60s.
story: The Rolling Stones recorded their first album at Regent Sound at No. 4, and the Sex Pistols lived and rehearsed at No. 6.

name: The 100 Club
why: A basement club on Oxford Street that has been putting on live music since 1942: jazz, then blues, then punk. Still a working venue.
line: A basement club on Oxford Street that has been putting on live music since 1942: jazz, then blues, then punk.
story: In September 1976 it hosted the Punk Special, with the Sex Pistols, the Clash and Siouxsie and the Banshees on the same bill.

name: Berwick Street
why: A Soho street of record shops and a daily market. Dig through vinyl at Sister Ray and Reckless Records.
line: A Soho street of record shops and a daily market.
story: It's the street on the cover of Oasis's (What's the Story) Morning Glory?

name: Carnaby Street
why: The centre of 'Swinging London' in the 1960s, when the mods and the bands of the day shopped here. Now a pedestrian shopping street.
line: The centre of 'Swinging London' in the 1960s, when the mods and the bands of the day shopped here.
story: The Who, the Small Faces and the Kinks all bought their clothes on and around this street.

name: The Marquee Club (site)
why: The Marquee at 90 Wardour Street was one of London's most famous rock clubs from 1964 to 1988. The club is long gone, but a blue plaque to The Who's Keith Moon marks the spot.
line: The Marquee at 90 Wardour Street was one of London's most famous rock clubs from 1964 to 1988.
story: The Who, David Bowie and Jimi Hendrix all played here on their way up.

name: John Lennon blue plaque
why: An English Heritage plaque at 34 Montagu Square in Marylebone, where John Lennon and Yoko Ono lived in 1968. Ringo Starr owned the flat.
line: An English Heritage plaque at 34 Montagu Square in Marylebone, where John Lennon and Yoko Ono lived in 1968.
story: Jimi Hendrix lived in this same flat a couple of years before Lennon. A busy little flat, that one.

name: Freddie Mercury's Garden Lodge
why: The house in Kensington where Freddie Mercury lived until his death in 1991. It's a private home behind a high wall, so please be respectful, but fans still visit the green door.
line: The house in Kensington where Freddie Mercury lived until his death in 1991.

name: Bob Marley blue plaque
why: An English Heritage plaque at 42 Oakley Street in Chelsea, where Bob Marley lived in 1977 while making the album Exodus.
line: An English Heritage plaque at 42 Oakley Street in Chelsea, where Bob Marley lived in 1977 while making the album Exodus.
story: He's said to have played football in Battersea Park, just over Albert Bridge at the end of the street.

name: Mozart in Belgravia
why: A plaque at 180 Ebury Street marks where an eight-year-old Mozart wrote his first symphony in 1764. There's a statue of the young Mozart in nearby Orange Square.
line: A plaque at 180 Ebury Street marks where an eight-year-old Mozart wrote his first symphony in 1764.

name: Marc Bolan Rock Shrine
why: A memorial by the tree in Barnes where T. Rex's Marc Bolan died in a car crash in 1977. Fans still leave messages and flowers.
line: A memorial by the tree in Barnes where T.

name: Bowie's Brixton
why: David Bowie was born at 40 Stansfield Road in Brixton in 1947. Opposite Brixton Underground station, the famous Bowie mural became a shrine after his death in 2016.
line: David Bowie was born at 40 Stansfield Road in Brixton in 1947.

name: The Roundhouse
why: A Victorian railway engine shed at Chalk Farm turned into a music venue. Still one of London's best places to see a gig.
line: A Victorian railway engine shed at Chalk Farm turned into a music venue.
story: Jimi Hendrix, the Doors and Pink Floyd all played here in the 1960s.

name: KOKO
why: A grand old Camden theatre turned music venue, with balconies all the way up. Once the Camden Palace.
line: A grand old Camden theatre turned music venue, with balconies all the way up.
story: Madonna played her first UK gig here in 1983, when it was the Camden Palace.

name: O2 Academy Brixton
why: One of London's best-loved gig venues, in a 1920s cinema with a sloping floor so everyone can see the stage.
line: One of London's best-loved gig venues, in a 1920s cinema with a sloping floor so everyone can see the stage.

name: Royal Albert Hall
why: The great domed concert hall in South Kensington, home of the BBC Proms every summer. Take a tour, or catch a concert.
line: The great domed concert hall in South Kensington, home of the BBC Proms every summer.
story: The Beatles sang about '4,000 holes' and how many it takes to fill the Albert Hall in 'A Day in the Life'.

name: Battersea Power Station
why: The giant brick power station by the river, now shops, restaurants and the Chimney Lift up one of the four chimneys.
line: The giant brick power station by the river, now shops, restaurants and the Chimney Lift up one of the four chimneys.
story: It's on the cover of Pink Floyd's Animals. During the photo shoot in 1976 the giant inflatable pig broke free and drifted over London.

name: Wembley Stadium
why: England's national stadium and London's biggest concert venue. Stadium tours run most days.
line: England's national stadium and London's biggest concert venue.
story: The old Wembley hosted Live Aid in July 1985, when Queen stole the show. Today's stadium was built on the same site.

name: Rough Trade West
why: The original Rough Trade record shop, in Notting Hill since 1978. Small, crammed and much loved by vinyl hunters.
line: The original Rough Trade record shop, in Notting Hill since 1978.

name: Sister Ray
why: One of Soho's best record shops, on Berwick Street: new and second-hand vinyl across every genre.
line: One of Soho's best record shops, on Berwick Street: new and second-hand vinyl across every genre.

name: The 606 Club
why: A basement jazz club in Chelsea with live music every night and dinner served while you listen.
line: A basement jazz club in Chelsea with live music every night and dinner served while you listen.

name: St Martin-in-the-Fields
why: The church on Trafalgar Square, famous for its concerts by candlelight and free lunchtime recitals. The café in the crypt is a good stop too.
line: The church on Trafalgar Square, famous for its concerts by candlelight and free lunchtime recitals.

name: Amy Winehouse statue
why: A life-size bronze of Amy Winehouse in Camden's Stables Market, close to the pubs and venues where she played and drank.
line: A life-size bronze of Amy Winehouse in Camden's Stables Market, close to the pubs and venues where she played and drank.
address: Stables Market, Chalk Farm Road, London NW1 8AH

name: Wembley Stadium Tour
why: Walk the players' tunnel, sit in the dressing rooms and lift the trophy at England's national stadium. Tours don't run on event days.
line: Walk the players' tunnel, sit in the dressing rooms and lift the trophy at England's national stadium.
story: The old Wembley's famous twin towers came down in 2003. The giant arch replaced them, and you can see it from all over London.

name: Emirates Stadium Tour
why: Arsenal's home: the dressing room, the tunnel and pitchside, with the museum next door.
line: Arsenal's home: the dressing room, the tunnel and pitchside, with the museum next door.
story: Arsenal moved here from Highbury in 2006. The old ground is now flats, and its pitch is a garden in the middle.

name: Tottenham Hotspur Stadium
why: Spurs' new stadium, with tours and the Dare Skywalk across the roof. It also hosts NFL games.
line: Spurs' new stadium, with tours and the Dare Skywalk across the roof.

name: Stamford Bridge Tour
why: Chelsea's dressing rooms, tunnel and museum.
line: Chelsea's dressing rooms, tunnel and museum.
story: Chelsea have played here since 1905, the year the club was formed.

name: London Stadium Tour
why: The 2012 Olympic Stadium in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, now West Ham's home.
line: The 2012 Olympic Stadium in Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, now West Ham's home.
address: Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, London E20 2ST

name: Lord's Cricket Ground
why: The home of cricket, with tours of the Pavilion and Long Room and the MCC Museum.
line: The home of cricket, with tours of the Pavilion and Long Room and the MCC Museum.
story: The Ashes urn lives in the MCC Museum here, even when Australia hold the Ashes.
address: St John's Wood Road, London NW8 8QN

name: The Kia Oval
why: South London's great cricket ground, by the famous gasholders.
line: South London's great cricket ground, by the famous gasholders.
story: It staged England's first home Test match, in 1880.

name: Allianz Stadium, Twickenham
why: The home of England rugby, with stadium tours and the World Rugby Museum.
line: The home of England rugby, with stadium tours and the World Rugby Museum.

name: Wimbledon Lawn Tennis Museum & Tour
why: Centre Court and the story of the Championships, open all year.
line: Centre Court and the story of the Championships, open all year.
story: In Championship fortnight you can join the Queue for on-the-day tickets – it's a famous British institution in its own right.

name: De Hems
why: A Dutch pub off Shaftesbury Avenue, famous for its atmosphere on big match nights.
line: A Dutch pub off Shaftesbury Avenue, famous for its atmosphere on big match nights.

name: The Maple Leaf
why: A Canadian pub in Covent Garden showing ice hockey and North American sports, with poutine and Canadian beer.
line: A Canadian pub in Covent Garden showing ice hockey and North American sports, with poutine and Canadian beer.

name: Fitzrovia Belle
why: A sports pub near Tottenham Court Road with seven screens and three separate sound zones, so more than one game can be on.
line: A sports pub near Tottenham Court Road with seven screens and three separate sound zones, so more than one game can be on.
address: Tottenham Court Road area (check exact address)

name: Passyunk Avenue
why: A Philadelphia-style bar for American sports – NFL, baseball, basketball – with Philly cheesesteaks. Several branches.
line: A Philadelphia-style bar for American sports – NFL, baseball, basketball – with Philly cheesesteaks.
address: Fitzrovia (also Waterloo, Nine Elms and Kensington; check exact addresses)

name: The Hercules Pillars
why: A Holborn pub with big-match screens and midweek deals.
line: A Holborn pub with big-match screens and midweek deals.

name: The Rocket
why: A big multi-sport pub by Euston station: Premier League and European nights.
line: A big multi-sport pub by Euston station: Premier League and European nights.

name: The Pavilion End
why: A Fuller's pub in the City, close to St Paul's, with Sky and TNT Sports. Staff will help find your match.
line: A Fuller's pub in the City, close to St Paul's, with Sky and TNT Sports.

name: Dickens Inn
why: A three-storey timber pub at St Katharine Docks by Tower Bridge, with five screens and pizza.
line: A three-storey timber pub at St Katharine Docks by Tower Bridge, with five screens and pizza.

name: Sixes Social Cricket
why: Play cricket in the indoor nets, then watch the game on the screens. Branches include London Bridge, Fitzrovia, Fulham, Stratford and Wembley.
line: Play cricket in the indoor nets, then watch the game on the screens.

name: Belushi's London Bridge
why: Lots of screens and two big projectors near Borough Market, with a late basement bar.
line: Lots of screens and two big projectors near Borough Market, with a late basement bar.

name: The Star of Kings
why: A King's Cross pub with projectors, a bookable area on match days and tacos on site.
line: A King's Cross pub with projectors, a bookable area on match days and tacos on site.
address: York Way, King's Cross (check exact address)

name: Café Kick
why: A little continental football bar on Exmouth Market, with table football and scarves from around the world.
line: A little continental football bar on Exmouth Market, with table football and scarves from around the world.

name: Bar Kick
why: Café Kick's bigger Shoreditch sister: table football, cocktails and Premier League, European and international games.
line: Café Kick's bigger Shoreditch sister: table football, cocktails and Premier League, European and international games.

name: Beechwood Sports Pub & Kitchen
why: A Shoreditch sports pub showing Premier League and Championship games. Book for big matches.
line: A Shoreditch sports pub showing Premier League and Championship games.

name: LaCage
why: A Montreal sports bar, its first outside Canada, opened September 2026 on two floors of the old Woolworths. Screens for football, rugby, F1 and darts, plus poutine and maple cocktails.
line: A Montreal sports bar, its first outside Canada, opened September 2026 on two floors of the old Woolworths.
story: The building opened as a Woolworths in the 1920s.

name: The Sydney Arms
why: A Chelsea pub for racing, rugby and football, with five screens and a good wine list.
line: A Chelsea pub for racing, rugby and football, with five screens and a good wine list.

name: Famous Three Kings
why: A big West Kensington sports bar with 13 screens and three projectors. Book for big tournaments.
line: A big West Kensington sports bar with 13 screens and three projectors.

name: The Cabbage Patch
why: A Twickenham rugby pub full of memorabilia, a favourite before and after England games. Book a table.
line: A Twickenham rugby pub full of memorabilia, a favourite before and after England games.

name: The Faltering Fullback
why: A much-loved Irish pub in Finsbury Park with a rambling multi-level garden. The place for the Six Nations.
line: A much-loved Irish pub in Finsbury Park with a rambling multi-level garden.

name: Princess of Wales, Blackheath
why: A pub on Blackheath with a famous rugby story and a good Sunday roast.
line: A pub on Blackheath with a famous rugby story and a good Sunday roast.
story: England's players met here in 1871 before the first ever international rugby match, and there's a little display about it inside.

name: The Auld Shillelagh
why: A narrow Irish pub in Stoke Newington with live music, a big covered garden and plenty of Guinness on Six Nations days.
line: A narrow Irish pub in Stoke Newington with live music, a big covered garden and plenty of Guinness on Six Nations days.
address: 105 Stoke Newington Church Street, London N16 0UD

name: Richmond Park
why: The biggest of the Royal Parks, with around 630 wild red and fallow deer roaming free. Keep at least 50 metres away, especially in the autumn rut and when the young are born in early summer.
line: The biggest of the Royal Parks, with around 630 wild red and fallow deer roaming free.
story: From King Henry's Mound there's a protected view through a gap in the trees all the way to St Paul's, 10 miles away.

name: Isabella Plantation
why: A woodland garden hidden inside Richmond Park, famous for its azaleas and rhododendrons. At its best from late April to May.
line: A woodland garden hidden inside Richmond Park, famous for its azaleas and rhododendrons.

name: Kew Gardens
why: The Royal Botanic Gardens: the Victorian Palm House, the Treetop Walkway and the Great Pagoda, across 300 acres by the river. Paid entry, and good in the rain thanks to the glasshouses.
line: The Royal Botanic Gardens: the Victorian Palm House, the Treetop Walkway and the Great Pagoda, across 300 acres by the river.
story: The Great Pagoda was built in 1762, and the dragons on it have been recreated after the originals disappeared, rumoured to have been sold to pay off a royal debt.

name: Hampstead Heath and Parliament Hill
why: 800 acres of wild heath, woods and ponds in north London. Climb Parliament Hill for one of the best free views of the city.
line: 800 acres of wild heath, woods and ponds in north London.
story: The view from Parliament Hill to St Paul's is protected by law, so nothing can be built to block it.

name: Hampstead Heath swimming ponds
why: Wild swimming in three ponds on the Heath – the men's, the women's and the mixed – open all year for the brave. Book online.
line: Wild swimming in three ponds on the Heath – the men's, the women's and the mixed – open all year for the brave.

name: Greenwich Park
why: The oldest enclosed Royal Park, on the hill above the river, with the Royal Observatory at the top and a view over Canary Wharf and the City.
line: The oldest enclosed Royal Park, on the hill above the river, with the Royal Observatory at the top and a view over Canary Wharf and the City.
story: It was enclosed in 1433, making it the oldest of the Royal Parks.

name: Bushy Park
why: The second-biggest Royal Park, next to Hampton Court Palace, with deer and the grand Chestnut Avenue. Combine it with a day at the palace.
line: The second-biggest Royal Park, next to Hampton Court Palace, with deer and the grand Chestnut Avenue.
story: Chestnut Avenue was laid out by Sir Christopher Wren as a grand approach to Hampton Court.

name: Victoria Park
why: East London's favourite park, known locally as the People's Park: lakes, a boating pond, cafés and a great playground.
line: East London's favourite park, known locally as the People's Park: lakes, a boating pond, cafés and a great playground.

name: Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park
why: The 2012 Olympic Park in Stratford: riverside paths, playgrounds, the ArcelorMittal Orbit and its giant slide, and the Aquatics Centre.
line: The 2012 Olympic Park in Stratford: riverside paths, playgrounds, the ArcelorMittal Orbit and its giant slide, and the Aquatics Centre.
story: Anyone can swim in the London Aquatics Centre, in the same pool as the Olympians.

name: Crystal Palace Park
why: A big south London park with a famous secret: life-size Victorian dinosaur sculptures around the lake, plus a maze and a farm.
line: A big south London park with a famous secret: life-size Victorian dinosaur sculptures around the lake, plus a maze and a farm.
story: The dinosaurs were made in 1854, the first dinosaur sculptures in the world. Some are a bit wrong, because scientists then had only bones to go on.

name: Chelsea Physic Garden
why: London's oldest botanic garden, founded in 1673 by the Apothecaries to grow medicinal plants, tucked behind a high wall by the river.
line: London's oldest botanic garden, founded in 1673 by the Apothecaries to grow medicinal plants, tucked behind a high wall by the river.
story: It is said to have the largest outdoor fruiting olive tree in Britain, thanks to its warm, sheltered walls.

name: Chiswick House and Gardens
why: An elegant 18th-century villa with free gardens, a camellia house and a lake – the birthplace of the English landscape garden.
line: An elegant 18th-century villa with free gardens, a camellia house and a lake – the birthplace of the English landscape garden.

name: Little Venice and the Regent's Canal
why: Where the canals meet near Paddington: colourful narrowboats, waterside cafés and a canal boat theatre. Walk the towpath to Camden in about an hour.
line: Where the canals meet near Paddington: colourful narrowboats, waterside cafés and a canal boat theatre.

name: Camley Street Natural Park
why: A small wildlife reserve on the canal right behind King's Cross station, with a floating boardwalk.
line: A small wildlife reserve on the canal right behind King's Cross station, with a floating boardwalk.

name: Phoenix Garden
why: A little community garden behind Shaftesbury Avenue, full of wildlife and quiet benches. A green escape in the middle of the West End.
line: A little community garden behind Shaftesbury Avenue, full of wildlife and quiet benches.

name: Golders Hill Park
why: A pretty park on the edge of Hampstead Heath with a free small zoo, a water garden and an ice cream café.
line: A pretty park on the edge of Hampstead Heath with a free small zoo, a water garden and an ice cream café.

name: Wimbledon Common
why: Over 1,000 acres of woods and heath, with a windmill museum. Home of the Wombles.
line: Over 1,000 acres of woods and heath, with a windmill museum.

name: Walthamstow Wetlands
why: A huge urban nature reserve across working reservoirs in east London, full of birds. Free.
line: A huge urban nature reserve across working reservoirs in east London, full of birds.

name: Serpentine Lido
why: Swim in the Serpentine in Hyde Park, open to the public in summer.
line: Swim in the Serpentine in Hyde Park, open to the public in summer.
story: The Serpentine Swimming Club has raced here every Christmas morning since 1864.

name: Parliament Hill Lido
why: An Art Deco open-air pool on Hampstead Heath. Unheated and open all year – a proper cold-water swim.
line: An Art Deco open-air pool on Hampstead Heath.

name: London Fields Lido
why: A heated 50-metre outdoor pool in Hackney, open all year.
line: A heated 50-metre outdoor pool in Hackney, open all year.
address: London Fields West Side, London E8 3EU

name: Brockwell Lido
why: A much-loved 1930s outdoor pool in Brockwell Park, Herne Hill, with a café.
line: A much-loved 1930s outdoor pool in Brockwell Park, Herne Hill, with a café.

name: Portobello Road Market
why: Antiques, vintage and street food along a mile of colourful houses. Saturday is the big day.
line: Antiques, vintage and street food along a mile of colourful houses.
story: Named after Porto Bello in Panama, captured by Admiral Vernon in 1739. The road was a country lane to a farm named after the victory.

name: Columbia Road Flower Market
why: Sundays only. A narrow street packed with flowers and plants, with traders calling out their deals. Go early for the best choice or late for bargains.
line: A narrow street packed with flowers and plants, with traders calling out their deals.
story: The story goes it moved to Sunday so Jewish traders could sell after their Sabbath. Stay till closing – the last buckets go for next to nothing.

name: Greenwich Market
why: A covered market of crafts, antiques and food stalls, a short walk from the Cutty Sark.
line: A covered market of crafts, antiques and food stalls, a short walk from the Cutty Sark.
story: There's been a market here since the 1700s. Look up for the old inscription over the entrance: 'A false balance is abomination to the Lord'.

name: Covent Garden Apple Market
why: Crafts, jewellery and gifts in the old market hall, with street performers on the piazza outside.
line: Crafts, jewellery and gifts in the old market hall, with street performers on the piazza outside.
story: London's fruit and veg market until 1974, when it moved to Nine Elms. It's where Eliza Doolittle sells her flowers at the start of Pygmalion and My Fair Lady.

name: Maltby Street Market
why: A narrow lane of food stalls and bars under the railway arches. Weekends only. A calmer choice than Borough.
line: A narrow lane of food stalls and bars under the railway arches.
story: Started around 2010 by food producers looking for a quieter spot than Borough Market, ten minutes' walk away.

name: Broadway Market
why: Saturday food and craft market between London Fields and the Regent's Canal. Pick up lunch and picnic in the park.
line: Saturday food and craft market between London Fields and the Regent's Canal.
story: Cabbie's tip: on a sunny Saturday the canal towpath here is the nicest way in – walk along from Victoria Park or Angel.

name: Brick Lane & Sunday UpMarket
why: Vintage clothes, food from all over the world and the famous 24-hour bagel shops. Sunday is the busy day.
line: Vintage clothes, food from all over the world and the famous 24-hour bagel shops.
story: Brick Lane is named after the brick and tile makers who worked here in the 1500s. The Sunday market fills the old Truman brewery.
address: Old Truman Brewery, 91 Brick Lane, E1 6QL

name: Berwick Street Market
why: One of the West End's oldest street markets, now mostly street food at lunchtime.
line: One of the West End's oldest street markets, now mostly street food at lunchtime.
story: Traders have worked this street since the 1700s. It's also the street on the cover of Oasis's (What's the Story) Morning Glory?

name: Southbank Centre Food Market
why: Street food stalls behind the Royal Festival Hall, Friday to Sunday. Good before a show or a walk along the river.
line: Street food stalls behind the Royal Festival Hall, Friday to Sunday.
story: The Royal Festival Hall next door was built for the Festival of Britain in 1951 and is the only building from it still standing.
address: Southbank Centre Square, Belvedere Road, SE1 8XX

name: Mercato Metropolitano
why: A huge, lively food hall with stalls from around the world, a brewery and plenty of seating.
line: A huge, lively food hall with stalls from around the world, a brewery and plenty of seating.
story: The original of Mercato Mayfair, set in an old paper factory. Mayfair's is in a church – both worth a look.

name: Eataly London
why: An Italian market, restaurants and wine bar under one roof, near Liverpool Street.
line: An Italian market, restaurants and wine bar under one roof, near Liverpool Street.
story: Eataly started in Turin in 2007. The London one has a pasta lab where you can watch it being made.

name: Arcade Food Hall
why: A smart food hall with counters from some of London's best cooks, at the foot of Centre Point.
line: A smart food hall with counters from some of London's best cooks, at the foot of Centre Point.
story: Centre Point famously stood empty for about ten years after it was finished in the 1960s.

name: Chinatown
why: Gerrard Street and its lanes – bakeries, dim sum, roast duck in the windows and Chinese supermarkets.
line: Gerrard Street and its lanes – bakeries, dim sum, roast duck in the windows and Chinese supermarkets.
story: London's first Chinatown was down by the docks in Limehouse. It moved to Soho after the war, when Gerrard Street was cheap.

name: Hyde Park Winter Wonderland
why: Seasonal: Christmas market, ice rink, rides and shows. Usually mid-November to early January – check dates each year.
line: Seasonal: Christmas market, ice rink, rides and shows.
story: Started in 2007 and now one of the biggest Christmas events in Europe. Book a time slot at weekends.

name: Liberty
why: A Tudor-style department store famous for its prints, fabrics and Christmas shop.
line: A Tudor-style department store famous for its prints, fabrics and Christmas shop.
story: Built in 1924 from the timbers of two old navy ships, HMS Impregnable and HMS Hindustan.

name: Burlington Arcade
why: A covered Regency arcade of jewellers, watchmakers and cashmere, opened in 1819.
line: A covered Regency arcade of jewellers, watchmakers and cashmere, opened in 1819.
story: Look for the Beadles in top hats – the arcade's own police. The old rules ban whistling, singing and running.

name: Lock & Co. Hatters
why: The world's oldest hat shop, trading since 1676. Worth a visit even just to look.
line: The world's oldest hat shop, trading since 1676.
story: Lock made the first bowler hat in 1849, for a gamekeeper's head. They still call it the 'Coke' after the man who ordered it.

name: Hatchards
why: London's oldest bookshop, since 1797, with creaky floors and signed copies.
line: London's oldest bookshop, since 1797, with creaky floors and signed copies.
story: Next door to Fortnum & Mason, and it holds royal warrants. Oscar Wilde and Lord Byron were customers.

name: Daunt Books Marylebone
why: An Edwardian bookshop with oak galleries and a long skylight. Travel books are arranged by country.
line: An Edwardian bookshop with oak galleries and a long skylight.
story: One of the prettiest shops in London. Pick up a book on where you're going next.

name: Foyles
why: Five floors of books on Charing Cross Road, with a café at the top.
line: Five floors of books on Charing Cross Road, with a café at the top.
story: Started in 1903 by two brothers who failed their civil service exams and sold their old textbooks.

name: James Smith & Sons Umbrellas
why: An umbrella shop since 1830 with a perfect Victorian shopfront.
line: An umbrella shop since 1830 with a perfect Victorian shopfront.
story: The shop front has hardly changed since the 1860s. In London, an umbrella is never a bad buy.

name: Berry Bros. & Rudd
why: Britain's oldest wine merchant, trading in St James's since 1698.
line: Britain's oldest wine merchant, trading in St James's since 1698.
story: Customers used to be weighed on the shop's giant coffee scales – Lord Byron's weight is still in the books.
address: 3 St James's Street / 63 Pall Mall (check which is open)

name: Jermyn Street
why: Shirtmakers, shoemakers, perfumers and the cheesemonger Paxton & Whitfield, all on one street.
line: Shirtmakers, shoemakers, perfumers and the cheesemonger Paxton & Whitfield, all on one street.
story: Look for the statue of Beau Brummell, the Regency dandy, at the Piccadilly Arcade end. Paxton & Whitfield have sold cheese here since 1797.

name: Savile Row
why: The home of made-to-measure tailoring. Peek in the basement windows to see suits being cut.
line: The home of made-to-measure tailoring.
story: The story goes the dinner jacket was first cut here, at Henry Poole, for the future Edward VII. Americans called it the tuxedo.

name: Bond Street
why: London's luxury shopping street – jewellers, fashion houses and auction rooms.
line: London's luxury shopping street – jewellers, fashion houses and auction rooms.
story: Look for the 'Allies' bench – Churchill and Roosevelt sitting together. There's room in the middle for a photo.

name: King's Road
why: Boutiques, homeware and cafés from Sloane Square to World's End.
line: Boutiques, homeware and cafés from Sloane Square to World's End.
story: Mary Quant opened her shop Bazaar here in 1955 – the miniskirt took off on this road. Later came punk, at Vivienne Westwood's shop.

name: Coal Drops Yard
why: Independent shops and restaurants in Victorian coal warehouses by the canal.
line: Independent shops and restaurants in Victorian coal warehouses by the canal.
story: Built in the 1850s to store coal that came in by train. The curving roofs were added by Thomas Heatherwick in 2018.

name: LEGO Store Leicester Square
why: The world's largest LEGO store, with London landmarks made of bricks.
line: The world's largest LEGO store, with London landmarks made of bricks.
story: Look for the full-size Tube carriage made of LEGO – you can sit inside it.

name: Harry Potter flagship store
why: A new Harry Potter store on Oxford Street, opening 4 Nov 2026 – check address and opening before publishing.
line: A new Harry Potter store on Oxford Street, opening 4 Nov 2026 – check address and opening before publishing.
story: Fans can also visit the shop at Platform 9¾ in King's Cross station.

name: Porchester Spa
why: Art deco Turkish baths with steam rooms, saunas and a plunge pool. Good value. Some days are women-only – check.
line: Art deco Turkish baths with steam rooms, saunas and a plunge pool.
story: Opened in 1929 and one of the last Turkish baths of its kind in London.

name: Ironmonger Row Baths
why: Restored 1930s Turkish baths with a steam room, saunas and a plunge pool, plus a swimming pool.
line: Restored 1930s Turkish baths with a steam room, saunas and a plunge pool, plus a swimming pool.
story: Opened in 1931 when most homes round here had no bath. Restored in 2012.

name: York Hall Spa
why: A small, good-value spa with Turkish baths beneath a famous boxing hall.
line: A small, good-value spa with Turkish baths beneath a famous boxing hall.
story: York Hall upstairs is a legendary boxing venue – plenty of champions fought their early fights here.

name: Bulgari Spa
why: A calm, luxurious spa with a 25-metre pool, in the Bulgari Hotel.
line: A calm, luxurious spa with a 25-metre pool, in the Bulgari Hotel.
story: One of the best hotel pools in London. Treatments include day access to the pool.

name: Mandarin Oriental Spa
why: A dark, peaceful spa with a pool, steam rooms and a vitality pool, by Hyde Park.
line: A dark, peaceful spa with a pool, steam rooms and a vitality pool, by Hyde Park.
story: Built in 1889 as a gentlemen's club and a hotel since 1902. Its park-side entrance is only used with the monarch's permission.

name: The Dorchester Spa
why: An art deco spa on Park Lane, with treatments and a relaxing lounge.
line: An art deco spa on Park Lane, with treatments and a relaxing lounge.
story: Pair it with afternoon tea in the Promenade – both are in the app.

name: Four Seasons Park Lane Spa
why: A spa on the top floor with views over Hyde Park.
line: A spa on the top floor with views over Hyde Park.
story: Few London spas have a view – this one looks over Hyde Park and the rooftops.

name: Akasha Spa, Hotel Café Royal
why: A spa with an 18-metre pool under Regent Street.
line: A spa with an 18-metre pool under Regent Street.
story: The Café Royal was where Oscar Wilde dined in the 1890s. Now a hotel, with a spa below.

name: The Lanesborough Club & Spa
why: A smart spa and gym at Hyde Park Corner. Treatments open to non-members.
line: A smart spa and gym at Hyde Park Corner.
story: The building was once St George's Hospital. It became a hotel in 1991.

name: K West Spa
why: A good-value spa with a 'snow paradise' room – you cool off in real snow between saunas.
line: A good-value spa with a 'snow paradise' room – you cool off in real snow between saunas.
story: Not many places in London let you roll in snow in July.

name: Banya No.1
why: A Russian-style bathhouse – very hot steam, birch-leaf treatments and a plunge pool.
line: A Russian-style bathhouse – very hot steam, birch-leaf treatments and a plunge pool.
story: Not for the faint-hearted. The birch-leaf 'venik' treatment is the thing to try.

name: Flight Club
why: Social darts with automatic scoring and private oches. Four sites: Bloomsbury, Shoreditch, Victoria and Islington (with a heated terrace).
line: Social darts with automatic scoring and private oches.
story: Want the real thing? The World Darts Championship is held at Alexandra Palace every December – see Ally Pally below.

name: Oche
why: Darts with a proper kitchen attached, just off the Strand.
line: Darts with a proper kitchen attached, just off the Strand.
story: Handy before or after a West End show – the theatres are all within a few minutes' walk.

name: Electric Shuffle – London Bridge & Canary Wharf
why: Shuffleboard with automatic scoring – two more sites to add alongside King's Cross (already in the app).
line: Shuffleboard with automatic scoring – two more sites to add alongside King's Cross (already in the app).
story: Same people as Flight Club. Good for groups – up to 32 at King's Cross.
address: London Bridge; Cabot Square, Canary Wharf

name: Boulebar South Bank
why: Pétanque on 20 gravel courts behind the National Theatre, with a courtside bar.
line: Pétanque on 20 gravel courts behind the National Theatre, with a courtside bar.
story: A taste of France on the Thames. A good one for a summer evening.

name: Boulebar Spitalfields
why: An underground pétanque bar with ten indoor courts.
line: An underground pétanque bar with ten indoor courts.
story: Pétanque under the streets of Spitalfields – rain or shine.

name: Crazy Boules
why: Boules on crazy-golf-style tracks, inside Mercato Metropolitano.
line: Boules on crazy-golf-style tracks, inside Mercato Metropolitano.
story: Eat in the food hall first – it's all under one roof.

name: Clays
why: Virtual clay pigeon shooting with automatic scoring and live leaderboards. Soho, the City (Moorgate) and Canary Wharf.
line: Virtual clay pigeon shooting with automatic scoring and live leaderboards.
story: Clay shooting without the mud, the cold or a trip to the countryside.

name: Rocket Room
why: Axe throwing, interactive darts, shuffleboard and beer pong, upstairs at Market Place Food Hall.
line: Axe throwing, interactive darts, shuffleboard and beer pong, upstairs at Market Place Food Hall.
story: Under-18s must be with an adult. Eat downstairs in the food hall – it's already in the app.
address: Market Place Food Hall, 20-21 Leicester Square

name: Boom Battle Bar
why: Axe throwing, AR darts, crazy golf, shuffleboard, karaoke and more. Sites on Oxford Street, Liverpool Street, the O2, Wandsworth and Ealing.
line: Axe throwing, AR darts, crazy golf, shuffleboard, karaoke and more.
story: Can't decide? Book a mix of games for the evening.
address: Oxford Street; Liverpool Street; The O2; Wandsworth; Ealing

name: Caddi Club
why: Indoor golf on Trackman simulators – play famous courses from around the world. Four clubs: Wimbledon (the biggest, 11 bays, with restaurant and terrace), Fulham (6 bays plus a VIP room), Waterloo (4 bays) and Chelsea (4 bays). Clubs provided, no experience needed, live sport in the lounge.
line: Indoor golf on Trackman simulators – play famous courses from around the world.
story: Rainy day? Play a round on a world-famous course without leaving London. The Wimbledon club is two minutes from the station – handy in tennis fortnight. (Matt's pick – spelt Caddi.)
address: Wimbledon: Top Floor, Wimbledon Quarter, 4 Queens Road, SW19 8YE; Fulham: Parrs Way, W6 9UQ; Waterloo: 4 Milner Place, SE1 7PE; Chelsea: 29 Imperial Road, SW6 2FR

name: Puttshack
why: High-tech crazy golf – the ball keeps your score. Three courses at Bank and at Westfield White City.
line: High-tech crazy golf – the ball keeps your score.
story: Started by the brothers who founded Topgolf.

name: Swingers West End
why: Nine-hole crazy golf with cocktail bars and street food traders.
line: Nine-hole crazy golf with cocktail bars and street food traders.
story: Crazy golf for grown-ups – a good one for birthdays and work nights out.

name: All Star Lanes
why: Boutique bowling with an American diner menu, cocktail bars and private karaoke booths. The Holborn original is in the basement of Victoria House, down steps off a side street. Also at Brick Lane, Westfield Stratford and Westfield White City. Holborn is open daily – late (till 2am) on Fridays and Saturdays.
line: Boutique bowling with an American diner menu, cocktail bars and private karaoke booths.
story: The Holborn one has a hidden speakeasy-style bar – most people walk straight past the entrance.
address: Victoria House, Bloomsbury Place, London WC1B 4DA (Holborn); also Brick Lane, Westfield Stratford, Westfield White City

name: Lane7
why: Bowling, mini golf, pool, ping pong and an 18+ arcade. Victoria and Camden.
line: Bowling, mini golf, pool, ping pong and an 18+ arcade.
story: Good for big groups – book bowling ahead at weekends.

name: Queens Skate Dine Bowl
why: An all-year ice rink, 17 bowling lanes, curling, darts and an arcade. Combo tickets available. All ages.
line: An all-year ice rink, 17 bowling lanes, curling, darts and an arcade.
story: Said to be London's oldest year-round indoor ice rink. Skate, then bowl, then eat on Queensway.

name: Hollywood Bowl at The O2
why: Thirteen tenpin lanes, duckpin bowling, an arcade and pool.
line: Thirteen tenpin lanes, duckpin bowling, an arcade and pool.
story: Pair it with Up at The O2 or the cable car for a full family day.

name: Rowans
why: An old-school bowling alley with karaoke and pool. Over-21s only after 7pm.
line: An old-school bowling alley with karaoke and pool.
story: A proper north London institution – no frills, lots of fun.

name: Roxy Ball Room
why: Duckpin bowling, pool, darts, karaoke and ice-free curling. Old Street, St Mary Axe (opposite the Gherkin) and Holborn.
line: Duckpin bowling, pool, darts, karaoke and ice-free curling.
story: Duckpin is bowling with small balls and short pins – easier for kids and beginners.
address: Old Street; St Mary Axe; Holborn

name: clueQuest
why: Six spy-themed escape rooms – 60 minutes to get out.
line: Six spy-themed escape rooms – 60 minutes to get out.
story: Pair it with lunch at Coal Drops Yard, a few minutes' walk away.

name: Escape Hunt
why: Six escape rooms including a Doctor Who room, opposite Tottenham Court Road station.
line: Six escape rooms including a Doctor Who room, opposite Tottenham Court Road station.
story: Doctor Who fans: the TARDIS was based on the old police call boxes – there's still one outside Earl's Court station.
address: Oxford Street, opposite Tottenham Court Road

name: Immersive Gamebox
why: Private game rooms with motion tracking and themed games – good for families.
line: Private game rooms with motion tracking and themed games – good for families.
story: No phones, no controllers – you move and the game follows you.

name: Omescape VR
why: Free-roam virtual reality games for 2 to 12 players.
line: Free-roam virtual reality games for 2 to 12 players.
story: A good one for teenagers who've done every escape room going.

name: Control Room B: Escape the Power Cut
why: An escape room in Battersea Power Station's real 1950s control room. 18+, weekends, cocktails included.
line: An escape room in Battersea Power Station's real 1950s control room.
story: Look up at the chimneys – the power station was on Pink Floyd's Animals cover, with a giant inflatable pig.

name: SPYSCAPE
why: An interactive spy experience – test your skills and find out what kind of spy you'd be. Check location before publishing.
line: An interactive spy experience – test your skills and find out what kind of spy you'd be.
story: Spy fans: the KGB's dead-letter lamp post in Mayfair is already in the app.

name: Alcotraz
why: A prison-themed cocktail experience – you bring the spirit, they make the cocktails. 18+.
line: A prison-themed cocktail experience – you bring the spirit, they make the cocktails.
story: You smuggle your own bottle in. It's all part of the act.

name: NQ64
why: Retro arcade machines, consoles and cocktails. Soho and Shoreditch. Under-18s Sundays 11am–3pm only.
line: Retro arcade machines, consoles and cocktails.
story: Pac-Man, Street Fighter and the games you played as a kid.

name: Fairgame
why: Grown-up fairground games with prizes and cocktails. Canary Wharf and One New Change by St Paul's. Adults only after 6pm.
line: Grown-up fairground games with prizes and cocktails.
story: After a game, take the lift to the free roof terrace at One New Change – a close-up view of St Paul's dome.
address: One New Change, EC4M; Canary Wharf

name: Lucky Voice
why: Private karaoke rooms, with drinks ordered from the room. Soho, Islington, Liverpool Street, Holborn and Waterloo.
line: Private karaoke rooms, with drinks ordered from the room.
story: The Waterloo one is under the station platforms – you might hear the trains between songs.
address: Soho; Islington; Liverpool Street; Holborn; Waterloo

name: Hijingo
why: High-tech bingo with live hosts, dancers and big screens.
line: High-tech bingo with live hosts, dancers and big screens.
story: Bingo calls are a London tradition – 'two fat ladies, 88', 'legs eleven'.

name: Dabbers Social Bingo
why: Social bingo with themed nights.
line: Social bingo with themed nights.
story: A good choice for a hen do or work night out.

name: Draughts
why: A board game café with over 1,000 games. Waterloo (in the Leake Street tunnel) and Stratford (Olympic Park). Under-12s free at Stratford.
line: A board game café with over 1,000 games.
story: The Waterloo café is in the graffiti tunnel under the station – Leake Street is already in the app.
address: Leake Street tunnel, Waterloo; Olympic Park, Stratford

name: Bounce
why: Ping pong bars with DJs and themed nights. Farringdon and Battersea Power Station.
line: Ping pong bars with DJs and themed nights.
story: Ping-pong started as a Victorian parlour game. A London firm, Jaques, registered the name 'Ping-Pong' in 1901.

name: Sixes Cricket
why: Indoor batting nets with smart bowling machines. London Bridge, Stratford and Boxpark Wembley. No skills needed.
line: Indoor batting nets with smart bowling machines.
story: Warm up here, then see the real thing at Lord's or the Oval – both in the app.

name: TOCA Social
why: Football games in private boxes with a ball machine and screen targets. The O2 and Westfield White City (the biggest, with VR).
line: Football games in private boxes with a ball machine and screen targets.
story: Good for football fans of every age – and you don't need to be any good.
address: The O2; Westfield London, White City

name: Gravity Max
why: Karting, bowling, VR and batting cages under one roof.
line: Karting, bowling, VR and batting cages under one roof.
story: A full day out for teenagers in one building.

name: Alexandra Palace Ice Rink
why: Year-round public ice skating, with views over London from the palace terrace outside.
line: Year-round public ice skating, with views over London from the palace terrace outside.
story: Ally Pally was where the BBC made the world's first regular TV broadcasts in 1936. Every Christmas it hosts the World Darts Championship.

name: Lee Valley Ice Centre
why: Two Olympic-size rinks with public skating and ice discos.
line: Two Olympic-size rinks with public skating and ice discos.
story: A cheaper, quieter skate than the seasonal rinks in central London.

name: Go Ape Battersea Park
why: Treetop rope courses and zip wires in Battersea Park. Check age and height limits when booking.
line: Treetop rope courses and zip wires in Battersea Park.
story: Battersea Park is already in the app – follow with the children's zoo or a pedalo on the lake.

name: Thames RIB Experience
why: A high-speed boat ride down the Thames past the City and Tower Bridge.
line: A high-speed boat ride down the Thames past the City and Tower Bridge.
story: The James Bond film The World Is Not Enough opens with a speedboat chase along this stretch of river.

name: Radio Rooftop
why: A 10th-floor rooftop on the Strand looking straight down the river to the London Eye and Big Ben. One of the best views in the West End.
line: A 10th-floor rooftop on the Strand looking straight down the river to the London Eye and Big Ben.

name: Madison
why: On top of One New Change, so close to St Paul's Cathedral you feel you could touch the dome. A great spot for a drink after visiting the cathedral.
line: On top of One New Change, so close to St Paul's Cathedral you feel you could touch the dome.
address: Rooftop Terrace, One New Change, London EC4M 9AF

name: 12th Knot
why: A rooftop cocktail bar on top of Sea Containers on the South Bank, reached by its own lift, with sweeping views up and down the Thames. Open Tuesday to Saturday.
line: A rooftop cocktail bar on top of Sea Containers on the South Bank, reached by its own lift, with sweeping views up and down the Thames.
address: Sea Containers London, 20 Upper Ground, London SE1 9PD

name: Seabird
why: A 14th-floor rooftop seafood restaurant and bar at the Hoxton Southwark, known for one of London's longest oyster lists and big views towards St Paul's.
line: A 14th-floor rooftop seafood restaurant and bar at the Hoxton Southwark, known for one of London's longest oyster lists and big views towards St Paul's.
address: The Hoxton Southwark, 40 Blackfriars Road, London SE1 8NY

line: London's most famous comedy club, just off Leicester Square, where generations of big-name comedians started out.

line: A pub off Essex Road in Angel with comedy seven nights a week and a beer garden.

line: Stand-up in Bethnal Green from Thursday to Saturday, many shows free, with dancing afterwards.

why: A small, much-loved comedy room in Crouch End, running since 1981.
line: A small, much-loved comedy room in Crouch End, running since 1981.

name: George Frideric Handel
why: Handel lived here from 1723 until his death in 1759 and wrote Messiah in the house. It's now the Handel half of Handel & Hendrix House.
line: Handel lived here from 1723 until his death in 1759 and wrote Messiah in the house.
story: Handel's neighbour, 200 years later, was Jimi Hendrix. It's one of the best two-plaque spots in London.

name: Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart
why: An eight-year-old Mozart wrote his first symphony here in 1764, when his family came to London.
line: An eight-year-old Mozart wrote his first symphony here in 1764, when his family came to London.
story: Pop round the corner to Orange Square, where there's a statue of the young Mozart with his violin.

name: Frédéric Chopin
why: Chopin stayed here in 1848 and left from this house to give his last ever public concert.
line: Chopin stayed here in 1848 and left from this house to give his last ever public concert.
story: Most people think of Chopin and Paris. Not many know his final performance was here in London.

name: Felix Mendelssohn
why: Mendelssohn stayed here on his first visit to London in 1829. He loved the city and came back again and again.
line: Mendelssohn stayed here on his first visit to London in 1829.
story: Queen Victoria was a big fan. He played for her at Buckingham Palace, just round the corner.

name: Ivor Novello
why: The songwriter and matinée idol lived in the flat above the theatre on the Aldwych for nearly 40 years. He wrote 'Keep the Home Fires Burning'.
line: The songwriter and matinée idol lived in the flat above the theatre on the Aldwych for nearly 40 years.
story: The theatre underneath is named after him now: the Novello. Look up next time you're going to a show there.

name: Marc Bolan
why: An English Heritage plaque to the T. Rex star and glam-rock pioneer, on his former home in Maida Vale.
line: An English Heritage plaque to the T.
story: Fans can pair it with the Marc Bolan Rock Shrine in Barnes, by the tree where he died in 1977.

name: Benjamin Britten
why: The composer lived here from 1931 to 1933 as a young music student.
line: The composer lived here from 1931 to 1933 as a young music student.
story: Twenty doors down at No. 153 is Alfred Hitchcock. Two plaques on the same stretch of the A4 that most people drive straight past.

name: Edward Elgar
why: Elgar's first London home, where he lived as a newly married man in 1890–91.
line: Elgar's first London home, where he lived as a newly married man in 1890–91.
story: He wrote the music for 'Land of Hope and Glory'. Think of him on the Last Night of the Proms.

name: Yehudi Menuhin
why: An English Heritage plaque to one of the greatest violinists of the 20th century, on his Belgravia home.
line: An English Heritage plaque to one of the greatest violinists of the 20th century, on his Belgravia home.

name: Sir Malcolm Sargent
why: The conductor who became the face of the BBC Proms lived and died in a flat right next to the Royal Albert Hall.
line: The conductor who became the face of the BBC Proms lived and died in a flat right next to the Royal Albert Hall.
story: You couldn't live much closer to work than that.
address: Albert Hall Mansions, Kensington Gore, London SW7 2AN

name: Adelaide Hall
why: The jazz singer who went from Harlem to London stardom. Her plaque went up in 2024, one of the newest in London.
line: The jazz singer who went from Harlem to London stardom.

name: Freddie Mercury
why: The Mercury family home from 1964, where a teenage Freddie started out in music. It's a private house near Heathrow, so one for real fans.
line: The Mercury family home from 1964, where a teenage Freddie started out in music.
story: Before Queen, Freddie worked as a baggage handler at Heathrow. Worth a thought next time you're on the way to the airport.

name: Charles Dickens
why: Dickens lived here from 1837 to 1839 and wrote Oliver Twist in the house. It's now the Charles Dickens Museum, so you can go inside.
line: Dickens lived here from 1837 to 1839 and wrote Oliver Twist in the house.
story: Dickens walked London for miles at night. He'd have made a fine cabbie with the Knowledge.

name: George Orwell
why: Orwell lived on the top floor here in 1935–36 and wrote most of Keep the Aspidistra Flying.
line: Orwell lived on the top floor here in 1935–36 and wrote most of Keep the Aspidistra Flying.
story: He was working in a bookshop in Hampstead at the time, which ended up in the novel.

name: Virginia Woolf
why: Woolf lived here from 1907 to 1911 and began her first novel, The Voyage Out, in the house.
line: Woolf lived here from 1907 to 1911 and began her first novel, The Voyage Out, in the house.
story: George Bernard Shaw lived in the same house years earlier, so there are two plaques on one front.

name: Agatha Christie
why: The Queen of Crime lived here from 1934 to 1941, at the height of her Poirot years.
line: The Queen of Crime lived here from 1934 to 1941, at the height of her Poirot years.
story: Her play The Mousetrap has been running in the West End since 1952, the longest-running play in the world.

name: Sylvia Plath
why: Plath lived here with Ted Hughes from 1960 to 1961, when her first collection of poems came out.
line: Plath lived here with Ted Hughes from 1960 to 1961, when her first collection of poems came out.
story: She later moved round the corner to 23 Fitzroy Road because it had W.B. Yeats's blue plaque on it. A plaque that led to another plaque.

name: John Keats
why: The house where Keats lived and fell in love with Fanny Brawne, the girl next door. It's now Keats House, open to visitors.
line: The house where Keats lived and fell in love with Fanny Brawne, the girl next door.
story: He's said to have written 'Ode to a Nightingale' under a plum tree in the garden.
address: Keats House, Keats Grove, London NW3 2RR

name: H.G. Wells
why: The author of The War of the Worlds and The Time Machine spent his last years here, overlooking Regent's Park.
line: The author of The War of the Worlds and The Time Machine spent his last years here, overlooking Regent's Park.
story: He stayed put right through the Blitz and wouldn't leave his house.

name: Mark Twain
why: Mark Twain lived here in 1896–97 while writing about his travels round the world.
line: Mark Twain lived here in 1896–97 while writing about his travels round the world.
story: It was during his London stay that a newspaper got hold of a rumour he was dying. His reply: reports of his death were an exaggeration.

name: Oscar Wilde
why: Wilde's family home from 1884 to 1895, where he wrote The Importance of Being Earnest.
line: Wilde's family home from 1884 to 1895, where he wrote The Importance of Being Earnest.
story: Tite Street is a cracker: Wilde here, the painter John Singer Sargent at No. 31, and Whistler lived on the street too.

name: Ian Fleming
why: An English Heritage plaque to the creator of James Bond, on his Belgravia home.
line: An English Heritage plaque to the creator of James Bond, on his Belgravia home.
story: Fleming gave Bond his own flat in Chelsea, just off the King's Road.

name: P.G. Wodehouse
why: The creator of Jeeves and Wooster lived here in Mayfair, right in the world he wrote about.
line: The creator of Jeeves and Wooster lived here in Mayfair, right in the world he wrote about.
story: Bertie Wooster's London was these few streets of Mayfair: the clubs, the flats and the butlers.

name: Rudyard Kipling
why: Kipling lived here from 1889 to 1891, when he first arrived in London and became famous almost overnight.
line: Kipling lived here from 1889 to 1891, when he first arrived in London and became famous almost overnight.
story: It's at the bottom of Villiers Street by Embankment station, so it's an easy one to look at on your way past.

name: J.M. Barrie
why: Barrie lived here, opposite Kensington Gardens, when he wrote Peter Pan.
line: Barrie lived here, opposite Kensington Gardens, when he wrote Peter Pan.
story: Cross into Kensington Gardens to find the Peter Pan statue. Barrie had it put up overnight in 1912 as a surprise for the children.

name: Bram Stoker
why: The author of Dracula lived here in Chelsea.
line: The author of Dracula lived here in Chelsea.
story: His day job was running the Lyceum Theatre, which is still going strong off the Strand.

name: A.A. Milne
why: Milne lived here in Chelsea, where he wrote the Winnie-the-Pooh stories.
line: Milne lived here in Chelsea, where he wrote the Winnie-the-Pooh stories.
story: The real Winnie was a bear at London Zoo that a young Christopher Robin loved to visit.

name: Alfred Hitchcock
why: Hitchcock lived here from 1926 to 1939, the years of his great British films like The 39 Steps and The Lady Vanishes.
line: Hitchcock lived here from 1926 to 1939, the years of his great British films like The 39 Steps and The Lady Vanishes.
story: Thousands drive past it every day on the A4 in from Heathrow and hardly anyone knows it's there. Next time you're on that road, look out for it.

name: Charlie Chaplin
why: Chaplin grew up poor in Lambeth and Kennington, and this plaque marks one of his early homes.
line: Chaplin grew up poor in Lambeth and Kennington, and this plaque marks one of his early homes.
story: From these streets to Hollywood. There's a statue of him in Leicester Square, too.
address: 15 Glenshaw Mansions, Brixton Road, London SW9 0DS

name: Laurence Olivier
why: An English Heritage plaque to Britain's most famous stage and screen actor, on his Pimlico home.
line: An English Heritage plaque to Britain's most famous stage and screen actor, on his Pimlico home.
story: Theatre's big awards, the Oliviers, are named after him, and so is the largest theatre at the National.

name: Vivien Leigh
why: The Gone with the Wind star lived in a flat here in Eaton Square.
line: The Gone with the Wind star lived in a flat here in Eaton Square.
story: She was married to Laurence Olivier for 20 years. Their two plaques are only a short ride apart.

name: Audrey Hepburn
why: An English Heritage plaque to the Roman Holiday and Breakfast at Tiffany's star, on her Mayfair home.
line: An English Heritage plaque to the Roman Holiday and Breakfast at Tiffany's star, on her Mayfair home.
story: Before Hollywood, she danced in the chorus of West End shows.

name: Ava Gardner
why: The Hollywood star made London her home for the last 20 or so years of her life, here in Knightsbridge.
line: The Hollywood star made London her home for the last 20 or so years of her life, here in Knightsbridge.

name: Tony Hancock
why: Hancock lived here from 1952 to 1958, the years of Hancock's Half Hour on radio and TV.
line: Hancock lived here from 1952 to 1958, the years of Hancock's Half Hour on radio and TV.

name: Kenneth Williams
why: The Carry On star lived in a flat here, just off Baker Street.
line: The Carry On star lived in a flat here, just off Baker Street.
story: It's right behind Madame Tussauds, so you can see the real famous faces and then the wax ones.
address: Farley Court, Allsop Place, London NW1 5LG

name: John Logie Baird
why: Baird gave the world's first demonstration of television here in 1926.
line: Baird gave the world's first demonstration of television here in 1926.
story: Bar Italia is underneath, open almost round the clock. Have a coffee where telly was born.

name: Sir John Gielgud
why: An English Heritage plaque to one of the great actors of the 20th century, on his Westminster home.
line: An English Heritage plaque to one of the great actors of the 20th century, on his Westminster home.
story: The Gielgud Theatre on Shaftesbury Avenue is named after him.

name: Charles Laughton
why: The actor lived here from 1928 to 1931. He went on to become the first British actor to win the Best Actor Oscar.
line: The actor lived here from 1928 to 1931.

name: Alastair Sim
why: Sim lived here from 1953 to 1975. Many people say his Scrooge in the 1951 film is the best ever.
line: Sim lived here from 1953 to 1975.
story: A perfect one to visit at Christmas.

name: Gracie Fields
why: The singer and film star, one of the biggest names in Britain in the 1930s, lived here on Upper Street.
line: The singer and film star, one of the biggest names in Britain in the 1930s, lived here on Upper Street.

name: Boris Karloff
why: Karloff was born here in 1887 as William Henry Pratt.
line: Karloff was born here in 1887 as William Henry Pratt.
story: Frankenstein's monster was a South London boy.

name: Sir Ralph Richardson
why: The actor lived here from 1944 to 1968.
line: The actor lived here from 1944 to 1968.
story: He was famous for riding his motorbike well into old age.
address: Bedegar's Lea, Kenwood Close, London NW3 7JL

name: Diana, Princess of Wales
why: Lady Diana Spencer's flat from 1979 to 1981, where she lived with friends before her engagement to Prince Charles.
line: Lady Diana Spencer's flat from 1979 to 1981, where she lived with friends before her engagement to Prince Charles.
story: In the run-up to the engagement, photographers camped outside every day waiting for her to come out.
address: Coleherne Court, Old Brompton Road, London SW5 0EF

name: Sir Winston Churchill
why: Churchill lived here after the war and died in the house in 1965.
line: Churchill lived here after the war and died in the house in 1965.
story: He bought No. 27 next door as well, for his staff and offices.

name: Mahatma Gandhi
why: Gandhi lived here as a young law student in London in the 1890s.
line: Gandhi lived here as a young law student in London in the 1890s.
story: There's a statue of him in Parliament Square, and another in Tavistock Square.

name: Charles de Gaulle
why: De Gaulle led the Free French from this building during the Second World War.
line: De Gaulle led the Free French from this building during the Second World War.

name: Karl Marx
why: Marx and his family lived in two rooms here in the 1850s, very short of money.
line: Marx and his family lived in two rooms here in the 1850s, very short of money.
story: Today the building is home to Quo Vadis, a smart Soho restaurant. He'd have been surprised.

name: Napoleon III
why: The future Emperor of France lived here in exile in 1848.
line: The future Emperor of France lived here in exile in 1848.
story: While he was in London he signed up as a special constable to help police the Chartist demonstrations.

name: Florence Nightingale
why: The founder of modern nursing lived here in Mayfair for over 40 years until her death in 1910.
line: The founder of modern nursing lived here in Mayfair for over 40 years until her death in 1910.
story: The Florence Nightingale Museum is across the river at St Thomas' Hospital.

name: Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst
why: A plaque to the leader of the suffragettes and her daughter, on their Notting Hill home.
line: A plaque to the leader of the suffragettes and her daughter, on their Notting Hill home.
story: There's a statue of Emmeline right next to Parliament, in Victoria Tower Gardens.

name: Jawaharlal Nehru
why: India's first Prime Minister lived here as a student in 1910 and 1912.
line: India's first Prime Minister lived here as a student in 1910 and 1912.

name: Simón Bolívar
why: The Liberator of Latin America stayed here in 1810.
line: The Liberator of Latin America stayed here in 1810.
story: There's a statue of him in Belgrave Square.

name: Charles Darwin
why: Darwin lived on this site from 1838 to 1842, soon after returning from his voyage on HMS Beagle.
line: Darwin lived on this site from 1838 to 1842, soon after returning from his voyage on HMS Beagle.
story: Fittingly, the plaque is now on a university biology building.
address: Biological Sciences Building, University College, Gower Street, London WC1E 6BT

name: Sir Alexander Fleming
why: The man who discovered penicillin lived here in Chelsea.
line: The man who discovered penicillin lived here in Chelsea.
story: He made the discovery at St Mary's Hospital in Paddington, where you can visit his little lab.

name: Sir Isaac Newton
why: Newton lived here on Jermyn Street in the early 1700s.
line: Newton lived here on Jermyn Street in the early 1700s.
story: Jermyn Street is London's famous street for shirtmakers, so it's a good one for a browse too.

name: Benjamin Franklin
why: Franklin lived here for nearly 16 years. It's the only home of his still standing anywhere, and it's now a museum you can visit.
line: Franklin lived here for nearly 16 years.
story: One of America's Founding Fathers, living a few minutes' walk from Trafalgar Square.

name: Michael Faraday
why: Faraday worked here as a young apprentice bookbinder, reading the science books he was binding.
line: Faraday worked here as a young apprentice bookbinder, reading the science books he was binding.
story: From binding books to inventing the electric motor. Not bad for a lad with little schooling.

name: Alan Turing
why: The codebreaker and computer pioneer was born here in 1912. The building is now a hotel.
line: The codebreaker and computer pioneer was born here in 1912.

name: Ada Lovelace
why: Lovelace, often called the first computer programmer, lived here on St James's Square.
line: Lovelace, often called the first computer programmer, lived here on St James's Square.
story: She worked with Charles Babbage, whose own plaque is in Marylebone.

name: Charles Babbage
why: The inventor of the first computing machines lived and worked here.
line: The inventor of the first computing machines lived and worked here.
story: He famously waged war on street musicians playing outside his window.

name: Rosalind Franklin
why: Franklin lived here from 1951 to 1958, when her X-ray photos helped reveal the structure of DNA.
line: Franklin lived here from 1951 to 1958, when her X-ray photos helped reveal the structure of DNA.
address: Donovan Court, Drayton Gardens, London SW10 9QS

name: Mary Seacole
why: The Jamaican-born nurse who cared for soldiers in the Crimean War lived here on Soho Square.
line: The Jamaican-born nurse who cared for soldiers in the Crimean War lived here on Soho Square.
story: Her statue stands outside St Thomas' Hospital, looking across the river at Parliament.

name: Vincent van Gogh
why: A young Van Gogh lodged here in 1873–74 while working for an art dealer in Covent Garden.
line: A young Van Gogh lodged here in 1873–74 while working for an art dealer in Covent Garden.
story: The story goes he fell for his landlady's daughter, who turned him down.

name: John Constable
why: Constable lived here in Hampstead and painted the skies over the Heath.
line: Constable lived here in Hampstead and painted the skies over the Heath.
story: Have a walk on Hampstead Heath afterwards and you'll see what he was painting.

name: Thomas Gainsborough
why: Gainsborough lived and worked here on Pall Mall for the last years of his life.
line: Gainsborough lived and worked here on Pall Mall for the last years of his life.
address: Schomberg House, 82 Pall Mall, London SW1Y 5ES

name: Canaletto
why: The Venetian painter lodged here while painting his famous views of London and the Thames.
line: The Venetian painter lodged here while painting his famous views of London and the Thames.

name: James McNeill Whistler
why: Whistler lived here on the river and painted his famous 'Whistler's Mother' while he was in Chelsea.
line: Whistler lived here on the river and painted his famous 'Whistler's Mother' while he was in Chelsea.
story: Cheyne Walk is full of plaques. Walk it from end to end and see how many you can spot.

name: Dante Gabriel Rossetti
why: The painter and poet lived here, sharing the house with the poet Swinburne.
line: The painter and poet lived here, sharing the house with the poet Swinburne.
story: He kept a menagerie of animals in the garden, including a wombat.

name: John Singer Sargent
why: The great portrait painter had his home and studio here for over 20 years.
line: The great portrait painter had his home and studio here for over 20 years.
story: Oscar Wilde lived a few doors along at No. 34.

name: Piet Mondrian
why: The Dutch painter lived here in Hampstead in the late 1930s, before leaving for New York.
line: The Dutch painter lived here in Hampstead in the late 1930s, before leaving for New York.

name: J.M.W. Turner
why: Turner designed and built this house himself as a country retreat. It's now Turner's House, open to visitors.
line: Turner designed and built this house himself as a country retreat.
story: You've probably got Turner in your wallet: he's on the £20 note.

name: William Blake
why: Blake stayed here in Hampstead as the guest of his friend, the painter John Linnell.
line: Blake stayed here in Hampstead as the guest of his friend, the painter John Linnell.
story: Blake wrote the words of 'Jerusalem'.
address: Old Wyldes', North End, London NW3 7HS

name: Trinity
why: Adam Byatt's much-loved restaurant on the edge of Clapham Old Town, long rated one of south London's best. Refined British cooking downstairs, and a more relaxed upstairs room where the short rib pie has a following of its own. One for a special occasion.
line: Adam Byatt's much-loved restaurant on the edge of Clapham Old Town, long rated one of south London's best.

name: Sorella
why: A lively little Italian on a back street off Clapham High Street. Arancini, proper pasta and a buzzy, romantic room. Book ahead.
line: A lively little Italian on a back street off Clapham High Street.

name: Minnow
why: A relaxed neighbourhood restaurant on the corner of Clapham Common, with a terrace looking over the Common. Good for brunch on a sunny weekend or an easy dinner.
line: A relaxed neighbourhood restaurant on the corner of Clapham Common, with a terrace looking over the Common.

name: Megan's on the Hill
why: A Balham favourite with fairy-tale interiors and a garden feel: brunch, coffee and cake by day, Mediterranean plates and cocktails in the evening. A short walk from Balham station.
line: A Balham favourite with fairy-tale interiors and a garden feel: brunch, coffee and cake by day, Mediterranean plates and cocktails in the evening.

name: The Umi
why: A small Balham Japanese in the izakaya style: Korean-spiced lamb chops, black-pepper squid and good sashimi. Relaxed and reasonably priced. (Address to confirm.)
line: A small Balham Japanese in the izakaya style: Korean-spiced lamb chops, black-pepper squid and good sashimi.

name: The Avalon
why: A big, handsome Balham pub with three outdoor spaces, including a large garden, and a kitchen that takes its food seriously. Popular for the Sunday roast, so book for a weekend.
line: A big, handsome Balham pub with three outdoor spaces, including a large garden, and a kitchen that takes its food seriously.

name: The Windmill
why: A Young's pub and inn right on Clapham Common, with a big garden for summer. Known for generous Sunday roasts and steaks. Perfect after a walk across the Common.
line: A Young's pub and inn right on Clapham Common, with a big garden for summer.
address: Clapham Common South Side, London SW4 9DE

name: The Bobbin
why: A cosy backstreet local in Clapham Old Town with a hidden garden out back, darts, a seasonal menu and a good Sunday roast. Feels a world away from the High Street.
line: A cosy backstreet local in Clapham Old Town with a hidden garden out back, darts, a seasonal menu and a good Sunday roast.

name: The Abbeville
why: The heart of Abbeville Village, the pretty little high street between Clapham and Balham. Fireside in winter, tables outside in summer, and a good-value pie-and-pint night on Mondays.
