why: A proper 1940s London caff behind Westminster, with black tiles outside and full English breakfasts inside. Order at the counter and listen for your name being shouted.
line: A proper 1940s London caff behind Westminster, with black tiles outside and full English breakfasts inside.
story: You might know it from the film Layer Cake. Closed Sundays.

name: E Pellicci
why: The East End café, run by the same family since 1900, with a listed Art Deco wood-panelled room. Full English in the morning, Italian home cooking at lunch, and a warm welcome from the Pelliccis. Breakfast and lunch only; closed Sundays.
line: The East End café, run by the same family since 1900, with a listed Art Deco wood-panelled room.
story: The Kray twins were regulars back in the day. The café is Grade II listed, so the wood panelling isn't going anywhere.

name: The Wolseley
why: A grand Viennese-style café on Piccadilly, in an old 1920s car showroom. Breakfast here is a London treat: eggs Benedict, kedgeree, pastries, all under a soaring black-and-gold ceiling. Afternoon tea too.
line: A grand Viennese-style café on Piccadilly, in an old 1920s car showroom.
story: The building started life as the showroom for Wolseley cars, then became a bank – look at the marble and the height of the ceiling.

name: Jack the Ripper Museum
why: A Victorian house on Cable Street telling the story of the 1888 Whitechapel murders over several floors – the suspects, the newspapers, the police, and the lives of the women themselves. You look at the evidence and decide who you think did it. Open daily 9.30am–6pm.
line: A Victorian house on Cable Street telling the story of the 1888 Whitechapel murders over several floors – the suspects, the newspapers, the police, and the lives of the women themselves.
story: Pair it with a walk round the Ripper streets and a drink at the Ten Bells on Commercial Street, where two of the victims are said to have drunk.

name: Golden Phoenix
why: Cantonese cooking and dim sum in Chinatown, with something rare: a separate gluten-free kitchen and a full gluten-free menu, so coeliacs can order dim sum and Chinese classics with confidence.
line: Cantonese cooking and dim sum in Chinatown, with something rare: a separate gluten-free kitchen and a full gluten-free menu, so coeliacs can order dim sum and Chinese classics with confidence.

name: Niche
why: A 100% gluten-free restaurant near Angel and Sadler's Wells, known for its pies and proper British comfort food, with nothing to worry about on the menu. A favourite with coeliacs.
line: A 100% gluten-free restaurant near Angel and Sadler's Wells – pies, fish and chips, Sunday roasts and puddings, with nothing to worry about on the menu.

name: Leggero
why: Fresh pasta in Soho where everything on the menu is gluten-free – a small, friendly Italian on Old Compton Street. Book ahead; it's tiny.
line: Fresh pasta in Soho where everything on the menu is gluten-free – a small, friendly Italian on Old Compton Street.

name: Indigo at One Aldwych
why: A smart hotel restaurant on a mezzanine above One Aldwych's lobby bar, where the whole menu is gluten-free and dairy-free. Handy for a pre-theatre dinner in Covent Garden.
line: A smart hotel restaurant on a mezzanine above One Aldwych's lobby bar, where the whole menu is gluten-free and dairy-free.

name: Jailhouse Bar at the Courthouse Hotel
why: Cocktails in the old holding cells of Old Street Magistrates' Court, now the Courthouse Hotel. Five original cells, heavy doors and all, have been turned into little booths for drinks. Book a cell for a group.
line: Cocktails in the old holding cells of Old Street Magistrates' Court, now the Courthouse Hotel.
story: The Kray twins were held in these cells before going up before the magistrates. The courtrooms upstairs are part of the hotel now.

name: Maria's Market Café
why: A proper market caff in the middle of Borough Market, famous for its bubble and squeak and big fry-ups. Traders have eaten here for years. Open Wednesday to Saturday.
line: A proper market caff in the middle of Borough Market, famous for its bubble and squeak and big fry-ups.
story: Maria herself has retired, but the café carries on under new owners – sit at the counter with the traders.
address: Three Crown Square, Borough Market, London SE1 9AL

name: Lantana London Bridge
why: Aussie café culture next to Borough Market – corn fritters, smashed avocado and good coffee, in a restored building with tables out front. Busy for weekend brunch.
line: Aussie café culture next to Borough Market – corn fritters, smashed avocado and good coffee, in a restored building with tables out front.

name: The Breakfast Club London Bridge
why: Pancakes, fry-ups and breakfast burritos in a fun, cluttered café a few steps from Borough Market. Expect a queue at weekends.
line: Pancakes, fry-ups and breakfast burritos in a fun, cluttered café a few steps from Borough Market.
story: Ask staff if you're 'here to see Mr Lucky' – it opens the way to a hidden bar.

name: Pavilion Café, Greenwich Park
why: All-day breakfasts in a little octagonal café inside Greenwich Park, a short walk from the Royal Observatory. Sit outside on a sunny morning.
line: All-day breakfasts in a little octagonal café inside Greenwich Park, a short walk from the Royal Observatory.
address: Charlton Way, Greenwich Park, London SE10 8QY

name: Royal Teas
why: A friendly little café on Royal Hill doing Belgian waffles, all-day breakfasts and good tea. Walk-ins only.
line: A friendly little café on Royal Hill doing Belgian waffles, all-day breakfasts and good tea.

name: Heap's Sausage Café
why: Greenwich's sausage specialist – proper bangers, full English and breakfast baps, just off the town centre.
line: Greenwich's sausage specialist – proper bangers, full English and breakfast baps, just off the town centre.

name: Sunday
why: A much-loved neighbourhood café in Barnsbury, famous for its brunch – smoked haddock rarebit, pancakes and generous fry-ups – and a garden out back. Be ready to queue at weekends.
line: A much-loved neighbourhood café in Barnsbury, famous for its brunch – smoked haddock rarebit, pancakes and generous fry-ups – and a garden out back.

name: The Breakfast Club Angel
why: Pancakes, fry-ups and breakfast burritos on pretty Camden Passage, among the antique shops. Busy at weekends.
line: Pancakes, fry-ups and breakfast burritos on pretty Camden Passage, among the antique shops.

name: Cinnamon Bazaar Richmond
why: Indian breakfasts by the Cinnamon Club team – Bombay scrambled eggs and stuffed parathas – a few minutes from Richmond station and on the way to Kew.
line: Indian breakfasts by the Cinnamon Club team – Bombay scrambled eggs and stuffed parathas – a few minutes from Richmond station and on the way to Kew.

name: Antipodea
why: An Aussie all-day brasserie on Hill Street, just up from the river – folded eggs, good coffee and a treacle-cured bacon sandwich.
line: An Aussie all-day brasserie on Hill Street, just up from the river – folded eggs, good coffee and a treacle-cured bacon sandwich.

name: The Black Cab Coffee Co
why: A bright café by the river at Nine Elms with an all-day breakfast – the eggs Benedict is the one to order. Handy for the US Embassy and Battersea Power Station.
line: A bright café by the river at Nine Elms with an all-day breakfast – the eggs Benedict is the one to order.
story: With a name like that, we had to put it in.

name: Megan's at Battersea Power Station
why: All-day brunch – shakshuka, pancakes and mezze – in Circus West Village, right under the Power Station's chimneys. Walk-in only at weekends until 4pm.
line: All-day brunch – shakshuka, pancakes and mezze – in Circus West Village, right under the Power Station's chimneys.

name: The Laundry
why: An easy-going all-day bistro on Coldharbour Lane – toasted banana bread, Turkish eggs and a good fry-up.
line: An easy-going all-day bistro on Coldharbour Lane – toasted banana bread, Turkish eggs and a good fry-up.

name: Parissi
why: A small Mediterranean café on Atlantic Road by Brixton market – breakfast plates in the week, pastries and frittatas at weekends.
line: A small Mediterranean café on Atlantic Road by Brixton market – breakfast plates in the week, pastries and frittatas at weekends.

name: Caravan Canary Wharf
why: All-day brunch from around the world and their own roasted coffee, by the water at Reuters Plaza.
line: All-day brunch from around the world and their own roasted coffee, by the water at Reuters Plaza.

name: Dishoom Canary Wharf
why: Dishoom's Bombay breakfast – bacon naan rolls, akuri and bottomless chai – in Wood Wharf. Breakfast until late morning. There's a separate gluten-free menu.
line: Dishoom's Bombay breakfast – bacon naan rolls, akuri and bottomless chai – in Wood Wharf.

name: Hideaway
why: A smart little café on Mount Street from Michelin-starred chef Ollie Dabbous, of Hide. Pastries baked every day, a smoked salmon bagel, and avocado toast you can top with caviar. Not cheap, but very good.
line: A smart little café on Mount Street from Michelin-starred chef Ollie Dabbous, of Hide.
story: Ollie Dabbous's Michelin-starred restaurant Hide is just round the corner on Piccadilly.

name: The Muffin Man Tea Shop
why: An old-fashioned tea room just off Kensington High Street, open since 1962 – breakfasts, scones, cakes and an affordable afternoon tea. Always busy, and it's easy to see why.
line: An old-fashioned tea room just off Kensington High Street, open since 1962 – breakfasts, scones, cakes and an affordable afternoon tea.
story: It calls itself the oldest tea room in Kensington.

name: Drury 188-189
why: A busy little brunch café on Drury Lane – eggs Benedict and Florentine with homemade hollandaise, and the famous baklava pancakes. No bookings, so expect a short queue.
line: A busy little brunch café on Drury Lane – eggs Benedict and Florentine with homemade hollandaise, and the famous baklava pancakes.

name: Comptoir Libanais Southbank
why: Lebanese breakfasts at the Southbank Centre from 9am – shakshuka, man'oushe flatbreads and a Lebanese full breakfast, with veggie and vegan versions.
line: Lebanese breakfasts at the Southbank Centre from 9am – shakshuka, man'oushe flatbreads and a Lebanese full breakfast, with veggie and vegan versions.
address: Southbank Centre, Belvedere Road, London SE1 8XX

name: The Victory, Waterloo
why: A pub above Waterloo station's Victory Arch that opens at 8am for a big classic fry-up – handy before a train or a morning on the South Bank.
line: A pub above Waterloo station's Victory Arch that opens at 8am for a big classic fry-up – handy before a train or a morning on the South Bank.
story: The Victory Arch below is Waterloo's memorial to railway staff who died in the First World War.

name: Riding House Bloomsbury
why: Brunch in the 1960s Brunswick Centre near Russell Square – malted pancakes and big breakfasts in a bright, buzzy room. Thanksgiving 2026: for the 15th year, a family-style feast with turkey, the sides and a vegetarian wellington at lunch and dinner on Thu 26 Nov at all three Riding House branches (Bloomsbury, Fitzrovia and Victoria), £65 a head.
line: Brunch in the 1960s Brunswick Centre near Russell Square – malted pancakes and big breakfasts in a bright, buzzy room.
address: 1 Brunswick Centre, Bernard Street, London WC1N 1AF

name: Salt & Pepper
why: A no-fuss café a minute from the British Museum – English breakfasts, eggs any way and a cup of tea before the crowds arrive.
line: A no-fuss café a minute from the British Museum – English breakfasts, eggs any way and a cup of tea before the crowds arrive.

name: Mildred's Camden
why: A colourful, all plant-based restaurant by the canal in Camden, with a popular weekend brunch.
line: A colourful, all plant-based restaurant by the canal in Camden, with a popular weekend brunch.

name: Bluebird Café
why: Breakfast from 9am in the café and courtyard of the Bluebird – a 1920s Art Deco garage on the King's Road.
line: Breakfast from 9am in the café and courtyard of the Bluebird – a 1920s Art Deco garage on the King's Road.
story: The building began life as a garage for Bluebird cars, named after Malcolm Campbell's record-breaking Bluebird.

name: Ottolenghi Belgravia
why: Yotam Ottolenghi's deli and café on smart Motcomb Street – colourful salads, pastries and a proper breakfast menu.
line: Yotam Ottolenghi's deli and café on smart Motcomb Street – colourful salads, pastries and a proper breakfast menu.

name: Dishoom Shoreditch
why: Dishoom's Bombay breakfast – bacon naan rolls and bottomless chai – with a lovely veranda, by Shoreditch's Boundary Street. There's a separate gluten-free menu.
line: Dishoom's Bombay breakfast – bacon naan rolls and bottomless chai – with a lovely veranda, by Shoreditch's Boundary Street.

name: The Cadogan Arms
why: A smart, proper pub on the King's Road, brought back to life by the team behind the Ivy Asia and JKS. The Sunday roast is one of the best in west London – book ahead.
line: A smart, proper pub on the King's Road, brought back to life by the team behind the Ivy Asia and JKS.

name: The Fox & Pheasant
why: A cosy, country-style pub tucked behind Stamford Bridge, with a fire, a garden and a well-loved Sunday roast. Packed on Chelsea match days.
line: A cosy, country-style pub tucked behind Stamford Bridge, with a fire, a garden and a well-loved Sunday roast.

name: The Mall Tavern
why: A Notting Hill Gate local just up from Kensington Palace, known for its Sunday roast and big cow pie.
line: A Notting Hill Gate local just up from Kensington Palace, known for its Sunday roast and big cow pie.

name: Hereford Arms
why: A friendly pub on Gloucester Road, a few minutes from the South Kensington museums – handy for a Sunday roast after the Natural History Museum.
line: A friendly pub on Gloucester Road, a few minutes from the South Kensington museums – handy for a Sunday roast after the Natural History Museum.

name: The Barley Mow, Westminster
why: A traditional pub on Horseferry Road, a short walk from Westminster Abbey, with a generous Sunday roast drowned in gravy.
line: A traditional pub on Horseferry Road, a short walk from Westminster Abbey, with a generous Sunday roast drowned in gravy.

name: The Goring Dining Room
why: Sunday lunch in grand style at The Goring, the royal family's favourite hotel, just behind Buckingham Palace. Roast beef carved at the table.
line: Sunday lunch in grand style at The Goring, the royal family's favourite hotel, just behind Buckingham Palace.
story: Kate Middleton spent the night before her wedding here.

name: The Colonel Fawcett
why: A smart, friendly Camden pub on a quiet corner, popular for its Sunday roast and gin list.
line: A smart, friendly Camden pub on a quiet corner, popular for its Sunday roast and gin list.

name: The Duke of Greenwich
why: A backstreet Greenwich pub doing roasts family-style – beef and lamb from a Dorset farm, with unlimited veg and gravy.
line: A backstreet Greenwich pub doing roasts family-style – beef and lamb from a Dorset farm, with unlimited veg and gravy.

name: The Albion, Islington
why: A wisteria-covered Georgian pub in Barnsbury with one of north London's best beer gardens and a much-loved Sunday roast.
line: A wisteria-covered Georgian pub in Barnsbury with one of north London's best beer gardens and a much-loved Sunday roast.

name: The Guinea Grill
why: A pub has stood on this Mayfair mews for centuries; the grill room behind it is famous for steak, steak and kidney pie, and roast beef on Sundays.
line: A pub has stood on this Mayfair mews for centuries; the grill room behind it is famous for steak, steak and kidney pie, and roast beef on Sundays.

name: Berners Tavern
why: A breathtaking dining room in The London Edition hotel, its walls covered floor to ceiling in pictures. The Sunday roast is a proper treat.
line: A breathtaking dining room in The London Edition hotel, its walls covered floor to ceiling in pictures.

name: Hawksmoor Spitalfields
why: The original Hawksmoor, by Spitalfields Market. Their Sunday roast – rump of beef with duck-fat potatoes and a big Yorkshire – is one of London's best known.
line: The original Hawksmoor, by Spitalfields Market.

name: Bread Street Kitchen Limehouse
why: Gordon Ramsay's riverside restaurant in Limehouse (once The Narrow), with a Sunday roast and Thames views.
line: Gordon Ramsay's riverside restaurant in Limehouse (once The Narrow), with a Sunday roast and Thames views.

name: Town of Ramsgate
why: An ancient, narrow riverside pub in Wapping, next to the old Wapping Stairs – a Sunday roast with centuries of history.
line: An ancient, narrow riverside pub in Wapping, next to the old Wapping Stairs – a Sunday roast with centuries of history.
story: Captain Bligh of the Bounty is said to have drunk here, and 'hanging judge' Jeffreys was caught here trying to flee in 1688.

name: The White Swan, Richmond
why: A pretty little pub on an old lane off Richmond Green, with a garden and a proper Sunday roast.
line: A pretty little pub on an old lane off Richmond Green, with a garden and a proper Sunday roast.

name: Masters Superfish
why: An old-school chippy on Waterloo Road with fish straight from Billingsgate, generous portions and crispy whitebait. A short walk from the Old Vic and Waterloo station.
line: An old-school chippy on Waterloo Road with fish straight from Billingsgate, generous portions and crispy whitebait.
story: Cabbies have been eating here for decades.

name: Fish Central
why: A family-run chippy near Old Street since 1968 – very fresh fish at fair prices, and a proper sit-down dining room.
line: A family-run chippy near Old Street since 1968 – very fresh fish at fair prices, and a proper sit-down dining room.

name: Seafresh
why: A Pimlico fish restaurant near Victoria station – big portions of very fresh fish, with table service and a wine list.
line: A Pimlico fish restaurant near Victoria station – big portions of very fresh fish, with table service and a wine list.

name: The Laughing Halibut
why: A traditional chippy on Strutton Ground market street, a few minutes from Westminster Abbey – takeaway or a seat at the back. Closed Sundays.
line: A traditional chippy on Strutton Ground market street, a few minutes from Westminster Abbey – takeaway or a seat at the back.

name: Poppies Fish and Chips Spitalfields
why: The original Poppies, by Spitalfields Market – 1950s décor, fish from Billingsgate and chips in mock newspaper.
line: The original Poppies, by Spitalfields Market – 1950s décor, fish from Billingsgate and chips in mock newspaper.
story: Founder Pat 'Pop' Newland started in the trade in 1945, aged 11.

name: Poppies Fish and Chips Camden
why: Poppies' retro chippy just off Camden Market – Billingsgate fish and chips in mock newspaper.
line: Poppies' retro chippy just off Camden Market – Billingsgate fish and chips in mock newspaper.

name: North Sea Fish Restaurant
why: A traditional sit-down fish restaurant on a quiet Bloomsbury street – fish fried or grilled, done properly.
line: A traditional sit-down fish restaurant on a quiet Bloomsbury street – fish fried or grilled, done properly.
story: Every cabbie learns this one on the Knowledge.

name: The Fryer's Delight
why: A 1962 chippy on Theobald's Road with Formica tables and chips fried in beef dripping. Cheap and proper.
line: A 1962 chippy on Theobald's Road with Formica tables and chips fried in beef dripping.

name: Sutton & Sons Islington
why: A fishmonger's chippy on Essex Road – very fresh fish, oysters, and good vegan 'fish' too.
line: A fishmonger's chippy on Essex Road – very fresh fish, oysters, and good vegan 'fish' too.

name: Sutton & Sons
why: The original Sutton & Sons on Stoke Newington High Street – fresh fish, local craft beers and sticky toffee pudding.
line: The original Sutton & Sons on Stoke Newington High Street – fresh fish, local craft beers and sticky toffee pudding.
address: 90 Stoke Newington High Street, London N16 7NY

name: Fish Lounge
why: A spotless chippy on Brixton Hill – light, crisp batter, thick chips, and extras like Jamaican patties.
line: A spotless chippy on Brixton Hill – light, crisp batter, thick chips, and extras like Jamaican patties.

name: Toff's
why: An award-winning, wood-panelled family chippy in Muswell Hill, open since 1968 – grease-free batter and sustainably sourced fish.
line: An award-winning, wood-panelled family chippy in Muswell Hill, open since 1968 – grease-free batter and sustainably sourced fish.

name: Kennedy's
why: A London fish and chip name going back about 150 years, when Kennedy's started as a butcher's famous for its sausages. Fish from British waters, proper pies and big portions. Two shops near the Barbican: Whitecross Street and Goswell Road.
line: A London fish and chip name going back about 150 years, when Kennedy's started as a butcher's famous for its sausages.
story: Recommended by a London cabbie.
address: 169 Whitecross Street, London EC1Y 8JT; also Goswell Road, EC1V 7DT

name: Senza Fondo
why: Italian-American and loud, with bottomless lasagne – slow-cooked beef shin and lots of béchamel, about £20 a head, as many slices as you can manage. Party music and cocktails; great for groups.
line: Italian-American and loud, with bottomless lasagne – slow-cooked beef shin and lots of béchamel, about £20 a head, as many slices as you can manage.
story: The record, apparently, is seven slices.

name: Gloria
why: A flamboyant 1970s Capri-style trattoria from the Big Mamma group – huge plates of pasta, wood-fired pizza and a famously tall lemon meringue pie.
line: A flamboyant 1970s Capri-style trattoria from the Big Mamma group – huge plates of pasta, wood-fired pizza and a famously tall lemon meringue pie.

name: Il Portico
why: Said to be London's oldest family-run restaurant – the Chiavarini family have run it since the 1960s, cooking simple food from Emilia-Romagna on Kensington High Street.
line: Said to be London's oldest family-run restaurant – the Chiavarini family have run it since the 1960s, cooking simple food from Emilia-Romagna on Kensington High Street.

name: Lina Stores King's Cross
why: Fresh pasta from the famous Soho deli, in Coal Drops Yard – quick, good and fairly priced.
line: Fresh pasta from the famous Soho deli, in Coal Drops Yard – quick, good and fairly priced.
story: Lina Stores has been selling Italian food on Brewer Street in Soho since 1944.

name: Spagnoletti
why: A friendly, family-run Italian on Euston Road, handy for King's Cross, St Pancras and Euston.
line: A friendly, family-run Italian on Euston Road, handy for King's Cross, St Pancras and Euston.

name: Luce e Limoni
why: A warm Sicilian restaurant on Gray's Inn Road – lemons everywhere, fresh pasta and Sicilian wines.
line: A warm Sicilian restaurant on Gray's Inn Road – lemons everywhere, fresh pasta and Sicilian wines.

name: Norma
why: Sicilian-inspired cooking in an elegant townhouse on Charlotte Street – crudo, pasta and Sicilian pastries, plus a weekend brunch.
line: Sicilian-inspired cooking in an elegant townhouse on Charlotte Street – crudo, pasta and Sicilian pastries, plus a weekend brunch.

name: Olivo
why: A long-running Sardinian restaurant near Victoria station – simple, very good food and Sardinian wines.
line: A long-running Sardinian restaurant near Victoria station – simple, very good food and Sardinian wines.

name: Gourmet Pizza Co.
why: A long-running pizza place in Gabriel's Wharf, right on the riverside walk between the National Theatre and the Oxo Tower.
line: A long-running pizza place in Gabriel's Wharf, right on the riverside walk between the National Theatre and the Oxo Tower.
address: Gabriel's Wharf, 56 Upper Ground, London SE1 9PP

name: Forza Wine National Theatre
why: An Italian wine bar and kitchen on the National Theatre's terrace – small plates, pasta and river views. Good before a show.
line: An Italian wine bar and kitchen on the National Theatre's terrace – small plates, pasta and river views.
address: National Theatre, Upper Ground, London SE1 9PX

name: Bianco43
why: Neapolitan pizza and Italian cooking a minute from the Cutty Sark, with ingredients brought in from Italy.
line: Neapolitan pizza and Italian cooking a minute from the Cutty Sark, with ingredients brought in from Italy.

name: Trullo
why: A much-loved Highbury Corner trattoria from the team behind Padella – hand-rolled pasta and meat from the charcoal grill.
line: A much-loved Highbury Corner trattoria from the team behind Padella – hand-rolled pasta and meat from the charcoal grill.

name: Purezza Camden
why: Award-winning vegan sourdough pizza on Parkway – and the whole menu is gluten-free too.
line: Award-winning vegan sourdough pizza on Parkway – and the whole menu is gluten-free too.
story: It was London's first all-vegan pizzeria.

name: Amerigo Vespucci
why: A long-established, classic Italian restaurant by the water at Canary Wharf, popular with regulars.
line: A long-established, classic Italian restaurant by the water at Canary Wharf, popular with regulars.

name: Alley Cats Pizza Chelsea
why: Big New York-style pizzas by the slice or whole, in a buzzy pizzeria on the King's Road.
line: Big New York-style pizzas by the slice or whole, in a buzzy pizzeria on the King's Road.

name: Gracey's Pizza
why: New Haven and New York-style pizza by the slice or whole pie – the NY cheese slice and the 'Smokey Ron' with smoked pepperoni are the ones to try. A cult favourite that started in St Albans, now inside Arcade food hall at Centre Point.
line: New Haven and New York-style pizza by the slice or whole pie – the NY cheese slice and the 'Smokey Ron' with smoked pepperoni are the ones to try.
story: Handy for a quick slice by Tottenham Court Road station.
address: Arcade Food Hall, Centre Point, 103 New Oxford Street, London WC1A 1DB

name: Emilia's Crafted Pasta Baker Street
why: Fresh pasta made in front of you at a live pasta station, at fair prices – a few minutes from the Sherlock Holmes Museum and Regent's Park.
line: Fresh pasta made in front of you at a live pasta station, at fair prices.

name: Nina
why: A glossy, buzzy basement on Thayer Street – leopard-print walls, a giant chicken Milanese to share, cacio e pepe and cocktails named after cigarette brands. Loud and fun, a big hit with a younger crowd.
line: A glossy, buzzy basement on Thayer Street.

name: The Cinnamon Club
why: Modern Indian cooking in the old Westminster Library, a few minutes from Parliament – the bookshelves are still on the walls. A favourite with politicians; good pre-theatre menus.
line: Modern Indian cooking in the old Westminster Library, a few minutes from Parliament.
story: Listen out for the division bell – MPs dine here and have minutes to get back to vote.
address: The Old Westminster Library, 30-32 Great Smith Street, London SW1P 3BU

name: Indian YMCA canteen
why: One of London's best-kept secrets: the canteen of the Indian YMCA student hostel on Fitzroy Square, open to everyone. Queue at the counter for home-style curries – the egg curry is the star – for well under £20.
line: One of London's best-kept secrets: the canteen of the Indian YMCA student hostel on Fitzroy Square, open to everyone.
story: It's been feeding Indian students in London since the 1950s.

name: Colonel Saab
why: A grand Indian restaurant in the old Holborn Town Hall – high ceilings, Indian art and generous, well-made curries.
line: A grand Indian restaurant in the old Holborn Town Hall.

name: Khan's
why: A huge, busy Bayswater institution since 1977 – a palm-tree dining room, big portions and fair prices. Alcohol-free.
line: A huge, busy Bayswater institution since 1977.

name: Tayyabs
why: A legendary Punjabi grill in Whitechapel – sizzling lamb chops, seekh kebabs and karahis, cheap and always packed. Bring your own drink.
line: A legendary Punjabi grill in Whitechapel.
story: Expect a queue at weekends – it's been a London favourite since 1972.

name: Zaffrani
why: A smart neighbourhood Indian on Cross Street, just off Upper Street – a well-liked local favourite.
line: A smart neighbourhood Indian on Cross Street, just off Upper Street.

name: Brigadiers
why: An Indian army-mess-style bar and restaurant in the City from the team behind Gymkhana – barbecue, curries, beers and sport on the screens.
line: An Indian army-mess-style bar and restaurant in the City from the team behind Gymkhana.
address: Bloomberg Arcade, Queen Victoria Street, London EC4N 8AR

name: Royal China Baker Street
why: A big, classic Cantonese dining room on Baker Street, famous for its dim sum since 2005 – great for families and groups. No alcohol served, but you can bring your own.
line: A big, classic Cantonese dining room on Baker Street, famous for its dim sum since 2005.

name: Dinings
why: A tiny, off-the-beaten-track Japanese place near Edgware Road, opened by two ex-Nobu chefs – superb sushi, sashimi and small plates. Pricey, but the food is top class.
line: A tiny, off-the-beaten-track Japanese place near Edgware Road, opened by two ex-Nobu chefs.

name: Donostia
why: Basque pintxos and tapas inspired by San Sebastián – sit at the counter for gildas, salt cod and a Basque cheesecake. In the Michelin Guide.
line: Basque pintxos and tapas inspired by San Sebastián.

name: Delamina
why: Bright, modern Eastern Mediterranean cooking on Marylebone Lane – mezze, grilled meats and lots for vegetarians.
line: Bright, modern Eastern Mediterranean cooking on Marylebone Lane.

name: BAO Marylebone
why: The cult Taiwanese bun bar's Marylebone branch – fluffy bao, fried chicken and a whisky list. Queue-worthy.
line: The cult Taiwanese bun bar's Marylebone branch.

name: Pollini at Ladbroke Hall
why: Seasonal Italian cooking by chef Emanuele Pollini in a stunning 1903 former car showroom in north Kensington, full of art. Named a Top Italian Restaurant abroad by Gambero Rosso and listed in the Michelin Guide – try the spaghetti with Gambero Rosso prawns.
line: Seasonal Italian cooking by chef Emanuele Pollini in a stunning 1903 former car showroom in north Kensington, full of art.
story: Gambero Rosso's 'Tre Forchette' (three forks) is Italy's own top food award – their answer to Michelin stars.
address: Ladbroke Hall, 79 Barlby Road, London W10 6AZ

name: Tiella
why: Chef Dara Klein's old-school trattoria on Columbia Road, named London's best new restaurant by Time Out – passatelli in brodo, a famous chicken Milanese and Campari-poached rhubarb with panna cotta.
line: Chef Dara Klein's old-school trattoria on Columbia Road, named London's best new restaurant by Time Out.
story: Make a Sunday of it: the flower market is right outside.

name: Burro
why: The first solo restaurant from Conor Gadd, chef and co-owner of Trullo – Italian food with Irish hospitality, tucked into Floral Court. Have the duck and porcini fettuccine, and finish with the tiramisu doughnuts.
line: The first solo restaurant from Conor Gadd, chef and co-owner of Trullo.
story: 'Burro' means butter in Italian.
address: 2 Floral Court, Floral Street, London WC2E 9FB

name: Auguste
why: Not your average Italian: food from Abruzzo by London Fields, built around flame-grilled arrosticini skewers – lamb, Suffolk wagyu, veal liver – plus a super-crispy crumbed pork chop finished in butter.
line: Not your average Italian: food from Abruzzo by London Fields, built around flame-grilled arrosticini skewers.

name: Osteria Angelina
why: Italian-Japanese sharing plates in a former cotton factory near Liverpool Street – the bigger, shinier sister of Dalston's much-loved Angelina.
line: Italian-Japanese sharing plates in a former cotton factory near Liverpool Street.
address: 1 Nicholls & Clarke Yard (off Blossom Street), London E1 6SH

name: Min Jiang
why: Fine Chinese dining on the 10th floor of the Royal Garden Hotel, looking over Kensington Gardens to the palace – famous for its wood-fired Beijing duck and dim sum.
line: Fine Chinese dining on the 10th floor of the Royal Garden Hotel, looking over Kensington Gardens to the palace.
story: Ask for a window table: you can see Kensington Palace across the gardens.
address: Royal Garden Hotel, 2-24 Kensington High Street, London W8 4PT

name: Maggie Jones's
why: A cosy, candlelit maze of rooms just off Kensington High Street, like a French farmhouse – onion soup, roast lamb, guinea fowl and apple crumble, with house wine in a magnum on the table (you pay for what you drink).
line: A cosy, candlelit maze of rooms just off Kensington High Street, like a French farmhouse.
story: The name is a nod to Princess Margaret, who's said to have booked tables here as 'Maggie Jones' in the 1960s.
address: 6 Old Court Place, Kensington Church Street, London W8 4PL

name: Wright Brothers South Kensington
why: Oysters, fresh fish and seafood platters from the Borough Market fishmongers, a few minutes from the South Kensington museums.
line: Oysters, fresh fish and seafood platters from the Borough Market fishmongers, a few minutes from the South Kensington museums.

name: Jacuzzi
why: The Big Mamma group's huge, over-the-top Italian in a former bank on Kensington High Street – big pasta, pizza and a chocolate fondue for pudding. Fun for groups.
line: The Big Mamma group's huge, over-the-top Italian in a former bank on Kensington High Street.

name: St Stephen's Tavern
why: A grand Victorian pub right opposite Big Ben, full of MPs, civil servants and visitors – etched mirrors, brass lamps and a high ceiling. Food from 10am, including a Sunday roast.
line: A grand Victorian pub right opposite Big Ben, full of MPs, civil servants and visitors.
story: Look up for the division bell on the wall: when it rings, MPs have eight minutes to finish their pint and get across the road to vote. The world's first traffic light stood just outside in 1868.

name: The Red Lion, Whitehall
why: A tall, narrow Victorian pub on Parliament Street, a few steps from Downing Street, with portraits of prime ministers on the walls and a carved mahogany bar.
line: A tall, narrow Victorian pub on Parliament Street, a few steps from Downing Street, with portraits of prime ministers on the walls and a carved mahogany bar.
story: When Gordon Brown was Chancellor, his team used it for off-the-record press briefings – it became known as the 'Treasury Annexe'.

name: Two Chairmen
why: A traditional little pub by St James's Park, popular with locals and handy after Buckingham Palace or Westminster Abbey.
line: A traditional little pub by St James's Park, popular with locals and handy after Buckingham Palace or Westminster Abbey.

name: Cellarium Café & Terrace
why: A café inside Westminster Abbey's medieval cellars, with a terrace looking up at the Abbey – breakfast, lunch and afternoon tea.
line: A café inside Westminster Abbey's medieval cellars, with a terrace looking up at the Abbey.
story: The vaulted room was the monks' store room in the 1300s.
address: 20 Dean's Yard, Westminster Abbey, London SW1P 3PA

name: Ma La Sichuan
why: Fiery Sichuan cooking a few minutes from Westminster Abbey – mapo tofu, dry-fried green beans and hot pot. A favourite with Westminster staff.
line: Fiery Sichuan cooking a few minutes from Westminster Abbey.

name: Caxton Grill
why: A smart steakhouse in the St Ermin's Hotel, near St James's Park station, with a lovely courtyard.
line: A smart steakhouse in the St Ermin's Hotel, near St James's Park station, with a lovely courtyard.
story: St Ermin's was a meeting place for British spies in the Second World War – the 'Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare' was set up here.
address: St Ermin's Hotel, 2 Caxton Street, London SW1H 0QW

name: Sapori
why: A friendly little Sicilian-run Italian on Great Peter Street – pasta, pizza and a warm welcome, a short walk from Parliament.
line: A friendly little Sicilian-run Italian on Great Peter Street.

name: The Kings Arms, Waterloo
why: A proper backstreet local on Roupell Street with a traditional two-bar interior, good cask ales and, surprisingly, a Thai restaurant in the conservatory at the back.
line: A proper backstreet local on Roupell Street with a traditional two-bar interior, good cask ales and, surprisingly, a Thai restaurant in the conservatory at the back.
story: Roupell Street is an almost untouched row of 1820s workers' cottages, and it is often used as a period film set. Turn the corner from Waterloo station and you step back 200 years.

name: The Hole in the Wall
why: A no-frills pub built into the railway arches by Waterloo station, with six cask ales, some of the cheapest pints round here and a tiny beer garden.
line: A no-frills pub built into the railway arches by Waterloo station, with six cask ales, some of the cheapest pints round here and a tiny beer garden.
story: It has been trading under the arches since just after the Second World War, and the trains still rumble overhead while you drink.

name: The Waterloo Tap
why: A craft beer bar in an old brick railway arch, with 26 cask and keg lines, the biggest beer choice around Waterloo.
line: A craft beer bar in an old brick railway arch, with 26 cask and keg lines, the biggest beer choice around Waterloo.
story: Sister to the Euston Tap and Farringdon Tap: three station bars for beer lovers who have a train to catch.

name: The Mulberry Bush
why: A friendly Young's pub on Upper Ground, just behind Gabriel's Wharf, with a back conservatory. The Sunday roast is a big one: aged Angus rump, pork belly or chicken with massive Yorkshires.
line: A friendly Young's pub on Upper Ground, just behind Gabriel's Wharf, with a back conservatory.

name: Doggett's Coat & Badge
why: A big riverside pub at the south end of Blackfriars Bridge, with a beer garden and upstairs bars looking across the Thames to St Paul's. Sunday roast of beef, chicken or a nut roast.
line: A big riverside pub at the south end of Blackfriars Bridge, with a beer garden and upstairs bars looking across the Thames to St Paul's.
story: It is named after the world's oldest rowing race, started in 1715 by the actor Thomas Doggett. Young Thames watermen still race from London Bridge to Chelsea every summer for the prize: a red coat and a silver badge.

name: Gillray's Steakhouse & Bar
why: A riverside steakhouse in County Hall looking straight at the London Eye and Big Ben, with steaks from a London butcher, a big gin bar and a Sunday roast.
line: A riverside steakhouse in County Hall looking straight at the London Eye and Big Ben, with steaks from a London butcher, a big gin bar and a Sunday roast.
story: It is named after James Gillray, the Georgian cartoonist who mocked kings and prime ministers. County Hall itself was the seat of London's government until Mrs Thatcher abolished the GLC in 1986.
address: County Hall, Westminster Bridge Road, London SE1 7PB

name: Hannah
why: A small, high-end Japanese restaurant at County Hall, recommended by the Michelin Guide. Chef-owner Daisuke Shimoyama serves an omakase of wagyu, sea bream and lobster, with a good sake list.
line: A small, high-end Japanese restaurant at County Hall, recommended by the Michelin Guide.
address: County Hall, Belvedere Road, London SE1 7PB

name: Roti King, Waterloo
why: Malaysian street food on Lower Marsh, famous for its flaky roti canai with curry, plus nasi lemak and laksa. Cheap, quick and always busy.
line: Malaysian street food on Lower Marsh, famous for its flaky roti canai with curry, plus nasi lemak and laksa.

name: Flat Iron, Waterloo
why: Good-value steak on The Cut, handy for the Old Vic and Young Vic: the signature flat iron cut, beef-dripping chips and free soft-serve ice cream.
line: Good-value steak on The Cut, handy for the Old Vic and Young Vic: the signature flat iron cut, beef-dripping chips and free soft-serve ice cream.

name: The Thames Indian
why: A long-running curry house on Waterloo Road, serving since 1985, with Indian and Bangladeshi dishes and a good-value set lunch. Handy for the IMAX and the Old Vic.
line: A long-running curry house on Waterloo Road, serving since 1985, with Indian and Bangladeshi dishes and a good-value set lunch.

name: Vaulty Towers
why: A quirky pub on Lower Marsh decorated with theatrical salvage, with comedy, live music, DJs and a pub quiz, plus playful food.
line: A quirky pub on Lower Marsh decorated with theatrical salvage, with comedy, live music, DJs and a pub quiz, plus playful food.

name: Limin Southbank
why: Home-style Trinidad and Tobago cooking near the river on Upper Ground: doubles, curries and rum punch, with a beach-club feel.
line: Home-style Trinidad and Tobago cooking near the river on Upper Ground: doubles, curries and rum punch, with a beach-club feel.

name: The Quality Chop House
why: A Victorian chop house on Farringdon Road with its original listed booths, now a much-loved modern British restaurant. The Sunday lunch, with rump, lamb shoulder and Yorkshire pudding, is one of the best in London.
line: A Victorian chop house on Farringdon Road with its original listed booths, now a much-loved modern British restaurant.
story: It opened around 1869 as a "Progressive Working Class Caterer", and that sign is still in the window. The wooden booths are listed, so they cannot be changed.

name: The Coal Shed, Tower Bridge
why: Steak and seafood cooked over coals at One Tower Bridge, by the bridge itself: 35-day dry-aged Lake District steaks, South Coast fish, and a sharing Sunday roast with all the trimmings.
line: Steak and seafood cooked over coals at One Tower Bridge, by the bridge itself: 35-day dry-aged Lake District steaks, South Coast fish, and a sharing Sunday roast with all the trimmings.
address: One Tower Bridge, 4 Crown Square, London SE1 2SE

name: The Wolseley City
why: The City sister of the famous Wolseley on Piccadilly, in a grand banking hall by Monument. It is the same Viennese grand café with an all-day menu, and a favourite for City power breakfasts.
line: The City sister of the famous Wolseley on Piccadilly, in a grand banking hall by Monument.

name: The Miniature St Paul's on Vauxhall Bridge
why: London's second St Paul's Cathedral, and probably its smallest. One of the giant bronze ladies on Vauxhall Bridge, 'Architecture' by Alfred Drury, is holding a little model of St Paul's in her hand.
line: One of the bronze statues on Vauxhall Bridge holds a little model of St Paul's Cathedral.
story: The bridge opened in 1906 with eight bronze figures on the piers (Agriculture, Architecture, Engineering, Pottery, Science, Fine Arts, Local Government and Education). You can't see them from the road. Lean over the upstream side and look down, or see them from a boat.

name: OXO Tower Restaurant & Brasserie
why: On the 8th floor of the OXO Tower, with a long glass wall and terrace looking across the Thames to St Paul's and the City. The Brasserie is the more relaxed side; the Restaurant is for a special occasion. Sunday lunch of beef, pork or chicken with Yorkshires.
line: On the 8th floor of the OXO Tower, with views across the Thames to St Paul's and the City.
story: In the 1920s the Liebig company, makers of Oxo cubes, were refused permission for an illuminated advert on the riverside. So the architect built the tower's windows in the shape of the letters O-X-O and lit them from inside – an advert that was, officially, just windows.
address: Oxo Tower Wharf, Barge House Street, London SE1 9PH

name: Ria's, Notting Hill
why: Detroit-style pizza on All Saints Road – square, light and crisp with a caramelised cheese crust, plus natural wine. Try the king prawn pizza. Just off Portobello Road, and a short bus or cab ride up from Kensington.
line: Detroit-style pizza on All Saints Road – square, light and crisp with a caramelised cheese crust.

name: The Parcel Yard
why: A big Fuller's pub upstairs at the back of King's Cross station, full of nooks, with a Sunday roast of beef, pork, chicken or all three. Perfect while you wait for a train north.
line: A big Fuller's pub upstairs at the back of King's Cross station, with a Sunday roast.
story: It's the station's old Victorian parcels office, a Grade I listed building. The timber beams and sorting rooms are still there.
address: King's Cross Station, Euston Road, London N1 9AL

name: The Betjeman Arms
why: A pub inside St Pancras International, with a terrace looking over the Eurostar trains. Sunday roasts include pork with crackling, West Country beef, or a whole lamb shoulder to share.
line: A pub inside St Pancras International, with a terrace looking over the Eurostar trains.
story: It's named after the poet Sir John Betjeman, who led the campaign that saved St Pancras from being knocked down in the 1960s. His statue, looking up at the roof, is on the upper concourse.
address: St Pancras International, Euston Road, London N1C 4QL

name: Namaaste Kitchen
why: A smart Indian restaurant on Parkway, a few minutes from Camden Town station, good for a date or a family meal. Try the tokri chaat and the apricot kofte.
line: A smart Indian restaurant on Parkway, a few minutes from Camden Town station, good for a date or a family meal.

name: Daphne
why: A family-run Greek-Cypriot restaurant over three floors on Bayham Street, cosy and old-fashioned, with photos of Cypriot villages on the walls. Order the crispy mini koubes and the meze.
line: A family-run Greek-Cypriot restaurant over three floors on Bayham Street, cosy and old-fashioned, with photos of Cypriot villages on the walls.

name: Andy's Taverna
why: A homely, good-value Greek taverna on Bayham Street that has been feeding Camden for decades: meze, charcoal grills and a little garden at the back.
line: A homely, good-value Greek taverna on Bayham Street that has been feeding Camden for decades: meze, charcoal grills and a little garden at the back.

name: Three Uncles, Camden
why: Hong Kong-style roast meats in the Hawley Wharf food hall at Camden Market: char siu, crispy pork belly and roast duck over rice or noodles. Quick, cheap and brilliant.
line: Hong Kong-style roast meats in the Hawley Wharf food hall at Camden Market: char siu, crispy pork belly and roast duck over rice or noodles.
address: Hawley Wharf, Camden Market, London NW1

name: Seto
why: A small, family-run Japanese restaurant near Camden Town station with home-style cooking: ramen, nigiri and sashimi, without the fancy prices.
line: A small, family-run Japanese restaurant near Camden Town station with home-style cooking: ramen, nigiri and sashimi, without the fancy prices.

name: Haché
why: Camden's long-running gourmet burger place on Inverness Street, by the market: steak burgers in a toasted ciabatta-style bun, and good chips.
line: Camden's long-running gourmet burger place on Inverness Street, by the market: steak burgers in a toasted ciabatta-style bun, and good chips.

name: The Edinboro Castle
why: A big Victorian pub between Camden and Regent's Park with one of the best beer gardens in north London and a Sunday roast.
line: A big Victorian pub between Camden and Regent's Park with one of the best beer gardens in north London, summer barbecues and a Sunday roast.
story: Built in 1839 and named after Edinburgh Castle, it once had its own little museum, art gallery and tea gardens. Grade II listed.

name: Lemonia
why: A big, lively Greek-Cypriot restaurant on Primrose Hill's main street, a local favourite for decades, with charcoal grills and huge meze. A 10-minute walk from Camden Lock.
line: A big, lively Greek-Cypriot restaurant on Primrose Hill's main street, open since the 1970s, with charcoal grills and huge meze.

name: Trattoria Brutto
why: A proper Florentine trattoria by Smithfield Market: checked tablecloths, candles in bottles, Florentine steak and cheap Negronis. Booking essential.
line: A proper Florentine trattoria by Smithfield Market: checked tablecloths, candles in bottles, bistecca and £5 Negronis.
story: It was the last restaurant opened by Russell Norman, the man behind Polpo, who modelled it on the old-school trattorias of Florence.

name: Luca
why: A smart Italian on St John Street in Clerkenwell, with a glass-roofed back room and a bar at the front. Famous for its parmesan fries.
line: A smart Italian on St John Street in Clerkenwell, with a glass-roofed back room and a bar at the front.

name: Sushi Tetsu
why: A tiny sushi counter tucked down a Clerkenwell alley, with only a handful of seats in front of the chef. One of London's best omakase meals, and hard to book.
line: A tiny sushi counter tucked down a Clerkenwell alley, with only a handful of seats in front of the chef.

name: Sweetings
why: A Victorian fish restaurant by Mansion House with no bookings, counter seats, and old-school dishes like potted shrimps, fish pie and Black Velvet in tankards. Lunch on weekdays only.
line: A Victorian fish restaurant by Mansion House with no bookings, counter seats, and old-school dishes like potted shrimps, fish pie and Black Velvet in tankards.
story: It has been serving City workers since 1889 and has barely changed since. Turn up early and queue like everyone else.

name: Sessions Arts Club
why: A beautiful, candlelit dining room on the top floor of an old courthouse on Clerkenwell Green, with peeling plaster walls and modern European cooking.
line: A beautiful, candlelit dining room on the top floor of an old courthouse on Clerkenwell Green, with peeling plaster walls and modern European cooking.
story: The building is the old Middlesex Sessions House, built in 1782, where magistrates once sat in judgement.

name: Piazza Italiana
why: A grand Italian restaurant in a former bank hall on Threadneedle Street, by the Bank of England: marble, high ceilings, classic dishes like ossobuco and vitello tonnato, and an Italian afternoon tea with baby calzone and mini tiramisu. Closed on Sundays.
line: A grand Italian restaurant in a former bank hall on Threadneedle Street, by the Bank of England.
story: The building was the London home of the British Linen Bank and is Grade II listed. The wine list runs to about 500 bottles, chosen by a sommelier once named the best in Italy.

name: Goddards at Greenwich
why: A wood-panelled pie and mash shop by Greenwich Market and the Cutty Sark: minced beef pie, mash and liquor (green parsley sauce), plus jellied eels and some unusual pies like lamb and rosemary.
line: A wood-panelled pie and mash shop by Greenwich Market and the Cutty Sark.
story: The Goddard family have been making pies since 1890, and the shop has been on King William Walk since 1952.

name: M. Manze, Tower Bridge Road
why: London's oldest surviving pie and mash shop, with green tiles, marble tables and long wooden booths. Pie, mash and liquor, jellied or stewed eels, and a scoop of ice cream to finish.
line: London's oldest surviving pie and mash shop, with green tiles, marble tables and long wooden booths.
story: Michele Manze, from Italy, opened here in 1902. The tiled interior is listed, and it has hardly changed in over 120 years.

name: F. Cooke, Hoxton
why: A bright, marble-topped pie and mash shop on Hoxton Street market, run by the Cooke family for generations. Crisp pastry, meaty mince and proper liquor.
line: A bright, marble-topped pie and mash shop on Hoxton Street market, run by the Cooke family for generations.

name: G. Kelly, Roman Road
why: A classic art deco pie and mash shop on Roman Road market in Bow, open since 1939, with crisp pastry and homemade apple crumble.
line: A classic art deco pie and mash shop on Roman Road market in Bow, open since 1939, with crisp pastry and homemade apple crumble.

name: Maureen's Pie & Mash
why: A family-run cockney food bar on Chrisp Street Market in Poplar, trading for over 50 years: pie and mash with plenty of gravy, and salt beef sandwiches.
line: A family-run cockney food bar on Chrisp Street Market in Poplar, trading for over 50 years: pie and mash with plenty of gravy, and salt beef sandwiches.

name: Arments Pie & Mash
why: A traditional pie and mash caff in Walworth, near Elephant & Castle, with cream tiles and wooden booths, run by the same family since 1914.
line: A traditional pie and mash caff in Walworth, near Elephant & Castle, with cream tiles and wooden booths, run by the same family since 1914.

name: Japes
why: Chicago-style deep-dish pizza by Greenwich Market, thick, cheesy and very filling. A good change from Neapolitan.
line: Chicago-style deep-dish pizza by Greenwich Market, thick, cheesy and very filling.

name: London Naru
why: A friendly Korean restaurant on Stockwell Street, by Greenwich station and the market: bibimbap, Korean fried chicken and barbecue.
line: A friendly Korean restaurant on Stockwell Street, by Greenwich station and the market: bibimbap, Korean fried chicken and barbecue.

name: Sefa
why: Turkish charcoal grills and meze on Trafalgar Road, a short walk east of the Old Royal Naval College. Good value and generous.
line: Turkish charcoal grills and meze on Trafalgar Road, a short walk east of the Old Royal Naval College.

name: The Tamil Prince
why: A Barnsbury backstreet pub that serves some of the best South Indian food in London: flaky roti, curries and tandoor dishes, alongside proper pints. Book ahead.
line: A Barnsbury backstreet pub that serves some of the best South Indian food in London: flaky roti, curries and tandoor dishes, alongside proper pints.

name: Bellanger
why: A grand Parisian-style brasserie on Islington Green, open from breakfast to late, with tarte flambée, steak frites and Alsace classics.
line: A grand Parisian-style brasserie on Islington Green, open from breakfast to late, with tarte flambée, steak frites and Alsace classics.

name: Santa Maria, Islington
why: Neapolitan pizza on Upper Street from one of the best-loved pizzerias in London: soft, blistered bases and proper Italian toppings.
line: Neapolitan pizza on Upper Street from one of the best-loved pizzerias in London: soft, blistered bases and proper Italian toppings.

name: Dzo Viet Kitchen
why: A friendly Vietnamese restaurant on Upper Street: pho, bun and crispy spring rolls at fair prices.
line: A friendly Vietnamese restaurant on Upper Street: pho, bun and crispy spring rolls at fair prices.

name: Llerena
why: A small, buzzing tapas bar on Upper Street with Spanish classics, good sherry and a short wine list.
line: A small, buzzing tapas bar on Upper Street with Spanish classics, good sherry and a short wine list.

name: Hanwoo Village
why: Korean barbecue near Angel, with grills at the table, banchan side dishes and soju. Fun for a group.
line: Korean barbecue near Angel, with grills at the table, banchan side dishes and soju.

name: Sasa Sushi
why: A tiny, much-loved sushi bar at the top of St John Street by Angel, with fresh nigiri and rolls at good prices.
line: A tiny, much-loved sushi bar at the top of St John Street by Angel, with fresh nigiri and rolls at good prices.

name: The Gun, Docklands
why: A historic riverside pub on the Isle of Dogs with a covered terrace looking across the Thames to the O2, Fuller's beers and modern British food, including a Sunday roast.
line: A historic riverside pub on the Isle of Dogs with a covered terrace looking across the Thames to the O2, Fuller's beers and modern British food, including a Sunday roast.
story: There has been a pub here since at least 1722, and it has been called The Gun since 1771. Lord Nelson is said to have met Lady Emma Hamilton in secret in the upstairs River Room. It's Grade II listed.

name: Roka Canary Wharf
why: Stylish Japanese cooking around a robata grill in the middle of Canary Wharf: black cod, sushi and grilled skewers. Good for a special night out.
line: Stylish Japanese cooking around a robata grill in the middle of Canary Wharf: black cod, sushi and grilled skewers.
address: Park Pavilion, 40 Canada Square, London E14 5FW

name: Goodman Canary Wharf
why: A serious steakhouse by the water at Canary Wharf, with dry-aged British and American beef cooked over charcoal.
line: A serious steakhouse by the water at Canary Wharf, with dry-aged British and American beef cooked over charcoal.

name: Iberica Canary Wharf
why: Spanish tapas and pinchos just around the corner from Canary Wharf station, with a terrace on Cabot Square.
line: Spanish tapas and pinchos just around the corner from Canary Wharf station, with a terrace on Cabot Square.

name: Big Easy Canary Wharf
why: American barbecue and crab shack at Crossrail Place, with live music most nights. Great for groups and hungry teenagers.
line: American barbecue and lobster shack at Crossrail Place, with live music most nights.

name: Foubert's Kensington
why: Family-run Italian on Kensington High Street, from the Foubert's family who have been making their own gelato in Chiswick since the 1970s. Thin pizzas and homemade pasta, with the ice cream to finish. A short walk from Kensington Gardens and the Royal Albert Hall.
line: Family-run Italian on Kensington High Street, from the Foubert's family who have been making their own gelato in Chiswick since the 1970s.

name: CeCe's
why: A glamorous Italian 'with a hint of Hollywood' from the team behind The Pelican and Canteen: copper panelling, green velvet banquettes and mirrors everywhere. Try the aubergine parmigiana, fonduta agnolotti or veal Milanese. Dinner only, closed Mondays.
line: A glamorous Italian 'with a hint of Hollywood' from the team behind The Pelican and Canteen: copper panelling, green velvet banquettes and mirrors everywhere.

name: Canteen
why: A walk-ins-only Italian at the top of Portobello Road, run by River Café alumni and holder of a Michelin Bib Gourmand. Thin crispy pizza, very good pasta and an olive-oil chocolate mousse people talk about. No bookings, so arrive early to get on the waitlist.
line: A walk-ins-only Italian at the top of Portobello Road, run by River Café alumni and holder of a Michelin Bib Gourmand.

name: Juno at Olympia
why: One of the biggest Italian restaurants in the UK, with 265 covers, inside Olympia's grand National Hall. Opened in October 2026 with Italian food, aperitivi and cocktails, live music and themed nights through the week.
line: One of the biggest Italian restaurants in the UK, with 265 covers, inside Olympia's grand National Hall.
address: National Hall, Olympia, Hammersmith Road, London W14 8UX

name: Brother Marcus Spitalfields
why: All-day Eastern Mediterranean brunch inside Spitalfields Market, with a heated terrace. Try the 'Step Sister': sweet potato, courgette and feta fritters with a poached egg. Other branches at Borough Yards, Angel and South Kensington.
line: All-day Eastern Mediterranean brunch inside Spitalfields Market, with a heated terrace.
address: 2 Crispin Place, Spitalfields Market, London E1 6DW

name: Brother Marcus Borough
why: The Borough Yards branch of the Eastern Mediterranean brunch favourite, a few minutes from Borough Market. Brunch classics include kefir fried chicken with potato rösti and the 'Marcus Breakfast', a Full English with merguez.
line: The Borough Yards branch of the Eastern Mediterranean brunch favourite, a few minutes from Borough Market.
address: 1 Dirty Lane, Borough Yards, London SE1 9PA

name: Serra at The Chancery Rosewood
why: All-day Southern Mediterranean restaurant inside the new Chancery Rosewood hotel on Grosvenor Square, inspired by the coasts of southern Italy and Greece. Sunday brunch with French toast, pancakes and seafood platters in five-star surroundings. Thanksgiving 2026: a traditional feast with whole-roasted bronze turkey and seasonal pies, £105 a head. Listings disagree on Thu 26 or Fri 27 Nov, so check when booking.
line: All-day Southern Mediterranean restaurant inside the new Chancery Rosewood hotel on Grosvenor Square, inspired by the coasts of southern Italy and Greece.
story: Until 2018 this building was the American Embassy. Cabbies of a certain age still call Grosvenor Square 'the Embassy'.
address: The Chancery Rosewood, 30 Grosvenor Square, London W1K 2HP

name: Straits Kitchen, Pan Pacific London
why: Pan Pacific London's Southeast Asian fusion restaurant by Liverpool Street, with a seasonal weekend brunch menu. A handy, calmer option in the City at the weekend.
line: Pan Pacific London's Southeast Asian fusion restaurant by Liverpool Street, with a seasonal weekend brunch menu.
address: Pan Pacific London, 80 Houndsditch, London EC3A 7AB

name: Roe
why: A huge, waterside sister to Fallow in St James's, on Wood Wharf beside South Dock, with a big terrace. Bottomless brunch every Saturday from 9.30am to 4pm, and dogs are welcome.
line: A huge, waterside sister to Fallow in St James's, on Wood Wharf beside South Dock, with a big terrace.
address: 5 Park Drive, Wood Wharf, London E14 9GG

name: Hexmoor: Wizarding Prison
why: The world's first immersive wizarding prison bar, from the team behind Alcotraz. You're handed a jumpsuit and locked in a cell with dark wizards, with three magical cocktails included. Allow about 1 hour 45 minutes. 18+.
line: The world's first immersive wizarding prison bar, from the team behind Alcotraz.

name: The Murdér Express
why: An immersive murder mystery aboard a recreated 1920s train in a railway arch off Brick Lane, with actors all around you and a three-course meal while you work out whodunnit.
line: An immersive murder mystery aboard a recreated 1920s train in a railway arch off Brick Lane, with actors all around you and a three-course meal while you work out whodunnit.
address: Pedley Street Station, Arch 63, Pedley Street, London E1 5BW

name: Prison Island
why: An immersive team challenge: race round themed 'cells', each with a different physical or mental puzzle, scoring points as you go. Good for groups, birthdays and office outings. Nearest tube: Holloway Road.
line: An immersive team challenge: race round themed 'cells', each with a different physical or mental puzzle, scoring points as you go.

name: Babylon Park
why: London's underground theme park beneath Camden: three space-themed floors with the city's only indoor rollercoaster, a drop tower, bumper cars, VR and hundreds of arcade games. Free to get in; you pay per ride. Fully indoors, so good whatever the weather.
line: London's underground theme park beneath Camden: three space-themed floors with the city's only indoor rollercoaster, a drop tower, bumper cars, VR and hundreds of arcade games.

name: Bunga 90
why: The old Bunga Bunga reborn as a 1990s time warp. Enter through a Blockbuster-style video shop to karaoke, retro cocktails, a claw machine that makes drinks and a Jurassic Park pinball machine. Bottomless 90s brunch on Saturdays; handy pre-theatre.
line: The old Bunga Bunga reborn as a 1990s time warp.

name: Savoy Grill by Gordon Ramsay
why: Thanksgiving week (Mon 23 – Thu 26 Nov 2026) brings an American-themed menu to one of London's grandest dining rooms: beer-brined prawns with caviar, Norfolk bronze turkey with green bean casserole, and pecan pie. Price to be confirmed, so check when booking.
line: Thanksgiving week (Mon 23 – Thu 26 Nov 2026) brings an American-themed menu to one of London's grandest dining rooms: beer-brined prawns with caviar, Norfolk bronze turkey with green bean casserole, and pecan pie.

name: CUT at 45 Park Lane
why: Wolfgang Puck's steakhouse does Thanksgiving properly on Thu 26 Nov 2026: Norfolk bronze turkey with all the sides, or Australian wagyu, then pumpkin or pecan pie. £220 a head, overlooking Hyde Park. The top-end choice.
line: Wolfgang Puck's steakhouse does Thanksgiving properly on Thu 26 Nov 2026: Norfolk bronze turkey with all the sides, or Australian wagyu, then pumpkin or pecan pie.

name: RAILS
why: Thanksgiving lunch and dinner on Thu 26 Nov 2026 for £49 a head: chowder, roast turkey with the trimmings and pecan pie, inside the old Great Northern railway hotel next to King's Cross. One of the best-value options, and handy if you're arriving by train.
line: Thanksgiving lunch and dinner on Thu 26 Nov 2026 for £49 a head: chowder, roast turkey with the trimmings and pecan pie, inside the old Great Northern railway hotel next to King's Cross.
address: Kaya Great Northern Hotel, Pancras Road, London N1C 4TB

name: The Surprise
why: A proper Chelsea backstreet pub doing Thanksgiving pub-style on Thu 26 Nov 2026: turkey crown or honey-roast ham with the sides. No set menu, so you can drop in and order what you fancy.
line: A proper Chelsea backstreet pub doing Thanksgiving pub-style on Thu 26 Nov 2026: turkey crown or honey-roast ham with the sides.

name: Lil' Nashville
